overview.title: ClickHouse Web Console
overview.description: Overview of the ClickHouse Web Console: one sign-in for the built-in web UIs, administration of users and access, data access policies, backups, clusters, and identity providers.
overview.html:
The ClickHouse Web Console is a single entry point to a ClickHouse server in a browser. It is served by the server itself at /console, for example http://localhost:8123/console, and needs no separate web server or database. You sign in once, as a ClickHouse user, and work in one window: the SQL Console, dashboards, and diagnostics, and the administration of users, roles, data access, backups, clusters, and identity providers.

The console is a user interface, not a security boundary. Every query and every administrative action runs with the credentials of the signed-in user, and the ClickHouse server authorizes each one with its own access control. What the console hides or shows never changes what a user can do.

Components

ComponentWhat it doesRuns where
ConsoleSign-in, home page, sidebar, and the panels: SQL Console, Dashboard, ClickStack, Web Terminal, Binary, Merges and Schema visualizers, Jemalloc, Processors profile, Reference.The browser; served by the server at /console.
AdministrationUsers, Roles & Permissions, Data Access Policies, Component Access, Profiles & Quotas, Audit Activity, Clusters, Backup & Restore.The browser. Changes are SQL statements run as the signed-in user; the console's own state is kept in tables of the admin_database.
Identity ProvidersThe LDAP page (LDAP and Active Directory user directories) and the SSO (Keycloak) page (OpenID Connect).The browser, and the server configuration.
Backup workerRuns backup schedules and retention, deletions, and server bundles (configuration, secrets, and Keeper data, encrypted).A Node.js process or the tools image.
Cluster agentCreates and operates clusters through Docker Compose or Kubernetes.A Node.js process or the tools image.
Access policy workerKeeps grants and row policies in line with the policy rules, and imports user attributes.A Node.js process or the tools image.
Token authenticatorChecks the single sign-on tokens of users for the server, and syncs users and roles from Keycloak groups.A Node.js process or the tools image.

The helper processes are optional. Each one is needed only for the features it serves, and each one connects to the server with a service account of its own.

Architecture

  • The browser talks only to ClickHouse (and to Keycloak when single sign-on is used). The console keeps the credentials in the memory of the tab, and sends them with each request.
  • Requests are the queue. The console records requests for long-running work, such as a backup schedule or a cluster operation, in console tables. The helper processes pick them up, do the work with their own service account, check the requester's privileges where it matters, and record the results. The console shows those results.
  • The server is the authority. Users, roles, grants, row policies, and settings profiles are native ClickHouse entities. The console creates them with CREATE USER, GRANT, CREATE ROW POLICY, and the like, so they work the same for every client.

Where to start

  • New to the console? Follow the Quick start, then the tutorial Set up the console as its first administrator.
  • Learning a feature? The tutorials walk through data access policies, backups, and single sign-on with Keycloak.
  • Using a page? The user guides explain each area: the console, users and roles, component access, data access policies, profiles and quotas, audit activity, backup and restore, clusters, and identity providers.
  • Doing a task? The how-to guides cover deployment with Docker Compose or Kubernetes, service accounts, LDAP and Active Directory, Keycloak single sign-on, user attributes, offboarding, recovering access, protecting backups, and recovering a server.
  • Integrating or operating it? The reference lists the configuration, the HTTP endpoints, the console tables, the privileges, the helper processes, and the token authenticator API.

Requirements

  • A ClickHouse server built with the web console. It serves the console on every HTTP port, at /console.
  • A recent desktop browser: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari. The console runs on the device of the user.
  • For the helper processes: Node.js 18 or later, or the tools image clickhouse-console-tools.
  • For single sign-on: an OpenID Connect provider (Keycloak 26 is tested) and the token authenticator.

The console needs no Internet access. The Binary visualizer and Jemalloc panels load libraries from public CDNs and do not work offline.

quick-start.title: Quick start
quick-start.description: Start a ClickHouse server with the web console in Docker, sign in, run a query, and set up the administration pages, in about ten minutes.
quick-start.html:
In this quick start you run the ClickHouse server image that includes the web console, sign in as the administrator, run a query, and set up the administration pages. It takes about ten minutes on a machine with Docker.

Before you begin

  • Docker 24 or later.
  • The image archive clickhouse-server-console-<version>-amd64.tar.gz and its SHA256SUMS, from the release of the console. To build them yourself, see Build and package the images.
  • A browser on the same machine.

If you already run a ClickHouse server built with the console, skip to Sign in: the console is at /console on its HTTP port.

Start the server

  1. Load the image

    Check the archive and load it:

    bash
    sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing
docker load -i clickhouse-server-console-<version>-amd64.tar.gz

    docker load prints Loaded image: clickhouse-server-console:<version>.

  2. Run the server

    Choose a password for the default user, and start the server. The HTTP port is published on 127.0.0.1 only, so the server is not reachable from other machines:

    bash
    docker run -d --name clickhouse-console \
    -p 127.0.0.1:8123:8123 \
    -e CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD='choose-a-password' \
    -e CLICKHOUSE_DEFAULT_ACCESS_MANAGEMENT=1 \
    --ulimit nofile=262144:262144 \
    clickhouse-server-console:<version>

    CLICKHOUSE_DEFAULT_ACCESS_MANAGEMENT=1 lets default create users and roles, which the administration pages need. The server image is the official clickhouse/clickhouse-server image with this build's binary, so all of its settings and environment variables apply.

  3. Check that it answers

    bash
    curl http://127.0.0.1:8123/ping

    The answer is Ok..

Sign in

Open http://localhost:8123/console. Sign in with the username default and the password you chose.

The home page lists the panels your user can open, grouped as in the sidebar: Workspace, Diagnostics, Administration, Identity Providers, and Resources. The console checks with the server which panels your user may use, so another user may see fewer of them.

Note

The password stays in the memory of the browser tab. Reloading the page signs you out.

Run a query

  1. Select SQL Console. The console signs in to it for you.

  2. Run:

    sql
    SELECT version(), uptime()

  3. Select Dashboard in the sidebar to see the server's metrics. Panels keep their state while you switch between them.

Set up the administration pages

The Users, Roles & Permissions, and Profiles & Quotas pages work at once. The audit log and the component access policy need tables, which you create once:

  1. In the sidebar, under Administration, select Component Access.
  2. Select Set up, keep the default retention of the audit records, and select Review.
  3. Read the statements that will run, and select Apply.

The console creates the database console_admin with its tables, a policy rule that lets every user open every component, and the role console_admin_reader. Nothing changes for users until you edit the policy.

Select Audit Activity: the setup is the first record.

Clean up

bash
docker rm -f clickhouse-console

Next steps

  • Create users and roles, and decide who sees which component: Set up the console as its first administrator.
  • Deploy for real, with the helper processes: Deploy with Docker Compose or Deploy on Kubernetes.
  • Learn the console: The console.

tutorials/first-administrator.title: Set up the console as its first administrator
tutorials/first-administrator.description: Set up the web console as its first administrator: create a role from a template and a user with it, decide which components users see, and follow the changes in the audit log.

headings.text: Create a role from a template
Create a user with the role
Follow the changes in the audit log

tutorials/first-administrator.html:
In this tutorial you prepare a ClickHouse server for an analyst, Maria, using only the console. You create a demo database, a role that reads it, and a user with that role. Then you decide which components of the console the users see, sign in as Maria to check the result, and find every change in the audit log.

It takes about twenty minutes.

Before you begin

  • A server with the console, and its default user with access management, as in the Quick start.
  • The administration pages set up: Component Access shows a Rules box. If it shows Set up instead, follow Set up the administration pages first.

Sign in to the console as default.

Create the demo data

  1. Open the SQL Console

    Select SQL Console in the sidebar.

  2. Create a database and a table

    Run:

    sql
    CREATE DATABASE sales;

CREATE TABLE sales.orders
(
    order_id UInt64,
    region LowCardinality(String),
    amount Decimal(12, 2),
    created_at DateTime
)
ENGINE = MergeTree
ORDER BY order_id;

INSERT INTO sales.orders
SELECT number, ['north', 'south', 'east', 'west'][number % 4 + 1], round(rand() % 100000 / 100, 2), now() - number * 60
FROM numbers(1000);

    SELECT count() FROM sales.orders returns 1000.

Create a role from a template

Role templates are starting points that the console offers for common jobs. Each one lists the exact privileges it grants before it creates anything.

  1. Open the role templates

    Select Roles & Permissions. Below the list of roles, the Role templates box lists the templates.

  2. Create an analyst role

    In the row Analyst ("Reads the tables of the chosen databases"), select Create role. Keep the role name analyst, and enter sales in Databases. Select Review.

    The review lists the statements that will run:

    sql
    CREATE ROLE `analyst`;
GRANT SHOW TABLES, SHOW COLUMNS, SELECT ON `sales`.* TO `analyst`;

    Select Apply. Each step shows Done.

The console runs these statements as you, and the server checks each one: you can only grant privileges you have WITH GRANT OPTION. See Users and roles.

Create a user with the role

  1. Open the user form

    Select Users, then Create user.

  2. Fill it in

    • Name: maria.
    • Password: select Generate a temporary password, and an expiry in Password expires (optional) if you want one.
    • Roles: select analyst. The role console_admin_reader is already selected: it lets the console apply its access policy to Maria. Keep Make the assigned roles default roles (active at login) selected.

    Select Review, read the statements, and select Apply.

  3. Note the password

    The console shows the generated password once. Copy it now: the server stores only its hash, and the console does not keep it.

Decide which components users see

The setup created a rule that lets all users open every component. Narrow it: everybody keeps the SQL Console and the Dashboard, and only analysts get the Schema visualizer.

  1. Narrow the rule for all users

    Select Component Access. In Rules for, keep All users. In the column Open, clear every component except SQL Console and Dashboard. Select Save rules, review, and apply.

  2. Add a rule for the analyst role

    In Rules for, choose the role analyst. Select Open for Schema visualizer, save, review, and apply.

A user may open a component when any rule allows it: the rule for all users, a rule for the user, or a rule for one of the user's enabled roles. Next to each component, the page shows the native privileges that govern what the user can actually do there. The policy only decides what the console lists: see Component access.

Check as Maria

  1. Select the Switch connection button (two arrows) at the top right, and sign in as maria with the generated password.
  2. The home page shows SQL Console, Dashboard, and Schema visualizer, and not the other panels or the administration pages.
  3. In the SQL Console, SELECT count() FROM sales.orders returns 1000.
  4. DROP TABLE sales.orders fails with ACCESS_DENIED: the role grants only reading. The server enforces this for every client, not only in the console.

Switch back to default.

Follow the changes in the audit log

Select Audit Activity. The console records each change it made: the role, the user, and the rules, with who made it, when, the result, and a correlation ID. Passwords are never recorded.

The server's own log lists access-management statements as well, including those made outside the console, when you can read system.query_log. See Audit activity.

Clean up

To remove what you created, as default:

sql
DROP USER maria;
DROP ROLE analyst;
DROP DATABASE sales;

Then, in Component Access, with Rules for set to All users, select Open for every component again (the box at the top of the column selects them all), and save.

What you learned

  • The console builds statements from forms and runs them as you; the server authorizes each one.
  • Role templates give least-privilege roles with the exact grants shown before they are applied.
  • The component access policy decides what the console lists for each user and role; native privileges decide what they can do.
  • Every change is in the audit log.

Next: protect individual columns and rows with Data Access Policies, or let users sign in with their company account through single sign-on.

tutorials/data-access-policies.title: Tutorial: protect a table of salaries
tutorials/data-access-policies.description: Protect a table of salaries with the Data Access Policies page of the web console: column grants, a row policy, access tests, and a policy rule on a user attribute.
tutorials/data-access-policies.html:
In this tutorial you protect a table of salaries so that two employees, alice in Finance and bob in Sales, read the salaries of their own department and never the bank accounts. You start with native controls (a column grant and a row policy), check them with Effective Access and access tests, then replace the hand-made row policy with a policy rule on the user attribute department, deploy it, and verify it as the users. At the end you remove everything you created.

The tutorial takes about 20 minutes. Every control you create is a native ClickHouse grant or row policy: the server enforces it for every client, not only for the console.

Prerequisites

  • A running web console that you can sign in to as an administrator who can create databases, users, roles, and row policies, and grant SELECT with the grant option, for example default in the Docker Compose deployment.
  • Data Access Policies set up: on Administration → Data Access Policies, the tabs Access Tests, Attributes & Classifications, Policy Rules, and Policy Deployments show their content, not Set up Data Access Policies. If they show it, select Set up and Apply on one of them.
  • A way to run SQL: the SQL Console panel of the console, or clickhouse-client.
  • For the steps that read as another user (Verify with the server and access tests), your administrator user needs IMPERSONATE on alice and bob. An administrator with ALL on *.*, such as default with access management, has it. The server setting allow_impersonate_user is enabled in the default config.xml of this build.

If the access policy worker runs, it may apply your rule before you select Deploy: History then shows a reconcile entry instead of your deploy. The result is the same.

Protect the table

  1. Create the demo database, table, users, and role

    As your administrator, run:

    sql
    CREATE DATABASE hr_demo;

CREATE TABLE hr_demo.salaries
(
    employee String,
    department String,
    salary UInt32,
    bank_account String
)
ENGINE = MergeTree
ORDER BY (department, employee);

INSERT INTO hr_demo.salaries VALUES
    ('Ann', 'Finance', 5200, 'DE00 1111'),
    ('Carl', 'Finance', 4800, 'DE00 2222'),
    ('Dina', 'Sales', 4500, 'DE00 3333'),
    ('Ed', 'Sales', 4700, 'DE00 4444'),
    ('Fay', 'Engineering', 6100, 'DE00 5555'),
    ('Gus', 'Engineering', 5900, 'DE00 6666');

CREATE USER alice IDENTIFIED WITH sha256_password BY 'Alice-demo-1';
CREATE USER bob IDENTIFIED WITH sha256_password BY 'Bob-demo-1';
CREATE ROLE salary_readers;
GRANT salary_readers TO alice, bob;

    If your user does not have IMPERSONATE through ALL, also run GRANT IMPERSONATE ON alice TO <your user> and GRANT IMPERSONATE ON bob TO <your user>.

    New users have all granted roles as default roles, so salary_readers is active when alice and bob sign in. The role has no privilege yet.

  2. Grant the columns

    1. Open Administration → Data Access Policies. The page opens on Column Permissions.
    2. Choose Database hr_demo and Table salaries. The Users matrix lists the users who can already read the table, such as your administrator, with ● in every column (a grant on the whole table or wider). alice and bob are not listed: they cannot read the table yet.
    3. Select Grant columns. In To, choose role salary_readers, and check employee, department, and salary. Leave bank_account unchecked.
    4. Select Review. The review shows the GRANT SELECT statement and warns that SELECT * will fail for this grantee, because it needs every column.
    5. Select Apply, then Close.

    The Roles matrix now shows salary_readers with ✓ under the three columns and — under bank_account. alice and bob appear in the Users matrix with the same marks: hover a ✓ to see that the grant comes through salary_readers. They have no grant of their own, so Direct column grants to users stays empty.

  3. Add a row policy for alice

    1. Select the Row Policies tab, then Create row policy.
    2. Fill in Name finance_only, Database hr_demo, Table salaries, Kind Permissive: joined with OR with other permissive policies, and Applies to These users and roles, then check user alice.
    3. Under Filter, keep Conditions (joined with AND). In the condition, choose Column department, Condition =, and type Finance in Values.
    4. Select Review. The warning lists the affected users with their filter before and after: alice goes from every row to department = 'Finance'.
    5. Select Apply, then Close.

    The Row policies list shows finance_only on hr_demo.salaries, Permissive (OR), applied to alice.

  4. Check the effect on the table

    In Effect on a table, choose Database hr_demo and Table salaries. The table shows:

    • alice: Rows visible Filtered, with the combined filter department = 'Finance' from finance_only.
    • bob and your administrator: All rows: no policy applies.

    This is the default behavior of ClickHouse: once a table has row policies, a user to whom none of them applies still reads every row. bob reads the salaries of every department. You fix this with a policy rule later.

  5. Explain the access of alice

    1. Select the Effective Access tab. Choose User alice, Database hr_demo, Table salaries, and Operation Read (SELECT).
    2. Under Roles, salary_readers is Active: it is a default role.
    3. In the per-column table, employee, department, and salary are Yes under At login (configured), and Given by names the SELECT grant and the role salary_readers. bank_account is No.
    4. Under Rows, At login shows department = 'Finance'.
    5. Select Verify with the server. The console runs EXECUTE AS alice CHECK GRANT for each column and counts the rows as alice: three columns are Allowed, bank_account is Denied, and Visible rows is 2.

    If the results are Unknown, your user lacks IMPERSONATE on alice: the evidence column shows the server's message.

  6. Add access tests

    1. Select the Access Tests tab, then Add test, and add these three tests. For each, fill in the fields, select Review, then Apply and Close.

      NameAs userDatabase, TableColumnsExpectedExpected rows
      alice reads Finance salariesalicehr_demo, salariesemployee, salaryAllowed2
      alice cannot read bank accountsalicehr_demo, salariesbank_accountDenied (ACCESS_DENIED)empty
      bob reads Sales salariesbobhr_demo, salariesemployee, salaryAllowed2

    2. Select Run all.

    The first two tests show Pass. The third shows Fail with allowed, 6 rows: bob reads every row, as Effect on a table showed. The test records the number of rows, never the data.

  7. Define the attribute department and set its values

    1. Select the Attributes & Classifications tab, then Define attribute.
    2. Fill in Attribute department, Category User, Source of truth console, and Owner HR. Leave Writer empty (any administrator who can write values), Fresh for (seconds) at 86400, and Evaluated per request unchecked.
    3. Select Review, then Apply and Close. The Attributes table lists department, fresh for one day.
    4. Under User attribute values, select Set value. Choose User alice and Attribute department (console), type Value Finance, then Review, Apply, and Close.
    5. Set the value Sales for bob the same way.

    Both values show Status Fresh. In production, an identity provider or HR import writes these values with its own account (see Import user attributes), and the definition names that account as its Writer.

  8. Create a policy rule that limits rows by department

    1. Select the Policy Rules tab, then New rule.
    2. Fill in:
      • Name: Salaries by department
      • Kind: Filter rows by an attribute
      • Users: department = Finance, Sales
      • Database hr_demo, Table salaries, Column department, Attribute department
      • Missing or stale attribute: Revoke what the rule gave (fail closed)
      • Exceptions: empty, and Enabled checked
    3. Select Review. The warning shows how the rule resolves now: 2 users matched (alice, bob), and 2 generated controls. Select Apply, then Close.

    The rule is listed with the business rule Users with department ∈ {Finance, Sales} read the rows of hr_demo.salaries where department equals their department. and the status 2 users.

    The Users selector matters: it puts only users with a department of Finance or Sales in the scope of the rule. With an empty selector, every user without a department, including your administrator, would get a policy that shows no row.

    Select Explain to see the matched users with their values and the two generated row policies, both Not deployed. Saving the rule changed nothing on the server yet.

  9. Remove the hand-made policy

    The rule replaces finance_only. On Row Policies, select Remove on finance_only, then Apply and Close. Until you deploy the rule, alice reads every row again.

  10. Deploy the rule

    1. Select the Policy Deployments tab. Planned changes lists two steps, one row policy per department, named dap_<rule>_<value hash>:
      text
      Create the row policy dap_…_… on hr_demo.salaries: `department` = 'Finance', for alice
Create the row policy dap_…_… on hr_demo.salaries: `department` = 'Sales', for bob

      Readers outside the rules may list your administrator: it reads the table, is not in the scope of the rule, and has no policy on it, so it sees every row. That is expected here.

    2. Select Deploy, review the statements (CREATE ROW POLICY OR REPLACE ... AS permissive TO ...), then Apply. Both steps show Done. Select Close.
    3. Planned changes now shows "None: the server matches the rules.", and History shows a deploy entry with the result success.
    4. Select Verify. The dialog reports "Every generated control is present, and no excluded user keeps the access elsewhere." Select Close. History shows a verify entry.

    The two policies are recorded in dap_owned: the platform owns them, and changes or removes them as the rule requires.

  11. Verify as the users

    1. On Access Tests, select Run all. All three tests show Pass: bob now reads 2 rows.

    2. Read as the users themselves, with their own credentials. With clickhouse-client (in the Docker Compose deployment, run it with docker compose exec clickhouse clickhouse-client):

      bash
      clickhouse-client --user bob --password 'Bob-demo-1' \
    --query "SELECT employee, department, salary FROM hr_demo.salaries"
      text
      Dina	Sales	4500
Ed	Sales	4700

    3. Try the column that is not granted, and SELECT *:

      bash
      clickhouse-client --user bob --password 'Bob-demo-1' --query "SELECT bank_account FROM hr_demo.salaries"
clickhouse-client --user bob --password 'Bob-demo-1' --query "SELECT * FROM hr_demo.salaries"

      Both fail with ACCESS_DENIED: SELECT * needs every column. The same query as alice returns the two Finance rows.

  12. Change an attribute and deploy again

    Move bob to Finance: on Attributes & Classifications, select Set value for bob, attribute department, value Finance, then Review, Apply, and Close.

    On Policy Deployments, Planned changes now updates the Finance policy for alice, bob and drops the Sales policy, which no rule wants any more. Select Deploy, then Apply and Close. bob now reads the Finance rows and no Sales row. With the access policy worker, the same change reaches the server within one interval, without anyone opening the console.

Clean up

Remove the generated policies before the users, so that the platform's ownership records stay consistent:

  1. On Policy Rules, select Delete on Salaries by department, then Apply and Close. The rule is now Deleted, but its policies still exist.

  2. On Policy Deployments, Planned changes lists Drop the row policy ... for the owned policies. Select Deploy, then Apply and Close.

  3. On Access Tests, select Remove on each of the three tests, then Apply. The runs stay in dap_test_runs.

  4. On Attributes & Classifications, select Remove on the values of alice and bob, then Apply. The page has no button to remove an attribute definition; to remove department, insert a row that marks it deleted (replace console_admin if your admin database has another name):

    sql
    INSERT INTO console_admin.dap_attributes (attribute, category, dynamic, source, writer, owner, max_age_seconds, description, deleted)
VALUES ('department', 'user', false, 'console', '', 'HR', 86400, '', true);

  5. Drop the demo entities:

    sql
    DROP USER alice, bob;
DROP ROLE salary_readers;
DROP DATABASE hr_demo;

What you learned

  • A column grant is positive: it restricts a user to some columns only when no broader grant gives the whole table, and SELECT * fails without every column.
  • A row policy filters reads only for the users it applies to: once a table has policies, other users with SELECT still read every row.
  • Effective Access explains configured access, and Verify with the server and access tests confirm it with EXECUTE AS as the user.
  • A policy rule turns trusted user attributes into native row policies. Saving it changes nothing; a deployment or the access policy worker applies it, changing only the entities the platform owns.

Read more:

  • Data Access Policies: every tab, the rule kinds, ownership, and limits.
  • Policy rules and Attributes and classifications.
  • Import user attributes from a feed or an LDAP directory.

tutorials/backups.title: Tutorial: back up and restore a database
tutorials/backups.description: Set up backups in the ClickHouse web console: a destination, a manual backup and restore, a daily schedule, the backup worker, a restore test, and an encrypted server bundle.
tutorials/backups.html:
In this tutorial, you protect a small database with the Backup & Restore page of the web console. You add a backup destination on a disk of the server, back up a demo database by hand, restore it under another name, schedule a daily backup with retention, run the backup worker once, verify a backup with a restore test, and finally back up the server configuration as an encrypted server bundle.

It takes about 30 minutes. Every step says what you should see.

Prerequisites

  • The server with the console and the backup worker, deployed with Docker Compose as in Deploy with Docker Compose. The commands below run in the deployment directory, next to compose.yaml and .env.
  • The service account backup_worker, created from service-accounts.sql with a role made with the Backup Administrator template, as in Create service accounts.
  • You are signed in to the console as default, or as another user with all privileges.

Tip

Without Docker, run the server as usual and the worker with node utils/web-console/backup_worker.mjs from a checkout of the repository; the steps in the console are the same.

Steps

  1. Give the server a backup disk

    A disk destination needs a disk of the server that is allowed in backups.allowed_disk. Create config.d/backups.xml in the deployment directory:

    xml
    <clickhouse>
    <storage_configuration>
        <disks>
            <backups>
                <type>local</type>
                <path>/var/lib/clickhouse/backups/</path>
            </backups>
        </disks>
    </storage_configuration>
    <backups>
        <allowed_disk>backups</allowed_disk>
    </backups>
</clickhouse>

    Mount it like web-console.xml: add this line to the volumes of the clickhouse service in compose.yaml:

    yaml
          - ./config.d/backups.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/backups.xml:ro

    Then recreate the server:

    bash
    docker compose up -d clickhouse

    The path is in the data volume of the server, which the backup-worker service also mounts, so that the worker can delete backups from it.

    You should see the disk in the list of disks:

    bash
    set -a; . ./.env; set +a
docker compose exec -T clickhouse clickhouse-client --password "$CLICKHOUSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD" --query "SELECT name, path FROM system.disks"
    text
    backups	/var/lib/clickhouse/backups/
default	/var/lib/clickhouse/

  2. Set up Backup & Restore

    In the console, open Administration → Backup & Restore. If the page shows Set up Backup & Restore, select Set up. The review lists the statements that create the database console_admin and five tables in it; select Apply.

    You should see the tabs Overview, Backups, Server state, Restore, Schedules, Destinations, Operations, and Recovery verification. The Overview shows the Scheduler worker box with the last heartbeat of the backup worker that docker compose up -d started.

  3. Add a disk destination

    On Destinations, select Add destination and fill in:

    FieldValue
    TypeServer backup disk
    Namelocal-disk
    Diskbackups (/var/lib/clickhouse/backups/)
    Prefixconsole (the default)
    Allowed databasesempty: any database

    Select Review, then Apply.

    You should see local-disk in the table, Disabled, with Never tested in Last test. A destination stays disabled until it passes a test and you enable it.

  4. Test and enable the destination

    On the row of local-disk, select Test. The server writes a small backup under console/_console_test/ and opens it.

    You should see write and read as ok, and list and delete as tested by the backup worker: the worker tests them with its own access when it next runs, and removes the test backup. Select Record result, then Apply.

    Then select Enable on the row, and Apply. You should see Enabled and a passed test.

  5. Optional: add an S3 destination

    To back up to an S3-compatible bucket as well, for example a MinIO server at http://10.0.4.20:9000 with a bucket backups:

    1. Choose a name for the credentials of the worker, for example BACKUP_S3_MAIN, and put the worker's key into backup-destinations.env in the deployment directory, then restart the worker with docker compose up -d backup-worker:

      text
      BACKUP_S3_MAIN_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
BACKUP_S3_MAIN_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...

    2. Select Add destination, with Type S3-compatible bucket, a Name such as minio, the Endpoint http://10.0.4.20:9000, the Bucket backups, the server's Access key ID and Secret access key, and the Worker credential reference BACKUP_S3_MAIN.

    3. Select Review. When the endpoint is not allowed yet, the review includes a step that allows it, with a warning; for plain HTTP, also a warning that data and credentials travel in clear text. Select Apply.

    4. Test and enable it as in the previous step.

    The secret key goes into a named collection on the server and is never shown again. See Destinations for the allowed endpoints.

  6. Create a demo database

    Create a database with one table of 100,000 rows:

    bash
    docker compose exec -T clickhouse clickhouse-client --password "$CLICKHOUSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD" --multiquery <<'EOF'
CREATE DATABASE demo;
CREATE TABLE demo.events (id UInt64, at DateTime, kind LowCardinality(String)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id;
INSERT INTO demo.events SELECT number, now() - number, ['view', 'click', 'buy'][number % 3 + 1] FROM numbers(100000);
EOF

    You can run the same statements in the SQL Console of the console instead.

  7. Back up the database

    On Backups, select New backup. The wizard has four steps:

    1. Scope: keep What to back up at Whole databases and select demo. Under Server objects, clear the option that includes the console's tables, to keep the backup small. Select Next.
    2. Destination: choose local-disk. Select Next.
    3. Type: keep Full backup, and keep the option that captures validation values: the row count and a fingerprint of each table, used later to check restores. Select Next.
    4. Review: the object demo.events with its engine MergeTree and 100,000 rows, and the consistency statement. Select Start backup.

    You should see the operation followed in a dialog until it is Succeeded. Closing the dialog does not stop the backup: it runs in the server. In the inventory, the backup has a row with its short ID, the scope demo, the type full, the destination, its size, and Can be deleted in Retention.

  8. Restore it under another name

    On Restore, select Restore… on the backup. The restore wizard has five steps:

    1. Backup and chain: the contents of the backup, the list of what it does not contain, and The backup and its chain open: 1 tables. Select Next.
    2. Target: the server, the version check, and the privileges, all Yes. Select Next.
    3. Names and options: the field demo → target database suggests restore_demo_<date>_<time>. Replace it with demo_restored. Select Next.
    4. Conflicts: No conflicts: demo_restored do not exist and are created by the restore. Select Next.
    5. Confirm: type demo_restored, and select Start restore.

    You should see the restore succeed, followed by the checks that compare the target with the backup: the tables and their engines, the row counts, and the fingerprints. Check the data yourself:

    bash
    docker compose exec -T clickhouse clickhouse-client --password "$CLICKHOUSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD" --query "SELECT count() FROM demo_restored.events"
    text
    100000

    A restore never writes into existing tables: had demo_restored existed, the Conflicts step would have stopped the restore.

  9. Schedule a daily backup with retention

    On Schedules, select Add schedule and fill in:

    FieldValue
    Namedemo-daily
    Destinationlocal-disk
    Databasesdemo
    StrategyFull backup each time
    FrequencyDaily
    Hour, Minute2, 0
    Time zoneUTC
    Keep7

    Select Review, then Apply.

    You should see demo-daily with daily at 02:00 (UTC), its next run, never as its last run, and keep 7 backups as retention. Retention preview shows No backups of the schedule here yet.

  10. Run the backup worker once

    Schedules are run by the backup worker, not by the browser. Run one cycle of it, next to the worker that is already running (several workers can run at the same time):

    bash
    docker compose run --rm backup-worker backup-worker --once
    bash
    CLICKHOUSE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8123 CLICKHOUSE_USER=backup_worker CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=... \
node utils/web-console/backup_worker.mjs --once

    The worker logs JSON lines and exits. A cycle records a heartbeat, tests listing and deleting at local-disk and removes the test backup, and submits the scheduled run that was due in the last day: a run missed because no worker made it is made once within its period. The worker of the deployment runs the same cycle every 30 seconds, so it may have done some of this already; a run is never submitted twice.

    You should see, after Refresh:

    • on Overview, Scheduler worker with Last seen a few seconds ago;
    • on Destinations, the last test of local-disk with list: ok, delete: ok;
    • on Backups, a second backup marked schedule demo-daily, and on Schedules, its state as the last run of demo-daily.

    From now on, the worker of the deployment makes a backup every day at 02:00 UTC, and deletes the oldest when there are more than 7.

  11. Verify a backup

    On Backups, select Check on the first backup. It opens the backup read-only and reads every table. You should see The backup opens, and every table was read completely., with demo.events and 100,000 rows read.

    Then select Test restore, and Run restore test. The console restores the backup into a new database console_verify_<id>_demo, compares it with the backup and with the values captured when it was made, and drops it.

    You should see The test databases were dropped., and in the inventory the badges Artifact opened and Restore test passed. The Recovery verification tab lists the test with its checks; Show in Checks lists each one.

  12. Back up the server configuration with a key file

    A database backup does not contain the server configuration or its secrets. The backup worker backs them up as encrypted server bundles. Here, you use a master key in a file.

    1. Create the key and staging directories, then the key, with the bundle overlay of the deployment:

      bash
      mkdir -p bundle-keys restore-staging && sudo chown 101:101 bundle-keys restore-staging && sudo chmod 700 bundle-keys restore-staging
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.bundles.yaml run --rm backup-worker backup-worker bundle-key-init --key-file /keys/bundle.key

      You should see Created /keys/bundle.key (readable by its owner only), fingerprint sha256:…, and the advice to copy the key out of band.

    2. Copy bundle-keys/bundle.key (readable only by the user 101, so read it with sudo) to a place outside this host and outside the backups, for example a password manager, and record the fingerprint with it. Without this key, no bundle can be decrypted.

    3. Check that the worker may store bundles. service-accounts.sql already contains this grant; if you created the account otherwise, run it:

      sql
      GRANT CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, INSERT, SELECT, BACKUP ON console_admin.server_bundle* TO backup_worker;

    4. Restart the worker with the overlay:

      bash
      docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.bundles.yaml up -d backup-worker

    5. On Server state, the Backup worker box shows the worker, Master key Key file on the worker host with the fingerprint you recorded, and Included /deploy/config.d. Select Back up the server state…, choose local-disk as the Destination, and select Request the bundle.

    6. Within 30 seconds, the worker makes the bundle. You should see, after Refresh, a row in Server bundles that is Succeeded, with its files, its encrypted size, and the key file with its fingerprint.

    7. Select Compare on the row, then Request the comparison. You should see under Restores, after the next cycle of the worker, a result such as 2 same, 0 changed, 0 missing on the host, 0 not in the bundle: the key, the bundle, and the destination all work.

Clean up

Drop the restored database when you no longer need it:

sql
DROP DATABASE demo_restored;

To remove the demo backups, select Delete on their rows and type their short IDs; the worker deletes them in its next cycle. Remove the schedule with Remove on Schedules.

What you learned

  • A destination is approved by an administrator, tested from the server, and enabled; users choose it by name.
  • A backup records its operation before it is submitted, runs in the server, and can capture values that later restores are checked against.
  • A restore always goes into new databases and stops on conflicts.
  • Schedules, retention, deletions, and destination checks are done by the backup worker.
  • A restore test proves that a backup opens and matches on this server.
  • Server bundles back up what BACKUP cannot reach, encrypted with a master key that you keep out of band.

Next:

  • Backup & Restore: every tab, state, and privilege.
  • Protect backups: choose a key provider, rotate it, and protect the backup storage.
  • Recover a whole server: the recovery procedure and its rehearsal.

tutorials/single-sign-on.title: Sign in with Keycloak
tutorials/single-sign-on.description: Run Keycloak in Docker on a test machine, set up a realm for the web console, and sign in to the console and to ClickHouse with Keycloak.

headings.text: Test the provider on the SSO page

tutorials/single-sign-on.html:
In this tutorial you set up single sign-on for the web console on one test machine. You run Keycloak in Docker, create a realm with the client of the console, a group, and a user, and start a ClickHouse server and the token authenticator next to it. The authenticator creates the ClickHouse user from the Keycloak group. Then you sign in to the console with Keycloak, and test the provider on the SSO (Keycloak) page.

It takes about thirty minutes. Everything runs on localhost over plain HTTP, which the console and the authenticator accept only for a provider on localhost. For a production setup, see Configure single sign-on with Keycloak.

Before you begin

  • Docker 24 or later, and a browser on the same machine.
  • The images clickhouse-server-console:<version> and clickhouse-console-tools:<version>, loaded with docker load (see Deploy with Docker Compose).
  • The image of Keycloak: docker pull quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.7.
  • The ports 8080 and 8123 free on 127.0.0.1. If the server of the Quick start still runs, remove it: docker rm -f clickhouse-console.

Work in a new, empty directory. In the commands, replace <version> with the version of the images.

How the containers connect

The browser, the server, and the token authenticator must all reach Keycloak at the same address, because the address is part of the issuer that every token carries. In this tutorial that address is http://localhost:8080. The server and the authenticator therefore run in the network namespace of the Keycloak container (--network container:...): inside it, localhost is the same for all three, and the ports 8080 (Keycloak) and 8123 (ClickHouse) are published on 127.0.0.1 of your machine by the Keycloak container.

Start Keycloak

  1. Write the realm

    Save this file as realm.json. It describes the realm clickhouse:

    • the public client of the console, clickhouse-console: the standard flow only, PKCE with S256, the redirect URI http://localhost:8123/console/oidc-callback, the post logout redirect URI http://localhost:8123/console/login, the web origin http://localhost:8123, a Group Membership mapper groups without the full path, and an Audience mapper that adds clickhouse-console to the access token;
    • the group clickhouse-analysts, and the user sam in it, with the password Sam-Kc-Pw-1;
    • the confidential client clickhouse-sso-sync of the user sync, with only a service account, which has the roles view-users and query-groups of realm-management.
    json
    {
  "realm": "clickhouse", "enabled": true, "sslRequired": "external", "registrationAllowed": false, "bruteForceProtected": true,
  "groups": [{"name": "clickhouse-analysts"}],
  "users": [
    {"username": "sam", "enabled": true, "emailVerified": true, "firstName": "Sam", "lastName": "Analyst", "email": "sam@example.org",
     "credentials": [{"type": "password", "value": "Sam-Kc-Pw-1", "temporary": false}], "groups": ["/clickhouse-analysts"]},
    {"username": "service-account-clickhouse-sso-sync", "enabled": true, "serviceAccountClientId": "clickhouse-sso-sync",
     "clientRoles": {"realm-management": ["view-users", "query-groups"]}}
  ],
  "clients": [
    {
      "clientId": "clickhouse-console", "enabled": true, "publicClient": true, "protocol": "openid-connect",
      "standardFlowEnabled": true, "implicitFlowEnabled": false, "directAccessGrantsEnabled": false, "serviceAccountsEnabled": false,
      "redirectUris": ["http://localhost:8123/console/oidc-callback"],
      "webOrigins": ["http://localhost:8123"],
      "attributes": {"pkce.code.challenge.method": "S256", "post.logout.redirect.uris": "http://localhost:8123/console/login"},
      "protocolMappers": [
        {"name": "groups", "protocol": "openid-connect", "protocolMapper": "oidc-group-membership-mapper",
         "config": {"claim.name": "groups", "full.path": "false", "id.token.claim": "true", "access.token.claim": "true", "userinfo.token.claim": "true"}},
        {"name": "audience", "protocol": "openid-connect", "protocolMapper": "oidc-audience-mapper",
         "config": {"included.client.audience": "clickhouse-console", "id.token.claim": "false", "access.token.claim": "true"}}
      ]
    },
    {
      "clientId": "clickhouse-sso-sync", "enabled": true, "publicClient": false, "secret": "tutorial-sync-secret",
      "serviceAccountsEnabled": true, "standardFlowEnabled": false, "implicitFlowEnabled": false, "directAccessGrantsEnabled": false,
      "protocol": "openid-connect"
    }
  ]
}

    The same settings can be made by hand in the Keycloak admin console; the file makes them exact and repeatable.

  2. Run Keycloak

    Run Keycloak in development mode, with the realm imported at the start. KC_HOSTNAME fixes the address in the issuer, and both ports are published on 127.0.0.1 only:

    bash
    docker run -d --name sso-keycloak \
    -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 -p 127.0.0.1:8123:8123 \
    -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD='choose-an-admin-password' \
    -e KC_HOSTNAME=http://localhost:8080 \
    -v "$PWD/realm.json:/opt/keycloak/data/import/realm.json:ro" \
    quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.7 start-dev --import-realm

    Keycloak takes about half a minute to start. Then:

    bash
    curl -s http://localhost:8080/realms/clickhouse/.well-known/openid-configuration | head -c 120; echo

    The answer starts with {"issuer":"http://localhost:8080/realms/clickhouse". The Keycloak admin console is at http://localhost:8080/admin, as admin.

Start the server

  1. Configure single sign-on

    Save this file as sso.xml. It declares the token authenticator as the HTTP authentication server sso, and makes the sign-in page of the console offer Keycloak:

    xml
    <clickhouse>
    <http_authentication_servers>
        <sso>
            <uri>http://127.0.0.1:29700/</uri>
            <connection_timeout_ms>1000</connection_timeout_ms>
            <receive_timeout_ms>2000</receive_timeout_ms>
            <send_timeout_ms>1000</send_timeout_ms>
            <max_tries>2</max_tries>
        </sso>
    </http_authentication_servers>
    <web_console>
        <sso_name>Keycloak</sso_name>
        <sso_issuer>http://localhost:8080/realms/clickhouse</sso_issuer>
        <sso_client_id>clickhouse-console</sso_client_id>
    </web_console>
</clickhouse>

  2. Run the server

    Run the server in the network namespace of Keycloak, with the file in config.d:

    bash
    docker run -d --name sso-clickhouse --network container:sso-keycloak \
    -e CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD='choose-a-password' -e CLICKHOUSE_DEFAULT_ACCESS_MANAGEMENT=1 \
    --ulimit nofile=262144:262144 \
    -v "$PWD/sso.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/sso.xml:ro" \
    clickhouse-server-console:<version>

    curl http://127.0.0.1:8123/ping answers Ok..

  3. Set up the administration pages

    Open http://localhost:8123/console (with localhost, which is the origin the Keycloak client allows) and sign in as default. The sign-in page already shows Sign in with Keycloak, below or: do not use it yet.

    Under Administration, select Component Access, then Set up, Review, and Apply, as in Set up the administration pages. This creates the database console_admin, with the audit log, and the role console_admin_reader, which the sync gives every SSO user.

  4. Create the role and the account of the sync

    The group clickhouse-analysts stands for the role analysts, which must exist on the server. The user sync signs in to the server as sso_sync, which may create and drop users and grant only the roles of the groups. Run:

    bash
    docker exec -i sso-clickhouse clickhouse-client --password 'choose-a-password' --multiquery <<'EOF'
CREATE ROLE analysts;
GRANT SELECT ON default.* TO analysts;

CREATE USER sso_sync IDENTIFIED WITH sha256_password BY 'choose-a-sync-password';
GRANT CREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER ON *.* TO sso_sync;
GRANT SHOW USERS, SHOW ROLES ON *.* TO sso_sync;
GRANT SELECT ON system.users TO sso_sync;
GRANT SELECT ON system.roles TO sso_sync;
GRANT SELECT ON system.role_grants TO sso_sync;
GRANT INSERT ON console_admin.audit_log TO sso_sync;
GRANT analysts, console_admin_reader TO sso_sync WITH ADMIN OPTION;
EOF

    These are the privileges of sso_sync in service-accounts.sql; see Create the service accounts.

Run the token authenticator

  1. Start it with the user sync

    bash
    docker run -d --name sso-authenticator --network container:sso-keycloak \
    -e SSO_ISSUER=http://localhost:8080/realms/clickhouse \
    -e SSO_CLIENT_ID=clickhouse-console \
    -e SSO_LISTEN=127.0.0.1:29700 \
    -e SSO_SYNC_CLIENT_ID=clickhouse-sso-sync -e SSO_SYNC_SECRET=tutorial-sync-secret \
    -e SSO_ROLE_PREFIX=clickhouse- -e SSO_DEFAULT_ROLES=console_admin_reader \
    -e CLICKHOUSE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8123 -e CLICKHOUSE_USER=sso_sync -e CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD='choose-a-sync-password' \
    clickhouse-console-tools:<version> sso-authenticator

    In production, keep the secret of the sync client in a file (SSO_SYNC_SECRET_FILE) instead of the environment.

  2. Check its log

    bash
    docker logs sso-authenticator

    The log is one JSON object per line. You see keys loaded with the issuer, listening with "sync":true, and users synced with "members":1.

  3. Check the user it created

    bash
    docker exec sso-clickhouse clickhouse-client --password 'choose-a-password' --query "SHOW CREATE USER sam"

    The statement contains IDENTIFIED WITH http SERVER 'sso': the password of sam is checked by the token authenticator. SHOW GRANTS FOR sam lists the roles analysts and console_admin_reader.

Sign in with Keycloak

  1. Sign out

    In the console, select Sign out. The sign-in page shows Sign in with Keycloak.

  2. Sign in as sam

    Select Sign in with Keycloak. A window opens with the sign-in page of the realm clickhouse. Sign in as sam with the password Sam-Kc-Pw-1. The window closes, and the console opens its home page, signed in as sam.

    If nothing opens, the browser blocked the window: allow pop-ups for http://localhost:8123, and try again.

  3. Look at what sam may do

    Open the SQL Console and run SELECT currentUser(): it returns sam. The console sent the access token of Keycloak as the password, and the server accepted it through the token authenticator.

    docker logs sso-authenticator shows no refused line for sam.

  4. Sign out again

    Select Sign out. The console also ends the session with Keycloak, and returns to its sign-in page.

Test the provider on the SSO page

  1. Set up the page

    Sign in as default. Under Identity Providers, select SSO (Keycloak). The page shows Set up single sign-on: select Set up, then Apply. This creates the table console_admin.idp_providers.

  2. Add Keycloak

    Select Add Keycloak… and enter:

    • Keycloak URL: http://localhost:8080
    • Realm: clickhouse

    Keep the other fields: Client ID clickhouse-console, User name claim preferred_username, Group claim groups, Role prefix clickhouse-. The issuer below the fields reads http://localhost:8080/realms/clickhouse. Select Add, review the statement, and select Apply.

  3. Test the connection

    On the provider, select Test connection. The report lists Discovery document, Issuer, Authorization Code flow, PKCE, Endpoints, Signing keys, and Roles for groups, each OK.

  4. Test a sign-in

    Select Test sign-in…, then Sign in with Keycloak, and sign in as sam in the window. Keycloak asks for the password even if you are still signed in there. The result shows Signed in as sam, the group clickhouse-analysts, Roles it would get analysts, the existing ClickHouse user, and an Access token that is valid, with the audience clickhouse-console.

  5. Find the user of single sign-on

    In the Signing in to ClickHouse box, Sign-in page shows the issuer and the client from sso.xml, and Users of single sign-on lists sam.

  6. Remove access in Keycloak

    In the Keycloak admin console (http://localhost:8080/admin), in the realm clickhouse, remove sam from the group clickhouse-analysts. Within a minute, the sync drops the user: docker logs sso-authenticator shows users synced with a change, and Users of single sign-on no longer lists sam after Refresh. Select Audit Activity to find the records of the sync.

Clean up

Remove the containers, Keycloak last, because the others use its network:

bash
docker rm -f sso-authenticator sso-clickhouse sso-keycloak

What you learned

  • The console signs users in with Keycloak as a public client, with the Authorization Code flow and PKCE, and uses the access token as the password of the session.
  • The server does not check tokens itself: the token authenticator does, as the HTTP authentication server sso, for the users IDENTIFIED WITH http SERVER 'sso'.
  • The user sync creates those users from the groups clickhouse-<role>, grants the roles, and drops the users who leave.
  • The SSO (Keycloak) page tests the provider and a sign-in, without storing any token.

Next:

  • Identity providers: the model and the limits of single sign-on.
  • Configure single sign-on with Keycloak: the production setup, with Docker Compose, and troubleshooting.
  • Token authenticator API: every check and setting.

guides/console.title: The console: sign-in, navigation, and panels
guides/console.description: How the web console shell works: signing in, the home page, the sidebar and its categories, panels and their states, the connection status, and the security model.

headings.text: Data in the browser's local storage

guides/console.html:
The web console is a single entry point for the web UIs built into the ClickHouse server. Every HTTP port of the server serves it at /console, for example http://localhost:8123/console. You sign in once with a ClickHouse user, and the console opens the SQL Console, the dashboards, the diagnostic pages, and its own administration pages next to a common sidebar, without a separate sign-in for each of them.

This page explains the shell of the console: how you sign in and out, what the home page and the sidebar show, how panels open and which states they can be in, and what the console does and does not protect. For the architecture and the list of components, see the overview.

Signing in and out

The sign-in form

The sign-in page, ClickHouse Console, asks for a Username (prefilled with default) and a Password, and signs in when you select Connect. The console always signs in to the server that serves it, at the address of the page. If that address uses plain HTTP and is not localhost, the form warns that the password is sent to the server in clear text.

The console checks the credentials with SELECT currentUser(), version(), hostName(), which needs no privileges. When the check fails, the form tells these cases apart:

  • The username or password is incorrect.
  • The user is not allowed to connect from your network address.
  • The user does not have the required permissions.
  • The server cannot be reached. Where the browser allows it, the message also tells a blocked HTTPS-to-HTTP request (mixed content), a CORS refusal, and an untrusted TLS certificate apart.

If you open the address of a panel, for example /console/merges, without being signed in, the form shows Sign in to open followed by the panel name, and opens that panel after the sign-in.

Single sign-on

When the server configuration sets web_console.sso_issuer and web_console.sso_client_id, the form also shows a Sign in with button for the identity provider, for example Sign in with Keycloak (the provider name comes from sso_name). See the configuration reference for these keys.

Selecting the button opens the provider's sign-in page in a pop-up window. If the browser blocks the pop-up, the form asks you to allow pop-ups for the page. After you sign in with the provider, the console uses the access token as the password of the session. The user name is the claim named by sso_username_claim (by default preferred_username). The server checks the token through the token authenticator, for users IDENTIFIED WITH http. If the server refuses the sign-in, the form says that the provider signed you in, and that the user must exist on the server with the token authenticator, which must be running.

While you are signed in, the console refreshes the access token before it expires and passes the new token to the native panels. The SQL Console, the Web Terminal, and ClickStack keep the token they started with, so reload them after it expires. When the provider refuses a refresh, for example because the session ended there or the user was disabled, the console signs you out and says that your session has ended. For the whole design, see Identity Providers.

Signing out and switching connection

Sign out in the header, and Switch connection (in the header and on the home page) to sign in as another user, close every panel. This ends their queries, timers, and terminal sessions. They also discard the password, and the ClickHouse connection that ClickStack stored for the current browser tab. After signing out, the browser's Back button does not restore the signed-in state.

With single sign-on, Sign out also ends the session with the provider and returns to the sign-in page. Switch connection then works like Sign out, because another user needs a new session with the provider.

The home page

After the sign-in, the console opens Home. Its connection overview shows:

FieldContent
StatusConnected, verified at a time, or Authentication failed or Connection lost with the time of the failure.
ServerThe URL the console is connected to.
Database userThe user the server reports with currentUser.
ClickHouse versionThe version of the server.
Host nameThe host name of the server.

Check connection checks the connection again, and Switch connection signs out so that you can sign in as another user. Below the overview, the home page shows a card for each destination the user can use, grouped by category. Each card has a description, its state, and a button: Open, Configure (for a destination without an address), or Details (for an unavailable one).

When the console access policy exists but cannot be read, the home page also says that the components it governs are hidden, and which privilege to ask for (see Component Access).

Connection status

The header shows the connection status as <user>@<host> followed by connected, checking…, authentication failed, or connection lost. The console checks the connection every minute while the tab is visible, and when you select Check connection. When the check fails, the open panel shows a notice that it may not work until the connection is restored. If authentication fails, the password may have changed: switch connection to sign in again.

The sidebar and its categories

The sidebar and the home page list the same destinations, in these categories:

CategoryDestinations
HomeHome.
WorkspaceSQL Console, Dashboard, ClickStack, Web Terminal.
DiagnosticsBinary visualizer, Merges visualizer, Schema visualizer, Jemalloc, Processors profile.
AdministrationUsers, Roles & Permissions, Data Access Policies, Component Access, Profiles & Quotas, Audit Activity, Clusters, Backup & Restore.
Identity ProvidersLDAP, SSO (Keycloak).
ResourcesConsole Guide, Source code, Documentation, Reference, Website, Cloud.

A category without any destination for the user is not shown. The button at the bottom of the sidebar collapses it to icons (Collapse sidebar, Expand sidebar); the browser remembers the choice. On a narrow screen, the menu button in the header shows and hides the sidebar.

The administration and identity provider pages are listed only for users who can read what they show, and when the console access policy allows them. Their own guides describe them: Users and roles, Component Access, Profiles and quotas, Audit activity, Data Access Policies, Backup & Restore, Clusters, and Identity Providers.

Console Guide shows this documentation inside the console, for every signed-in user. It is embedded in the server, so it works without Internet access and describes the console of this build.

  • Its home page has a search box, the Get started actions (the quick start and the overview), and a card for each page, by section: Tutorials, User guides, How-to guides, and API reference. A card shows the type of the page and what it covers; select it anywhere to open the page. More resources links to the ClickHouse documentation and to the Reference panel.
  • Each page fills the width of the window: the navigation of the guide on the left, with Guide home at the top and a search box, the article, and On this page on the right (at the top of the article in a narrower window). The previous and next pages are at the end of the article.
  • The header of each administration and identity provider page has a Guide button that opens the guide of that page.

The links of Resources come from the web_console section of the server configuration. A path on the server opens inside the console; an absolute HTTP or HTTPS URL opens in a new tab and is marked External. External links open with noopener and noreferrer and carry no credentials, queries, or database names. See the configuration reference.

Panels

A panel is a web UI of the server shown inside the console: the SQL Console (/ui), Dashboard (/dashboard), ClickStack (/clickstack or clickstack_url), Web Terminal (/webterminal), the diagnostic pages (/binary, /merges, /schema, /jemalloc, /processors-profile), and Reference (/docs). The console passes the connection to each of them, so they do not ask for credentials (see the embedding contract). ClickStack is the exception: it keeps its own connection settings, which you enter in ClickStack on first use.

Each panel has a refreshable address under /console, for example /console/merges, and the browser's Back and Forward buttons move between panels. The pages also keep working on their own at their original paths.

The panel bar

Above an open panel, the panel bar shows the name of the panel and these controls:

  • Console: shows or hides the console header and sidebar (see Focus mode).
  • Reload panel: loads the panel again with the current connection.
  • Standalone page: opens the page outside of the console, in a new tab. It asks for credentials separately.

Focus mode

When a panel opens, the console header and sidebar hide, so that the panel, with its own navigation, uses the whole window. To return to the console navigation, select Console (the arrow at the start of the panel bar); select the same button again to hide it. The console navigation then stays visible for that panel until you select another one.

Home, the administration pages, and the messages shown instead of a panel (for example when it is restricted or not configured) always show the console navigation. In the Web Terminal, Escape moves the keyboard focus to the Console button.

Panels that stay loaded

The SQL Console, Dashboard, ClickStack, Web Terminal, and Reference stay loaded when you switch to another destination: their queries, tabs, results, and terminal sessions survive. The other panels are unloaded, which stops their timers and requests, and are loaded again each time they are opened.

Panel states

After the sign-in, the console runs a LIMIT 0 query for each panel that needs privileges or system tables, with the same privileges and tables the panel needs. It also checks whether /webterminal and the ClickStack bundle answer. The result gives each destination one of these states:

StateMeaningWhat the address shows
Checking…The checks are still running.Checking whether this panel is available for your user.
Not listed (restricted)The server denies the check query: the user has no privileges for the panel. The card and the sidebar entry are not shown.is restricted, the answer of the server, and Open anyway: the server still checks every query and rejects those the user is not allowed to run.
UnavailableA system table or function the panel needs does not exist, for example system.part_log when it is not configured. The Web Terminal is unavailable when the enable_webterminal server setting disables it, and when the console is connected to a server other than the one that serves it. ClickStack is unavailable when the server build has no ClickStack bundle.is unavailable and the reason.
Not configuredAn administrator removed the address of the destination, or set an invalid one.is not configured, with an example of the configuration that sets the address.
Not verifiedThe check failed for another reason, for example a timeout. The panel can still be opened.The panel.
Not allowed by policyThe console access policy does not allow the user to open the component. It is not listed.is not allowed, and a note that the server still decides what the user can query.

Two more badges describe a destination, not its state: External for a destination that opens in a new tab, and Needs Internet for a page that loads a library from a public CDN. The Binary visualizer loads Leaflet, and Jemalloc loads uPlot. Every other panel and the console itself work without Internet access.

If the page inside a panel navigates away from its own address, for example when you use the SQL Console's own sign-out, the console unloads the panel and offers Reload panel.

Security model

The sign-in screen is a convenience of the user interface, not an access control. The console page and the embedded pages are public static files, like the other web UIs of the server. Every query is authorized by the ClickHouse server, with the credentials of the signed-in user. Hiding or marking a panel in the console does not change what the user can do.

The console handles credentials as follows:

  • It keeps the password, or the access token with single sign-on, in the memory of the browser tab. It never writes them to the address bar, the browser history, cookies, or browser storage. Reloading the page signs you out.
  • It sends the credentials in the X-ClickHouse-User and X-ClickHouse-Key headers, never in the URL.
  • Embedded pages get the credentials from the console without going through a URL, a storage, or a message to another origin. Some of them send the credentials to the server as user and password URL parameters, as they do when opened on their own. The server masks the password in its logs, but a reverse proxy may record such URLs: do not log query strings on a proxy in front of ClickHouse.
  • Links to external destinations open in a new tab with noopener and noreferrer, and carry no credentials, queries, or database names.
  • The console page is served with Cache-Control: no-store, X-Frame-Options: DENY, and a Content-Security-Policy that allows only inline code, same-origin frames, and requests to ClickHouse servers. To override any of these headers, set it in a console handler of http_handlers (see the configuration reference).
  • The embedded pages are loaded in same-origin frames. Do not set X-Frame-Options: DENY or frame-ancestors 'none' on them, or they cannot be embedded.

The administration pages follow the same model: each change is a SQL statement that the server authorizes with your privileges (see Users and roles). The console access policy only lists or hides components; see Component Access.

Data in the browser's local storage

The SQL Console keeps its saved queries, query history, and open tabs in the browser's local storage, per server URL and user, also when it is used inside the console. Signing out of the console does not delete them. Use a browser profile of your own on a shared computer.

The console itself stores only two preferences in local storage: the theme (light or dark, shared with the other web UIs of the server) and whether the sidebar is collapsed.

Limitations

  • The console and the panels share the origin of the ClickHouse HTTP port. Any page on that origin, including ClickStack and the SQL Console, can read the memory of the console. Do not serve untrusted content from the ClickHouse HTTP port.
  • Navigation inside an embedded page, for example opening a query in the SQL Console, also adds entries to the browser history.
  • Panels other than the SQL Console, Dashboard, ClickStack, Web Terminal, and Reference are reloaded each time they are opened, which stops their background refresh while they are hidden.
  • A theme change applies to panels opened after it. Panels that are already open keep their theme until they are reloaded.
  • The Merges visualizer does not display query errors, including permission errors.
  • With single sign-on, the SQL Console, the Web Terminal, and ClickStack keep the access token they started with: reload them after it expires.
  • The SQL Console has no embedding interface: the console fills in its connection form and submits it. If that does not succeed, the console shows a notice above the panel, and you can sign in with the form of the SQL Console.

guides/users-and-roles.title: Users and roles
guides/users-and-roles.description: How the Users and Roles & Permissions pages of the web console manage ClickHouse users, roles, and privileges, and how the server authorizes each change.

headings.text: Changes made outside of the console

guides/users-and-roles.html:
The Users and Roles & Permissions pages, in the Administration category, manage the users, roles, and privileges of the ClickHouse server the console is connected to. They are a front end to the SQL statements CREATE USER, ALTER USER, GRANT, REVOKE, and their relatives: the console builds the statements from validated form fields, shows them to you, and runs them with your credentials. The server decides whether each one is allowed.

This page explains the model behind the pages and what each action does. For a step-by-step procedure, see Offboard a user and the tutorial Your first administrator. For the privileges each page needs, see the privileges reference.

Identity and authorization model

The console has no identity store and no server-side session of its own: you sign in as a ClickHouse user, and the password stays in the memory of the browser tab. Every administrative action is a statement such as CREATE USER or GRANT, built by the console from validated form fields (it never runs SQL typed by the user), and run with your credentials. ClickHouse authorizes each statement:

  • Granting a privilege needs that privilege WITH GRANT OPTION, so you cannot hand out more than you have.
  • Granting a role needs ROLE ADMIN, or that role granted to you WITH ADMIN OPTION.
  • User management can be limited to names: GRANT CREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER ON app_* TO ... allows managing only the users whose names start with app_. The pages then say which names you can manage.

The console asks the server what you can do (with CHECK GRANT, and LIMIT 0 reads of system tables) to decide which pages and buttons to offer. A button you cannot use is disabled, with the reason in its tooltip. The server still checks every statement, so a direct request without the console is rejected in the same way. See the SQL reference for undefined and undefined.

A ClickHouse user is a database identity. Creating one does not create an account in ClickStack or in any other separately deployed service, and the console does not synchronize identities with them. ClickHouse does not store e-mail addresses, creation dates, or the time of the last login, so the console does not show them. The last successful login is shown from system.session_log when that log is enabled and readable.

Reviewing and applying a change

Every change goes through the same steps:

  1. A form collects the values, and Review validates them.
  2. The review dialog lists the steps, the statements (with passwords replaced by [HIDDEN]), and the server or cluster they run on. If the console audit log is not set up, or you cannot write to it, the dialog says that the change is not recorded there.
  3. Apply (or Suspend, Delete, Revoke for destructive changes) runs the statements one after another and stops at the first failure.
  4. The result is Applied., Not applied (the first statement failed, so nothing changed), or Partially applied with the steps that took effect. ClickHouse has no transactions for access entities, so a partial change is not rolled back.

Each change has a correlation ID, which the console sets as the log_comment of its statements (console-admin:<id>) and writes to the audit log.

Management sources

Each user and role shows its source, which decides whether SQL can change it:

SourceMeaningIn the console
SQLCreated with SQL, stored on this server.Editable.
SQL (replicated)Created with SQL, stored in a replicated user directory and replicated through Keeper.Editable.
SQL (memory)Created with SQL and kept in memory only: lost when the server restarts.Editable.
ConfigurationDefined in a configuration file (users.xml).Read-only: change it in the file.
LDAPProvided by an LDAP server for the time of a session.Read-only: manage it in the directory.

The console does not move users between sources. Users of an LDAP directory appear in the list once they have signed in since the server started; they cannot be suspended or deleted in the console (see Identity Providers).

Users of single sign-on are SQL users IDENTIFIED WITH http, created by the user sync of the token authenticator. The console does not set a password for them, because their credentials are managed outside of ClickHouse. The sync also manages their roles: at each run it grants the roles of their groups in the identity provider and revokes every other role, so a role you assign them in the console does not last. Manage their roles with the groups of the provider (see Identity Providers and the user sync reference).

The Users page

The list shows the users of the server, searchable by name and paginated by 50, with these columns:

ColumnContent
UserThe name, and the stable ID (UUID).
AuthenticationThe authentication methods. Methods whose credentials live outside of ClickHouse (ldap, kerberos, ssl_certificate, ssh_key, http, jwt) are highlighted.
SourceThe management source (see Management sources).
RolesThe granted roles; default roles are marked as active at login.
HostsThe allowed hosts.
Profiles & quotasThe settings profiles and quotas that apply.
StateActive, Suspended, Expired, Partly expired, Expires with a date, or No allowed hosts.

Columns that your user cannot read show not readable. Selecting a user opens its page, with the tabs Overview, Roles, Permissions, Profiles & quotas, Component access, and Audit activity, and the actions Edit, Password, Suspend or Reactivate, and Delete.

The Overview tab shows the name, stable ID, management source, authentication methods with their expiry, allowed hosts, default database, default roles, the users it can grant privileges to, the account state, the last successful login, and the definition as the server reports it (SHOW CREATE USER, which never shows passwords or hashes).

User lifecycle

  • Create user: a name, a password, an optional expiry, the allowed hosts, a default database, roles, and a settings profile. The password is either typed twice (Enter a password) or generated in the browser (Generate a temporary password) and shown once after the user is created, with a Copy button. When the server has more than one writable user directory, Stored in chooses it. Once the console is set up, the role console_admin_reader is preselected if you can grant it (see Component Access).
  • Edit: rename, allowed hosts, and default database. Renaming keeps the ID, roles, and privileges; clients must sign in with the new name. Changing the allowed hosts applies to new logins; open sessions are not closed.
  • Password: set a new password or generate a temporary one, with an optional expiry. This replaces every authentication method of the user. ClickHouse cannot force a password change at the next login; use an expiry instead. Users authenticated with LDAP, Kerberos, certificates, SSH keys, JWT, or HTTP cannot get a password in the console. A suspended user stays suspended: the new password gets the same expiry.
  • Roles tab: Assign role, Default roles, and Revoke. Default roles are active when a session starts; other granted roles become active only after SET ROLE. Revoking a role takes effect for open sessions of the user at their next query.
  • Suspend and Reactivate: see Suspending a user.
  • Delete: see Deleting a user.

You cannot suspend or delete your own user. Passwords are sent to the server only in the statement that sets them, never in a URL. The server stores a hash and masks the password in system.query_log and its logs. The console does not write passwords to the audit log, to error messages, or to browser storage, and removes a generated password from the page when its dialog closes.

Suspending a user

ClickHouse has no statement that disables a user. The console suspends a user with ALTER USER name VALID UNTIL '2000-01-01 00:00:00 UTC', which makes every authentication method of the user expire. Then:

  • New logins are rejected over every interface. HTTP requests are authenticated one by one, including those with a session_id, so HTTP clients of the user, including the console, stop working at their next request.
  • Native connections that are already open, such as clickhouse-client, the Web Terminal, and pooled driver connections, keep working until they disconnect. ClickHouse has no statement that closes another user's connection. To cut them off at once, revoke the user's roles and privileges as well: revocations apply to open sessions at their next query.
  • Running queries finish, unless you also select Also stop the queries the user is running now (KILL QUERY), which runs KILL QUERY and needs the KILL QUERY privilege.
  • Roles, privileges, and settings stay unchanged.

Reactivate sets VALID UNTIL 'infinity', or a date you choose in Credentials expire (optional). Expiry dates that the user had before the suspension are overwritten; they are kept in the audit record and shown when reactivating.

The console refuses to suspend a protected account and the last platform administrator.

Deleting a user
