Delete first shows what depends on the user: its granted roles, direct privileges, views and tables that run as the user (SQL SECURITY DEFINER), quotas and row policies that name it, and its running queries. Views that use the user as definer stop working until their definer is changed. To confirm, you type the name of the user.

Deleting removes the credentials, direct privileges, role assignments, and settings of the user. Open sessions are not closed, but lose all privileges at their next query. This cannot be undone: a user created again with the same name gets a new ID.

The Roles & Permissions page

The list shows the roles with their source, their members (users and roles), how many members can grant the role (the admin option), and the number of direct privileges, with how many of them are delegable. Create role creates an empty role; the role templates below the list create a role with privileges.

A role's page has the tabs Permissions, Granted roles (roles granted to this role, whose privileges its members also get), Members (Add member, Revoke), Profiles & quotas, and Component access, and a Delete action. Deleting a role shows its members and the console policy rules for it, which then no longer apply to anyone.

Permissions

The Permissions tab of a user or role shows three views:

  • Direct privileges: granted to the user or role itself, from system.grants, with Revoke, Revoke grant option, and Grant back for a partial revoke. The statements are also shown as SHOW GRANTS, including user and role management scoped by name.
  • Inherited from roles: privileges of the roles granted to it, directly or through other roles, with the role path and, for a user, whether the role is active at login or needs SET ROLE.
  • Effective: computed by the server with SHOW GRANTS ... FINAL. For your own user, the console also lists the roles active in the console session.

Grants with the grant option and roles with the admin option are marked, because they allow delegation.

Granting a privilege

Grant privilege offers the privileges and groups of the server version (from system.privileges) and the scopes that apply to the chosen privilege:

ScopeStatement target
Everything (*.*)ON *.*
One databaseON db.*
One tableON db.table (a table, view, or dictionary)
Some columns of a table(col1, col2) ON db.table
Users or roles by nameON app_*, for user and role management

WITH GRANT OPTION lets the grantee pass the privilege on. The review warns when you grant a broad administrative privilege, such as ALL, ACCESS MANAGEMENT, ROLE ADMIN, CREATE USER, ALTER USER, SYSTEM, or INTROSPECTION, on everything.

Role templates

The role templates are proposals of the console, not built-in ClickHouse roles. None includes the grant option or unrestricted administrative rights. Each template has a suggested role name, which you can change; the console shows its exact privileges before creating a role, and the server refuses any privilege you do not hold WITH GRANT OPTION. In the table, <db> is the console database (console_admin by default).

TemplateSuggested namePrivileges
Platform Administratorconsole_platform_adminSELECT, INSERT on <db>.component_policy, <db>.protected_accounts, and <db>.audit_log; SHOW USERS, SHOW ROLES ON *.*. Changes the console access policy and the protected accounts, and reads the audit log; cannot manage users, roles, or data.
ClickHouse Access Administratorconsole_access_adminCREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER ON <pattern>; SHOW USERS, SHOW ROLES, SHOW SETTINGS PROFILES, SHOW QUOTAS ON *.*; SELECT, INSERT on the audit log and SELECT on the policy and the protected accounts; the chosen roles and, once the console is set up, console_admin_reader WITH ADMIN OPTION; optionally KILL QUERY ON *.*, to complete suspensions.
Database AdministratordbaOn each chosen database: SHOW, SELECT, INSERT, ALTER, CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, CREATE DICTIONARY, DROP TABLE, DROP VIEW, DROP DICTIONARY, TRUNCATE, OPTIMIZE, and SYSTEM MERGES, SYSTEM TTL MERGES, SYSTEM MOVES, SYSTEM FETCHES, SYSTEM REPLICATION QUEUES, SYSTEM SYNC REPLICA, SYSTEM RESTART REPLICA.
DeveloperdeveloperOn each chosen database: SHOW, SELECT, INSERT, ALTER TABLE, ALTER VIEW, CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, DROP TABLE, DROP VIEW, TRUNCATE, OPTIMIZE; CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE ON *.*.
AnalystanalystSHOW TABLES, SHOW COLUMNS, SELECT on each chosen database.
OperatoroperatorSELECT on system.dashboards, metric_log, asynchronous_metric_log, metrics, events, asynchronous_metrics, part_log, merges, mutations, replicas, parts, disks, clusters, tables, columns, dictionaries, jemalloc_stats, and documentation; optionally system.processes, query_log, and processors_profile_log (they contain the queries of all users), and INTROSPECTION for the Binary visualizer.
Backup Viewer, Backup Operator, Restore Operator, Backup Administratorbackup_viewer, backup_operator, restore_operator, backup_adminThe privileges of Backup & Restore; see Backup & Restore.
Cluster Viewer, Cluster Operator, Cluster Administratorcluster_viewer, cluster_operator, cluster_adminThe cluster tables and capabilities; see Clusters.
AuditorauditorSHOW USERS, SHOW ROLES, SHOW SETTINGS PROFILES, SHOW QUOTAS, SHOW ROW POLICIES ON *.*; SELECT on the three console tables, system.query_log, and system.session_log. Cannot change anything.

For the ClickHouse Access Administrator, the pattern * lets the role change any user, including administrators, and the review warns about it: prefer a prefix such as app_*. The role can only hand out the roles chosen in the template, so it cannot give anyone more than those roles contain.

Protected accounts and platform administrators

Protected accounts are users that the console does not delete or suspend, for example break-glass and service accounts. A protected user's page says so, with the reason, and the Suspend and Delete actions are disabled. You protect a user and remove the protection on the Component Access page. Users defined in configuration files cannot be changed with SQL at all, which makes them the most robust break-glass accounts.

Platform administrators are the users who can change the console access policy: INSERT on <db>.component_policy, directly, through roles, or through broader grants. The console estimates them from system.grants, lists them on the Component Access page, and refuses to:

  • delete or suspend the last platform administrator;
  • revoke the last role that makes someone a platform administrator;
  • delete such a role.

These safeguards are applied by the console only. A user with the privileges can still make the same changes with SQL directly. To recover when they were bypassed, see Recover access to the console.

Applying changes to a cluster

Changes apply to the server the console is connected to. When the server has clusters and its SQL-managed users are not in a replicated user directory, the Users, Roles & Permissions, Profiles & Quotas, and Data Access Policies pages offer Apply changes to: This server, followed by its host name, or ON CLUSTER with each cluster of system.clusters. Each statement then runs with ON CLUSTER and distributed_ddl_output_mode = 'never_throw', and the result shows every server with its outcome (Done, Failed, or Unfinished).

  • A server that does not answer within 30 seconds is shown as Unfinished: it executes the statement when it processes the distributed DDL queue.
  • A change that fails on some servers is reported as partially applied; it is not rolled back.
  • When users are stored in a replicated user directory, every change reaches all servers that share it through Keeper, and the console does not offer ON CLUSTER.

The console's own tables, such as the audit log and the protected accounts, are stored on the server the console is connected to and are not replicated.

Changes made outside of the console

The pages always read the current state from the server, so a change made with SQL or another tool is shown on the next load or Refresh. If a user or role was renamed or deleted meanwhile, its page says so. Access-management statements made outside of the console are listed on the Access changes seen by the server tab of Audit activity.

guides/component-access.title: Component Access
guides/component-access.description: How the Component Access page of the web console decides which components each user and role can open, how it relates to native ClickHouse privileges, and how to set it up.

headings.text: How the console applies the policy
Native privileges next to the policy

guides/component-access.html:
The Component Access page, in the Administration category, holds the console access policy: which console components (panels, links, administration pages, and identity provider pages) each user and role can open. Next to each rule it shows the native ClickHouse privileges that actually govern what the component can do, and it keeps the list of protected accounts and platform administrators.

The policy decides what the console lists and opens. It is not a security boundary on its own: the SQL Console, the standalone pages, and other clients reach the server directly, where only native privileges apply. This page explains the model, the setup, and what the policy does not cover. For the tables it uses, see the console tables reference.

The policy model

Subjects

A rule is written for one subject, chosen in Rules for:

  • All users: applies to everyone.
  • Role followed by a name: applies to the users who have that role enabled in their session.
  • User followed by a name: applies to that user.

A user gets the capabilities of the rules for all users, for the user, and for the roles enabled in the session, which at sign-in are the default roles. Rules only allow: a capability is allowed when any of these rules allows it. The Component access tab of a user shows the result both with the default roles and with every granted role, and marks capabilities that the user gets only after SET ROLE.

Components and capabilities

Each rule allows four capabilities of a component:

CapabilityWhat it meansWho enforces it
OpenThe component is listed on the home page and in the sidebar, and its address opens it.The console only.
View dataThe component can show the data it reads.Native privileges, listed next to the rule.
Run queriesThe component can run queries, for example the SQL Console or editable Dashboard charts.Native privileges.
AdministerThe component can change server state, for example SYSTEM JEMALLOC for Jemalloc.Native privileges.

The other capabilities need Open: ticking one of them also ticks Open, and clearing Open clears them. A box in the header of each column selects or clears that capability for every component it applies to, and shows whether all, some, or none of them have it.

The policy governs:

  • the panels of Workspace and Diagnostics, and the Reference panel;
  • the links of Resources: Source code, Documentation, Website, and Cloud;
  • the administration pages: Users, Roles & Permissions, Data Access Policies, Profiles & Quotas, Audit Activity, Clusters, and Backup & Restore;
  • the Identity Providers pages: LDAP and SSO (Keycloak).

For a link, an administration page, and an identity provider page, only Open applies (the other columns show —). What a user can do on such a page is decided by native privileges, as on every page: the page is listed only when the user can also read what it shows, and each action is a statement the server authorizes.

To give an administration or identity provider page to some roles only, clear Open for all users and tick it for those roles.

Components that are not governed

  • Home is not governed.
  • Component Access itself is not governed: it stays available to the users who can change the policy (INSERT on the policy table) or set it up, so that a policy mistake cannot lock them out of correcting it.
  • A component that no rule mentions yet, such as one added to the console after the policy was set up, is open to everyone. On the page it is marked No rules yet: open to everyone. Saving the rules for all users turns that into a rule.

How the console applies the policy

At sign-in, the console reads the policy and the roles enabled in the session. A governed component that the user may not open is not listed, and its address says that it is not allowed by the console policy. While the policy loads, panels wait; links to public sites stay usable and disappear if the policy hides them.

The policy has these states, shown on the page under Policy storage:

StateEffect
Not set upThe console shows every component to every user. Set up creates the tables.
No rulesThe table exists but is empty: the console shows every component to every user.
ActiveThe rules apply. Components without a rule that allows Open are hidden.
UnreadableThe table exists, but the user cannot read it. The console fails closed: it hides every governed component, and the home page asks for SELECT on the policy table.

The policy is stored on the server the console is connected to only. Other servers of a cluster have their own copy of these tables.

Native privileges next to the policy

The column Enforced outside the console by shows, for each component, what governs it on the server, for example:

ComponentNative privileges
DashboardView data: SELECT on system.dashboards, system.metric_log, system.asynchronous_metric_log.
Binary visualizerView data: INTROSPECTION.
Merges visualizerView data: SELECT ON system.part_log.
Schema visualizerView data: SELECT on system.tables, system.columns, system.dictionaries.
JemallocView data: SELECT on system.jemalloc_stats, system.asynchronous_metrics. Administer: SYSTEM JEMALLOC.
Processors profileView data: SELECT on system.processors_profile_log, system.query_log.
ReferenceView data: SELECT ON system.documentation.
SQL ConsoleEvery query is authorized by the grants on the tables it uses.

For ClickStack, the Web Terminal, the links, and the administration pages, the column explains instead why the policy only hides them in the console. ClickStack has its own connection settings and authorization. The Web Terminal runs clickhouse-client on the server as the signed-in user; the enable_webterminal server setting turns it on or off for everyone, and /webterminal stays reachable to anyone with valid credentials. Hiding a link only removes it from the console: anyone who knows the address of an external site can still visit it.

When Rules for is a role or a user, a Native privileges column also shows whether its grants (direct and through roles) give the privileges of each capability: granted, partly granted, or not granted. Where the policy and the grants disagree, it offers to make them agree:

  • The policy allows a capability, but the privileges are missing: Grant grants the missing privileges. You need them WITH GRANT OPTION.
  • The policy does not allow a capability, but the grants give it: the data is reachable outside of the console. Revoke direct grants revokes the grants made directly to the subject; privileges from broader grants or roles must be changed on the Permissions tab.

Setting up

The Users, Roles & Permissions, and Profiles & Quotas pages work without setup. The audit log, the component access policy, and the protected accounts need tables. On the Component Access page, select Set up. The dialog asks:

  • Keep audit records for (days): the retention of the audit log, 365 by default; a TTL removes older records.
  • Whether to assign the role console_admin_reader to the existing users and roles created with SQL, so that the console can apply the policy to them.

Review shows the statements, which:

  1. create the database named by the admin_database setting (by default console_admin);
  2. create the tables audit_log, component_policy, and protected_accounts;
  3. add the initial rules: all users can open every governed component, with View data and Run queries for the panels and no Administer, so nothing changes for users until you edit the policy;
  4. create the role console_admin_reader (named <admin_database>_reader) with SELECT on the policy table, and assign it if you chose so;
  5. record the setup in the audit log.

The setup needs CREATE TABLE on the database, and CREATE DATABASE if it does not exist. The statements use IF NOT EXISTS, so you can run the setup again after fixing an error. To set up without the console, run the statements shown in the review step with clickhouse-client.

The reader role

Users who cannot read the policy table do not see the components it governs. The role console_admin_reader gives them SELECT on it, and it must be among a user's default roles to apply at sign-in. Users defined in configuration files get this grant in those files.

When you create a user in the console, this role is preselected if you can grant it. A role is used instead of a direct grant because assigning a role needs only the admin option on it, while granting SELECT on the table would need it WITH GRANT OPTION. The ClickHouse Access Administrator role template includes it WITH ADMIN OPTION.

Editing rules

  1. Choose the subject in Rules for.
  2. Tick or clear the capabilities.
  3. Select Save rules, review the changes, and apply them.

Remove the rules of this subject removes every rule of a role or user. Changing the policy needs INSERT on the policy table; without it, the page is read-only. A change to your own rules warns that it changes what the console shows to you. Each change is recorded in the audit log.

Deleting a role keeps its rules in the table, but they no longer apply to anyone.

Protected accounts

The Protected accounts section lists the users that the console does not delete or suspend, with the reason and who protected them. Protect a user asks for the user and a reason; Remove protection removes it. Changing them needs INSERT on protected_accounts. This protection is applied by the console only: DROP USER run directly still works for anyone with the privilege. See Protected accounts and platform administrators.

Platform administrators

The Platform administrators section lists the users who can change the policy: INSERT on the policy table, directly, through roles, or through broader grants, estimated from system.grants. The console refuses to delete or suspend the last of them, or to revoke the last role that makes someone one. It cannot stop the same changes made with SQL directly. To recover, see Recover access to the console.

Limitations

  • The console enforces only Open. The other capabilities are enforced by native privileges on every access path.
  • The policy tables are local to one server. Other servers of a cluster have their own policy.
  • The tables are ordinary tables: users with ALTER, TRUNCATE, or DROP on them can change or remove rows. Grant only SELECT and INSERT on them.

guides/data-access-policies.title: Data Access Policies
guides/data-access-policies.description: How the Data Access Policies page of the web console controls which columns and rows each user can read, with native grants, row policies, and attribute-driven rules.
guides/data-access-policies.html:
The Data Access Policies page of the Administration category controls which columns and rows of tables each user can read, explains the effective access of a user, and provisions native controls from trusted user attributes. Everything it enforces is a native ClickHouse control: column grants and row policies, which the server applies to every client that reaches it, including the SQL Console, BI tools, drivers, the HTTP interface, and the native protocol. Hiding a component in the console is not data authorization: only the server controls on this page are (see Security model).

To try the page on a demo table, follow the tutorial Protect a table of salaries. To fill user attributes from an identity source, see Import user attributes.

Five mechanisms

The page keeps five mechanisms apart:

MechanismWhat it isEnforced byTabs
Column permissionsNative GRANT SELECT(column) ON db.tableThe server, for every queryColumn Permissions, Effective Access
Row policiesNative CREATE ROW POLICY ... USING <filter>The server, for every SELECTRow Policies, Effective Access
Attribute-driven provisioningRules on user attributes, translated into native roles, grants, and row policiesThe server, after a deployment or reconciliationAttributes & Classifications, Policy Rules, Policy Deployments
Dynamic, request-time ABACA decision per query from attributes of the request (purpose, device, time, network)Not providedRules on such attributes are refused
Column maskingReturning a transformed value instead of the stored oneNot provided: native masking policies are refused by this buildNot offered

Attribute-driven provisioning is not per-query ABAC: a change of an attribute takes effect when the rules are deployed or reconciled, not on the next query. The console does not present views as masking policies.

The page

The page has seven tabs: Column Permissions, Row Policies, Effective Access, Access Tests, Attributes & Classifications, Policy Rules, and Policy Deployments. The header has:

  • Apply changes to, shown when the server has clusters and no replicated user directory: This server or ON CLUSTER <cluster>. Statements of grants, row policies, and deployments run with this scope. With a replicated user directory, the header says that changes reach every server that shares it through Keeper.
  • Refresh, which reads the state from the server again.
  • Audit records, which opens Audit Activity filtered on dap_, when you can read the audit log.

The console shows the page to users who can read system.grants and system.role_grants. The first three tabs read only system tables and need no console table. Access Tests, Attributes & Classifications, Policy Rules, and Policy Deployments need the data access tables in the admin database: until they exist, these tabs show Set up Data Access Policies with a Set up button, which creates them with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS and changes no grant or policy. Set up needs CREATE TABLE on the admin database.

Each button is enabled by a privilege that the console checks with the server (CHECK GRANT); the server still authorizes every statement:

ActionNeeds
Read the tabs that use console tablesSELECT on every dap_* table
Define attributeINSERT on dap_attributes
Set value, Remove a valueINSERT on dap_user_attributes
Classify columnINSERT on dap_classifications
New rule, Edit, Enable, Disable, DeleteINSERT on dap_rules
Deploy, Verify, AdoptINSERT on dap_owned
Add test, Remove a testINSERT on dap_access_tests

The full list of privileges per page is in Privileges. Every change opens a review dialog that lists the steps and the statements; Apply runs them. The statements run as the signed-in user, so the server checks that user's own privileges, including the grant option for GRANT.

Column permissions

Column Permissions shows, for a table chosen with Database and Table, who can read each of its columns, from system.grants and system.role_grants:

  • Users and Roles: a matrix of users and roles against columns. ✓ marks a column grant, ● a grant on the whole table, the database, or every database, and parentheses, for example (✓), a grant through a role that is not a default role, active only after SET ROLE. A dash means no access. Hovering a mark shows its source and role path.
  • Broader grants: grants that give every column of the table, with the role path (Through), whether they also cover objects created later (Covers future objects), and whether they override column grants of the same user or role (Overrides column grants).
  • Direct column grants to users, with Revoke. Prefer granting columns to a role and the role to users.
  • Grants on columns that no longer exist, with Revoke: left behind by a renamed or dropped column. They give nothing today, but apply again to a new column of the same name.

Grant columns opens a dialog with To (a role, or a user for a direct grant) and the Columns to grant. It runs GRANT SELECT(<columns>) ON db.table TO <grantee>. The review warns when the grantee already reads every column through a broader grant, so that the grant changes nothing until that grant is revoked, and when SELECT * will fail for the grantee.

Column grants are positive: a narrow grant never cancels a grant on the whole table or a wider one, which still gives every column. To restrict a user to some columns, revoke the broader grant (or add a partial revoke), then grant the columns, preferably to a role. The behavior on this server version, also listed on the tab under How column grants behave:

  • SELECT of granted columns works; SELECT of any other column fails with ACCESS_DENIED.
  • SELECT * fails unless every column of the table is granted: it does not return only the granted columns.
  • A filter, ORDER BY, or join on a column that is not granted fails too, so its values cannot be probed through WHERE.
  • count() works with a grant on any one column, so the number of rows is visible.
  • A column added later is not covered by existing column grants; table, database, and global grants cover it, and tables created later too.
  • A renamed column keeps its grants only under the old name.

See undefined for the syntax.

Row policies

A row policy is a read filter that the server adds to every SELECT of the table by the users it applies to, from any client. Permissive policies are joined with OR, restrictive ones with AND; policies on a whole database (ON db.*) combine with those of the table. A row policy does not restrict INSERT, ALTER UPDATE, or ALTER DELETE, nor reads through views that run as their definer.

The Row policies box lists every row policy of the server from system.row_policies, with Policy and its source, On, Kind (Permissive (OR) or Restrictive (AND)), Filter, and Applies to. Policies stored with SQL have Edit and Remove; policies from configuration files are read-only.

Create row policy opens a dialog with:

FieldMeaning
NameThe short name of the policy.
Database, TableThe table. Every table of the database (ON db.*) creates the policy on db.* instead.
KindPermissive: joined with OR with other permissive policies, or Restrictive: joined with AND.
Applies toThese users and roles (chosen below), All users, or All users except (chosen below).
FilterConditions (joined with AND), or Expression (advanced).

A condition has a Column, a Condition (=, ≠, is one of, is none of, or = the user name (currentUser())), and Values, separated by commas. Values are quoted for the type of the column. Add condition adds a condition; for columns named like branch, company, tenant, tenant_id, region, country, or department, a preset button (for example + department) adds a condition on that column.

An expression can be typed only by administrators who can create and alter row policies on every table (CREATE ROW POLICY, ALTER ROW POLICY ON *.*). It is checked with the server's parser (EXPLAIN AST, EXPLAIN QUERY TREE) and refused when it contains subqueries, table functions, or references to other tables.

The dialog writes CREATE ROW POLICY <name> ON db.table USING <filter> AS permissive|restrictive TO <targets>, or ALTER ROW POLICY for an edit. The review lists the affected users with their combined filter before and after the change. Removing a policy runs DROP ROW POLICY: the users it applied to see the rows it allowed no more, or, when it was their only policy, every row of the table.

Effect on a table

Effect on a table shows, for a chosen table, each user who can read it or to whom a policy applies, with the roles the user has at login (default roles):

ColumnMeaning
Can read the tableYes, or No SELECT when a policy applies but the user has no SELECT on the table.
Rows visibleAll rows (no row policy exists on the table), All rows: no policy applies (policies exist, but none applies to the user), No rows, or Filtered.
Combined filterThe permissive policies joined with OR, and the restrictive ones with AND.
From policiesThe policies that make up the filter.

The combined filter assumes the server default access_control_improvements.users_without_row_policies_can_read_rows = true, under which a user to whom no policy of the table applies reads every row. SQL cannot read this setting: confirm it with an access test.

Below the users, the box lists:

  • Paths that can undermine the filter (bypass paths): views that run as their definer (SQL SECURITY DEFINER or NONE), materialized views, and Distributed, Merge, and Buffer tables whose definition names the table. A match by name is a candidate for review, not a proof.
  • Users who can change rows: users with INSERT, ALTER UPDATE, ALTER DELETE, or wider grants, who can write rows outside their filter.

Row policies on a cluster

Row policies are evaluated by the server that reads the table. Create them ON CLUSTER (choose the cluster in Apply changes to) or in a replicated user directory, so that every shard has them, and configure an interserver <secret> for the cluster so that the shards know the initial user. Shards apply their own row policies for the connecting user and those of the initial user, if a user of that name exists on the shard. Column grants are checked on the Distributed table, not on the shard's table.

Effective access

Effective Access explains, for a User, a Database and Table, and an Operation (Read (SELECT) or Write (INSERT)), what the user can do and why:

  • Identity: the user, its source (SQL, configuration, LDAP), state, and default roles.
  • Roles: the roles granted to the user with their paths, whether each is active at login (Active) or only after SET ROLE (After SET ROLE), and their source.
  • Per column: At login (configured), With all granted roles, and Given by, the grant that gives the column, directly or through which role path.
  • Rows: the row filter at login and with all granted roles, and the policies with their sources.
  • Conflicts: column grants made ineffective by a broader grant, several permissive policies, a filter that changes with SET ROLE, and column clearance rules whose intent other grants contradict.
  • Verification: Verify with the server, and the recent access tests of the user.

The tab shows the state of the server the console is connected to only. Other servers keep their own users, grants, and policies unless the user directory is replicated.

Verification with the server

Inspecting grants is not a proof. The page distinguishes the configured entitlement (what the grants say), the access in the default-role context (At login), the result verified by the server, and what is unknown.

Verify with the server asks the server as the user, with EXECUTE AS:

  • EXECUTE AS <user> CHECK GRANT <operation>(<column>) ON db.table for every column: Allowed or Denied, marked "Verified at runtime";
  • for SELECT, EXECUTE AS <user> SELECT count() FROM db.table: the number of rows visible with the user's grants, default roles, and row policies.

EXECUTE AS needs the server setting allow_impersonate_user (enabled in the default config.xml of this build) and IMPERSONATE ON <user> granted to the signed-in user. Grant IMPERSONATE only on dedicated test users: it lets the grantee act as that user. Without it the result is Unknown, with the server's message.

Access tests

Access Tests stores approved positive and negative tests in dap_access_tests. Add test opens a dialog with:

FieldMeaning
NameA name for the test.
As userThe user who reads. Use a dedicated synthetic user: running the test needs IMPERSONATE on it.
Database, TableThe table to read.
ColumnsComma-separated columns. Empty: count the rows only.
ExpectedAllowed, or Denied (ACCESS_DENIED).
Expected rowsFor an allowed read, the number of rows the user must see. Empty: any.

Run runs one test and Run all runs every test. A run reads the table as the user, with EXECUTE AS <user> SELECT count() FROM (SELECT <columns> FROM db.table), so the server applies that user's grants, default roles, and row policies as for a direct connection. The outcome is:

  • Pass: the read was allowed with the expected number of rows (or any number), or denied with ACCESS_DENIED when Denied was expected;
  • Fail: the read was allowed when it should be denied, returned another number of rows, or was denied when it should be allowed;
  • Error: any other error, including a missing IMPERSONATE grant. An error is never a pass.

A run records the outcome and the number of rows in dap_test_runs, never the data. Runs are kept for 365 days. The browser acceptance checks (utils/web-console/data_access_e2e.mjs) repeat the checks over HTTP and with the native client, as the synthetic users themselves.

Attributes and classifications

Attributes & Classifications holds the inputs of the policy rules: attribute definitions, attribute values of users, and labels of columns.

Attribute definitions

Define attribute opens the dialog Define an attribute:

FieldMeaning
AttributeThe name: letters, digits, and underscores, for example department.
CategoryUser, Resource, Operation, or Environment. Only user attributes select users in rules.
Evaluated per requestThe value changes per query (purpose, device, time, network). Native controls cannot follow it, so rules on it are refused.
Source of truthThe name of the source that reports the values, for example hr-feed or ldap. A value counts only when its source is this one.
WriterThe database user whose writes are trusted, typically the account of the identity import. Empty: any administrator who can write values.
OwnerWho is responsible for the attribute.
Fresh for (seconds)How long a value stays fresh after it was last confirmed. Default 86400; 0: never stale.
DescriptionFree text.

The Attributes table shows each definition, with a Per request badge for attributes evaluated per request, and Fresh for: Always for 0.

Attribute values

User attribute values lists the values of dap_user_attributes with their user, source and writer, the time they were last confirmed, and a Status:

  • Fresh: the value is trusted.
  • Not trusted: the attribute is not defined; the value was reported by another source than the definition's; it was written by another user than the definition's writer; or it is older than the freshness limit. Hovering the badge shows the reason. A value that is not trusted is treated as missing.

The server records who wrote each value (updated_by, MATERIALIZED currentUser()), so the writer of a value cannot be forged with the value. ClickHouse does not read identity provider claims itself: values reach it only through this table, and nothing a browser sends is taken as evidence.

Set value sets a value of a user attribute whose writer is you or empty (any administrator); attributes written by an import are set by the import (see Import user attributes). Remove marks a value deleted: rules that need the attribute treat the user as missing it at the next deployment. Rules use a new or removed value at the next deployment or reconciliation, not immediately.

The reserved user attribute employment_status disables an identity for every rule when its fresh value is disabled, suspended, terminated, or inactive.

Data classifications

Data classifications labels columns (for example pii, financial, or secret) with their source and owner. Classify column opens a dialog with Database, Table, Column, Label (letters, digits, dashes, and underscores), Source (default console), and Owner. A label does not hide a column by itself: column clearance rules give access to the columns of a label through a generated role, and a change of the labels changes the grants of that role at the next deployment.

Policy rules

Policy Rules lists the rules with their kind, revision, author, a Business rule in plain words, and a Status: the number of users the rule matches (hover for the number excluded), Disabled, Deleted, or Not representable with the reason. Each rule has Explain, Edit, Disable or Enable, and Delete.

New rule opens the dialog New policy rule:

FieldMeaning
NameThe name of the rule.
KindGrant a role, Filter rows by an attribute, or Columns of a label need a clearance.
UsersThe selector: one condition per line, attribute = value, value. All conditions must hold; a condition holds when the user's value is one of the listed values.
RoleFor Grant a role: an existing role. The rule grants it; it never changes the role's privileges.
Database, Table, Column, AttributeFor Filter rows by an attribute: each user reads the rows whose column equals the user's value of the attribute.
Label, Clearance attribute, Values that clearFor Columns of a label need a clearance: users whose clearance attribute has one of the values read the columns of the label.
Missing or stale attributeRevoke what the rule gave (fail closed) (default), or Keep what was provisioned until the value is fresh again.
ExceptionsComma-separated users the rule never provisions.
EnabledWhether deployments include the rule.

The review shows how the rule resolves now: the users matched, the users excluded, and the number of generated controls. Saving a rule changes nothing on the server: the rules take effect when they are deployed or reconciled by the access policy worker.

Generated native controls

Each kind translates into native controls. <rule> is the first 8 hexadecimal digits of the rule ID, and <value hash> a stable hash of an attribute value:

KindExampleGenerated native controls
Grant a roleAnalysts in department Finance get the role finance_reportsGRANT finance_reports TO <user> per matched user
Filter rows by an attributeBranch staff read only the rows of their branchOne permissive row policy per value, dap_<rule>_<value hash>, USING branch = '<value>' TO <users>; and dap_<rule>_none, USING 0, for users in scope without a trusted value and for disabled identities
Columns of a label need a clearanceUsers without clearance secret cannot read columns labeled secretA role dap_<rule>_cleared with SELECT(<column>) on every column of the label, granted to the cleared users

Who a rule selects

For each user of the server, a rule decides:

  • A user whose fresh employment_status disables the identity is excluded, but stays in scope: a row filter rule gives it the policy that shows no row.
  • A user listed in Exceptions gets nothing from the rule, not even the policy that shows no row.
  • A user who has none of the selector's attributes, or whose fresh values do not satisfy the selector, is not in scope.
  • A user in scope whose attribute is missing or not trusted is excluded. With Revoke, what the rule gave is removed, and a row filter rule gives the user the policy that shows no row, because without any policy the user would read every row. With Keep, what was provisioned from the last known value stays until the value is fresh again; nothing new is provisioned from a stale value, and a missing value is not held.
  • Every other user in scope is matched.

Warning

A rule with an empty Users selector has every user of the server in scope. For a row filter rule, every user without a trusted value of the attribute, including administrators and service accounts, gets the policy dap_<rule>_none and reads no row of the table. Select the users with a condition, for example department = Finance, Sales.

Rules add access

Rules only add access. A rule never removes a grant made outside the platform, so this is not deny-overrides: a user who lacks a clearance still reads the classified columns through a broader grant. Effective Access and Verify report such conflicts.

A rule is refused, not approximated with a permanent grant, when it uses an attribute that is not defined, an attribute evaluated per request, or an attribute that is not a user attribute, or when a field of its kind is missing. Such a rule is shown as Not representable and contributes nothing to deployments.

Revisions and explanation

Every change of a rule, including Enable, Disable, and Delete, is a new revision in dap_rules with its author, recorded by the server (created_by). The author of the current revision matters: the access policy worker applies the rule with that user's privileges.

Explain shows the business rule, the resolved attributes of each matched user, the excluded users with the reason and the effect (Keeps what was provisioned, Sees no row (fail closed), or Gets nothing from this rule), the generated controls with their state on this server (Deployed, Exists, not owned, or Not deployed), and the last deployment with its scope and verification.

Policy deployments

Policy Deployments computes the difference between the desired state of every enabled rule and the server, and shows it before anything changes. The Deploy the rules box shows when the state was observed, the scope (this server, or ON CLUSTER <cluster> from Apply changes to), and the number of enabled and not representable rules, then:

  • Planned changes: the steps, in order (roles, grants, role grants, row policies, then removals in reverse order), or "None: the server matches the rules."
  • Deploy: reviews and runs the steps.
  • Verify: checks the result (see Verification of a deployment).
  • Left alone: entities that exist but were not created by the platform, with Adopt for generated names, and role grants that a user already has from elsewhere.
  • Removed outside the platform: owned entities that no longer exist.
  • Rules not deployed: rules that are not representable, with the reason.
  • Readers outside the rules: users who can read a table filtered by a rule, are not in the rule's scope, and have no other policy on it, so they see every row.
  • Disabled identities: users whose employment_status disables them.

The generated statements are idempotent: CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS, CREATE ROW POLICY OR REPLACE, DROP ROLE IF EXISTS, DROP ROW POLICY IF EXISTS, GRANT, and REVOKE, with ON CLUSTER for a cluster scope. Deploying again repairs a partial deployment. With a cluster scope, the result shows each server, and a server that did not answer within 30 seconds is shown as unfinished.

History lists the deployments, reconciliations by the worker, verifications, and adoptions of dap_deployments, with the time, kind, author, scope, result, rules with their revisions, and the steps and verification in Steps and verification.

Ownership

Only entities the platform owns, recorded by stable key in dap_owned, are changed or removed:

  • An entity that exists but was not created by the platform is left alone and listed. Remove or rename it, or Adopt it to record it as owned, so that the platform changes or removes it as the rules require.
  • A role that a rule grants and that a user already has from a grant made outside the platform is reported and kept when the rule stops applying.
  • An owned entity that was removed outside the platform is reported and not restored, unless Restore entities that were removed outside the platform is chosen. To revoke an entitlement on purpose, add an exception to the rule instead.
  • An owned entity that no rule wants any more is removed; one that no longer exists is forgotten.

Only steps that took effect become owned: the ownership records are written after the statements, from the outcome of each step.

Verification of a deployment

Verify checks, on the server the console is connected to, that every generated control is present; for role and clearance rules, that no user known to the identity sources keeps the access through another grant; and, when you can read system.processes, which affected users still have running queries. It is recorded in dap_deployments as a verify entry. A revocation is reported complete only when these checks pass; other servers of a cluster are covered by the per-server results of the deployment.

Access policy worker

utils/web-console/access_policy_worker.mjs keeps the server in line with the rules when nobody has the console open. Each cycle it imports the attribute feed (when configured), computes the desired state with the same functions as the console, which it loads from console.html, applies the difference, and records ownership, the deployment (kind reconcile), and an audit record (action dap_reconcile). It runs in the tools image as access-policy-worker, or directly with Node.js 18 or later:

bash
CLICKHOUSE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8123 CLICKHOUSE_USER=access_policy_worker CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=... \
    ATTRIBUTE_FEED=/var/lib/clickhouse-console/hr-feed.json ATTRIBUTE_FEED_SOURCE=hr INTERVAL_SECONDS=60 \
    node utils/web-console/access_policy_worker.mjs

--once runs one cycle and exits. The environment variables are listed in Helper processes.

The worker is not an escalation path: it holds no privilege to grant anything. Each statement runs as EXECUTE AS <author>, the user who wrote the current revision of the rule, so the server checks that user's own privileges, including the grant option and CLUSTER for ON CLUSTER. Its account needs:

sql
GRANT SELECT ON console_admin.* TO access_policy_worker;
GRANT INSERT ON console_admin.dap_owned TO access_policy_worker;
GRANT INSERT ON console_admin.dap_deployments TO access_policy_worker;
GRANT INSERT ON console_admin.audit_log TO access_policy_worker;
GRANT INSERT ON console_admin.dap_user_attributes TO access_policy_worker;  -- only with an attribute feed
GRANT SELECT ON system.users TO access_policy_worker;
GRANT SELECT ON system.roles TO access_policy_worker;
GRANT SELECT ON system.role_grants TO access_policy_worker;
GRANT SELECT ON system.grants TO access_policy_worker;
GRANT SELECT ON system.row_policies TO access_policy_worker;
GRANT SHOW USERS, SHOW ROLES, SHOW ROW POLICIES ON *.* TO access_policy_worker;
GRANT IMPERSONATE ON <each rule author> TO access_policy_worker;

deploy/service-accounts.sql creates this account (see Create service accounts). Replace console_admin if the admin database has another name.

Like Policy Deployments, the worker changes only owned entities, and never restores an owned entity that was removed outside the platform: that needs a deployment with Restore entities that were removed outside the platform. A rule whose author is unknown fails its steps: there is no user to act as.

Revocation latency

An attribute change reaches the server within one interval after it is written or the feed reports it (INTERVAL_SECONDS, 60 seconds by default), plus the delay of the feed itself. Without the worker, it reaches the server at the next Deploy. Grants and row policies are checked when a query starts: a running query finishes with the access it started with, and new queries of open sessions use the new access.

Identity source outage

When the feed cannot be read, nothing is written and the values age. Until they pass the freshness limit of their attribute, the access already provisioned stays active. After that, each rule applies its setting: Revoke removes the access (row filters show no row), Keep holds what was provisioned. Set the freshness limit to the longest outage you accept.

Disabled identities

A ClickHouse user authenticates with its own credentials, not with the identity provider. Disabling the identity (employment_status) removes what rules gave and makes row filter rules show no row, but the user can still sign in and use grants made outside the platform until the account is suspended on the Users page (see Suspending a user) or dropped.

Verified behavior

These are the behaviors of the server version the page was built for, checked on it with synthetic users and data. Confirm them on another release with access tests.

RequirementExisting capabilityEnforcement pointAdded by the consoleVersion limitation
Read only some columnsGRANT SELECT(col, ...)Query analysis on the server that runs the queryColumn matrix, grant and revoke with review, broader-grant detectionSELECT * fails unless every column is granted; count() works with any column grant
Read only some rowsCREATE ROW POLICY ... AS permissive / restrictive on a table or db.*Every SELECT on the server that reads the tableStructured filter editor, combined filter per user, bypass pathsFilters reads only; not INSERT, ALTER UPDATE, or ALTER DELETE
Users without a matching policyaccess_control_improvements.users_without_row_policies_can_read_rows (default true)Server configurationFlagged per user as All rows: no policy appliesThe setting cannot be read with SQL: the console assumes the default
Explain effective accesssystem.grants, system.role_grants, system.row_policies, SHOW GRANTS ... FINAL—Role paths, default and activatable roles, conflicts, sourcesShows one server; sessions of other users are not observable
Verify access at runtimeEXECUTE AS <user> with IMPERSONATE ON <user>The server, with the target user's grants, default roles, and row policiesVerify with the server, access testsNeeds allow_impersonate_user and IMPERSONATE per target user
Distributed readsShards apply their own row policies for the connecting user and those of the initial user, if a user of that name exists on the shardEach shardDistributed tables listed as bypass pathsColumn grants are checked on the Distributed table, not on the shard's table
Reads through viewsSQL SECURITY DEFINER and NONE views read as their definerThe viewListed as bypass pathsRow policies of the reader on the base table do not apply inside the view; currentUser() inside still returns the reader
MaskingCREATE MASKING POLICY—Not offeredRefused: "Masking Policies are available only in ClickHouse Cloud"

Dynamic access and masking

Request-time ABAC and column masking need an enforcement boundary that sees every query. Findings on this server version:

  • Native masking is refused in this build (SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED: "Masking Policies are available only in ClickHouse Cloud"). The statement is parsed, so its syntax is no evidence of support. While checking it, CREATE MASKING POLICY ... TO NONE raised a logical error (inconsistent AST formatting of TO NONE): an exception in a release build.
  • Controlled views with SQL SECURITY DEFINER read the base table as the definer while currentUser() returns the reader, so a view can decide per user, for example if(currentUser() IN (SELECT user_name FROM <entitled users>), ssn, concat('***-', right(ssn, 2))). Checked on synthetic data: the entitled reader gets the value and the others the mask; a filter on the real value through the view matches nothing, because filters, joins, grouping, and ordering operate on the masked value; but whatever the mask leaves visible can be probed (LIKE '***-1%' matched), and the base table's row policies do not apply inside the view (the reader saw 2 rows instead of 1), so they must be repeated in the view. Such a view is safe only when the readers have no grant on the base table, and no other path (another view, a Distributed or Merge table, a dictionary, a materialized view, remote with other credentials) reaches it. Hashing is not anonymization: a hash of a low-entropy value, such as a national identifier, is reversed by enumerating the values.
  • A query gateway enforces only if no client can reach the server directly; ClickHouse has no mechanism that confines users to a gateway except network rules and the users' allowed hosts. Rewriting SQL needs the server's parser, not regular expressions.
  • An engine enhancement (planner-level masking and request attributes) is the only option that covers every protocol and distributed execution; it is upstream work.

Keep authorization in native controls: column grants, row policies, and attribute-driven provisioning. For masking, use controlled definer views only for named tables whose base-table access is revoked for all readers, and verify the absence of other paths with Paths that can undermine the filter on Row Policies and with access tests. The console does not provide request-time ABAC or masking, and nothing on the page is presented as such.

Performance

A row policy adds its filter to every query of the users it applies to, as if they had written it: on 50 million rows, sum(v) took 0.15 s with a policy branch = 'north' against 0.17 s with the same WHERE written by hand (median of 5 runs, on the development server). A policy disables the answer of count() from the table's metadata: count() took 0.10 s with the policy against 0.01 s without. Index the columns used in filters (the primary key or a skip index) on large tables.

Console tables and audit

The page keeps attribute definitions (dap_attributes), attribute values (dap_user_attributes), classifications (dap_classifications), rule revisions (dap_rules), ownership (dap_owned), deployments (dap_deployments), access tests (dap_access_tests), and test runs (dap_test_runs) in the admin database. Their columns are in Console tables. As for the other console tables, the writer and time of each row are filled in by the server. Grant SELECT on them to the readers of the page, INSERT on the tables of each task to its administrators, and keep ALTER and DROP to the server administrators.

Administrative changes are recorded in the console audit log with actions dap_*: search for dap_ on Audit Activity. Query-time decisions are kept apart: Audit Activity → Access decisions shows reads the server refused (ACCESS_DENIED in system.query_log, with the literals of queries replaced by ?) and the runs of access tests.

Runbooks

  • A user reads columns it should not. Open Effective Access for the user and table: Given by names the grant and role path. Revoke the broader grant; a column grant does not narrow it.
  • A user sees every row. Row Policies → Effect on a table shows All rows: no policy applies: add the user (or a role it has at login) to a policy, or to the scope of a rule.
  • A user sees no row. Effective Access → Rows names the policies. A dap_<rule>_none policy means the user is in the scope of a row filter rule without a trusted value: check Status of the value on Attributes & Classifications, and the selector of the rule.
  • A deployment is partly applied. History shows the failed step and the servers. Fix the cause (often the author's missing grant option or CLUSTER privilege), then deploy again: the statements are idempotent.
  • An entity is reported as existing but not owned. Remove or rename it, or Adopt it to let the platform manage it.
  • Revocation is not complete. Verify lists the other grants that still give the access, and running queries. Revoke the other grants, or suspend the user.
  • The worker reports a failure. The audit record names the step and the server's message; the worker acts as the rule author, so the author needs the privileges for every generated statement, and the worker needs IMPERSONATE on the author.
  • To migrate or recover, back up the admin database with the other console tables. The native entities (roles, grants, row policies) are backed up with the access entities of the server (see Backup and restore). After a restore, run Verify: drift between dap_owned and the server is reported, not silently repaired.

guides/profiles-and-quotas.title: Profiles and quotas
guides/profiles-and-quotas.description: How the Profiles & Quotas page of the web console manages settings profiles, setting constraints, and quotas, and where they apply.
guides/profiles-and-quotas.html:
The Profiles & Quotas page, in the Administration category, manages the resource limits of the server: settings profiles, with their settings and constraints, and quotas, with their intervals and limits. Its two tabs are Settings profiles and Quotas.

Resource limits do not replace privileges: a user with a strict quota can still read every table it has SELECT on. Each change is a CREATE, ALTER, or DROP statement for a SETTINGS PROFILE or QUOTA, reviewed and run like every change of the administration pages (see Users and roles). When the server has clusters, Apply changes to runs the statements ON CLUSTER (see Applying changes to a cluster).

The page is listed for users who can read system.settings_profiles and system.settings_profile_elements, or system.quotas and system.quota_limits. Creating, changing, and deleting need CREATE, ALTER, and DROP SETTINGS PROFILE or QUOTA. Profiles and quotas defined in configuration files are marked Read only.

Settings profiles

A settings profile is a named set of settings and constraints. Users and roles get profiles assigned, and a profile can inherit other profiles. Changes apply to new sessions; sessions that are already open keep their settings.

The list shows each profile with its source, its settings, and what it is assigned to (users and roles, or all users with exceptions). The actions are Edit, Assign, and Delete.

Creating and editing a profile

Create profile opens a form with one row per setting:

FieldMeaning
SettingThe name of a setting of the server, with suggestions from system.settings.
ValueThe value. Integer settings accept byte units, such as 10GiB.
Minimum, MaximumConstraints: users cannot set the setting outside of them.
UsersUser can change, Cannot be changed (fixes the value), or Changeable in readonly.

Add setting adds a row, and Inherit profiles chooses profiles to inherit. The form validates each value with the type of the setting, and the server validates it again. Saving an existing profile replaces all of its settings.

For the common resource limits, the form explains what each setting limits:

SettingLimits
max_execution_timeSeconds a query may run.
max_memory_usageMemory of one query on one server, in bytes.
max_memory_usage_for_userMemory of all running queries of the user on one server, in bytes.
max_threadsThreads of one query.
max_concurrent_queries_for_userQueries of the user running at the same time on one server.
max_result_rows, max_result_bytesRows or bytes in the result of one query.
max_rows_to_read, max_bytes_to_readRows or bytes one query may read.
max_query_sizeBytes of the query text.
readonly1: only reading queries, and settings cannot be changed; 2: reading queries, and settings can be changed.

For every setting, see the settings reference.

Assigning a profile

Assign on a profile, or Assign profile on the Profiles & quotas tab of a user or role, adds the profile with ALTER USER ... ADD PROFILES or ALTER ROLE ... ADD PROFILES. The other settings and profiles of the user or role stay. Only users and roles that can be changed with SQL are offered.

The Profiles & quotas tab of a user or role shows the settings and profiles that apply to it, with where each comes from (the user or role itself, or a role it has), and Remove for a profile assigned to it directly. Without any setting or profile, the server default profile (default_profile in the server configuration) applies.

Quotas

A quota counts usage per key (by default per user) over time intervals, and rejects queries once a limit is reached, until the interval ends. Each server counts separately. Queries that read no table, such as SELECT 1, are not counted.

The list shows each quota with its source, its key, its limits per interval, and what it applies to, with Edit and Delete. Deleting a quota stops its limits from applying immediately.

Creating and editing a quota

Create quota asks for:

FieldMeaning
NameThe name of the quota. It cannot be changed later.
Count usage perUser name, Client IP address, Forwarded IP address, Client key, Client key, else user name, Client key, else IP address, or Not keyed (one shared counter).
Every, UnitThe length of an interval: a number of seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, quarters, or years. Randomized start randomizes the start of the interval. Add interval adds another interval.
Limitsqueries, query selects, query inserts, errors, result rows, result bytes, read rows, read bytes, execution time (in seconds), written bytes, and failed sequential authentications. An empty limit is not limited; an interval without limits only tracks usage. Byte limits accept units such as 10GiB.
Applies toThe selected users and roles, All users, All users except the selected, or Nobody yet.

When you edit a quota, intervals you remove are removed from the quota, and the usage counted so far is kept for intervals that stay.

The Profiles & quotas tab of a user or role lists the quotas that apply to it, directly or through its roles.

Limitations

  • Settings and profile changes apply to new sessions only.
  • Quotas count per server: on a cluster, each server has its own counters.
  • Quotas do not count queries that read no table.

guides/audit-activity.title: Audit activity
guides/audit-activity.description: What the Audit Activity page of the web console shows: the console audit log, the access-management statements the server logged, and query-time access decisions.

headings.text: Access changes seen by the server
What is recorded, and what never is

guides/audit-activity.html:
The Audit Activity page, in the Administration category, shows who changed access, when, where, and with what result. It has three tabs, each with its own source:

TabSourceCovers
Console actionsThe console audit log, console_admin.audit_log.Changes made in the console and by its helper processes.
Access changes seen by the serversystem.query_log of the connected server.Access-management statements, including those made outside of the console.
Access decisionssystem.query_log, and the access test runs of Data Access Policies.Queries the server refused, and access test results.

The page is listed for users who can read the audit log or system.query_log. It opens on Console actions when you can read the audit log, and on Access changes seen by the server otherwise. The Audit activity tab of a user shows the console records whose target is that user, and the server statements of the last 30 days that contain its name (see Users and roles).

The pages always read the current state from the server, so a change made outside of the console is shown on the next load or Refresh.

Filters

Each tab has:

  • Search: on Console actions, the actor, target, action, summary, or correlation ID; on the other tabs, the user or the text of the statement.
  • Period: Last day, Last 7 days, Last 30 days, or Last year. The default is 30 days for Console actions and 7 days for the other tabs.
  • Result, on Console actions only: Any result, Success, Partly applied, or Failed.

Each tab shows at most 500 records, the newest first. Times are in UTC.

Console actions

After each change, the console writes a record to the audit log, which you set up on the Component Access page. Each record has:

FieldContent
Time (UTC)When the record was written.
ActorThe user who made the change.
ActionThe summary, the target type and name, and the action, for example user alice · suspend_user.
ResultSuccess, Failed, or Partly applied.
WhereThe server, and the scope: this server, or ON CLUSTER with the cluster name.
DetailsThe correlation ID, a sanitized error, the steps with the outcome of each (and of each server for ON CLUSTER), and details of the action, such as the expiry dates a suspension overwrote or the dependencies of a deleted user.

The actor, the time, and the server are filled in by the server (MATERIALIZED currentUser(), now64(), and hostName()), and CHECK constraints reject other values, so a user who can insert into the log cannot write records in another user's name.

Each change has a correlation ID, which the console also sets as the log_comment of its statements, as console-admin:<id>. The result of a change in the console shows it. Use it to find the statements of a change on the server tab.

The helper processes of the console write to the same log with their own service account as the actor: for example, the user sync of the token authenticator records sso_create_user, sso_grant_roles, sso_revoke_roles, and sso_drop_user (see Helper processes).

A change is not recorded in the audit log when the log is not set up or the user cannot write to it (INSERT on it). The review dialog says so before the change, and the result gives the correlation ID, so that the statements can still be found in system.query_log. If the change succeeds but its record cannot be written, the result says so.

Access changes seen by the server

This tab lists the CREATE, ALTER, and DROP statements for users, roles, settings profiles, quotas, row policies, and masking policies, and GRANT, REVOKE, and SET DEFAULT ROLE, from system.query_log of the server the console is connected to, including rejected attempts. Each row shows the time, the user, the statement, and the outcome: Done, or Failed with the error code and message.

The Origin column marks statements with a console correlation ID as Console, and all others as Outside the console (run with SQL directly, or by another tool). Statements of the access policy worker run as EXECUTE AS <rule author> and appear here.

This tab does not cover:

  • other servers of a cluster: each has its own log;
  • users or sessions with log_queries disabled;
  • changes to configuration files;
  • statements older than the query_log retention.

The server flushes the log every few seconds, so the newest statements can be missing.

Access decisions

This tab shows query-time authorization decisions, apart from administrative changes:

  • reads the server refused with ACCESS_DENIED, from system.query_log, with the literals of the queries replaced by ? so that values typed in a query are not shown, and the privilege that was missing;
  • the runs of access tests of Data Access Policies, with their result.

It is readable by users with SELECT on system.query_log and on the access test runs. Refused queries are kept as long as the query_log retention, and test runs for 365 days.

What is recorded, and what never is

The console never writes passwords, password hashes, or tokens to the audit log, to error messages, or to browser storage:

  • Passwords are sent to the server only in the statement that sets them. The review dialog and the audit details replace them with [HIDDEN], as well as any literal after BY, HASH, SALT, or PASSWORD in an error message.
  • The server stores a hash and masks the password in system.query_log and its logs, so the server tab shows the statement without it.
  • With single sign-on, the access token is kept in the memory of the browser tab only. The connection test of an identity provider checks the tokens and then drops them; they are never stored.

The audit log is an ordinary table on the server the console is connected to, and it is not replicated. Users with ALTER, TRUNCATE, or DROP on it can change or remove records, so it is not tamper-proof: grant only SELECT and INSERT on it, and keep ALTER and DROP to the server administrators.

Retention

Records older than the retention chosen at setup (365 days by default) are removed by a TTL. To change the retention later, run:

sql
ALTER TABLE console_admin.audit_log MODIFY TTL toDateTime(event_time) + INTERVAL 730 DAY

To keep the records before removing the console data, back up the database, for example with BACKUP DATABASE console_admin TO Disk('backups', 'console_admin.zip') on a server with a backups disk configured (see Backup and restore).

guides/backup-and-restore.title: Backup & Restore
guides/backup-and-restore.description: How the Backup & Restore page of the ClickHouse web console works: destinations, backups, restores, schedules, retention, restore tests, server bundles, the backup worker, and privileges.
guides/backup-and-restore.html:
The Backup & Restore page of the Administration category runs the native BACKUP and RESTORE statements of ClickHouse (see Backup and restore). It does not copy data itself. It adds what the statements lack: a list of approved destinations, a durable record of every operation, schedules, retention that keeps incremental chains intact, restores that never touch existing data, restore tests, and encrypted backups of the server state that BACKUP cannot reach.

The console only records requests and submits statements. What a browser cannot do, such as running schedules, deleting backups, and reading files on the server host, is done by the backup worker, a process next to the server.

For a guided first run, see the backup tutorial. For the exact columns of the tables the page uses, see Backup tables.

Tabs

TabWhat it shows
OverviewOperations of the last 7 days (total, failed or unknown, running), available backups and how many passed a restore test, the last heartbeat of the backup worker (Scheduler worker), the Resilience (3-2-1-1) check, recent failures, schedules, and destinations.
BackupsThe inventory: one row per backup with its scope, type and base, destination, status, size and duration, and retention state.
Server stateThe server bundles of the backup worker, and their restores.
RestoreThe successful backups that can be restored, each with Restore….
SchedulesSchedules with their next runs, last runs, and retention.
DestinationsThe approved destinations, their test results and protection, and the allowed S3 endpoints.
OperationsEvery backup, restore, restore test, deletion, and destination test, with its state and the source of that state.
Recovery verificationThe restore tests and their checks.

The page needs the console tables. When they are missing, the page shows Set up Backup & Restore: Set up creates the database admin_database (by default console_admin) if needed and five tables in it. It creates no destination or backup. Setting up needs CREATE TABLE on the admin_database.

Tables created by an earlier version may need an update, offered where it is needed: Update the operations table on the Server state tab adds the operation kinds of server bundles, and Update the table on the Schedules tab adds the column for second copies. Neither changes data.

Recovery coverage

A backup contains what BACKUP copies: nothing more. Plan the recovery of the rest separately. The note at the top of the page, the scope step of the backup wizard (Never in a backup made here), and the first step of the restore wizard (Not in this backup) say the same.

ObjectCovered by a database backup
Tables of the MergeTree family, Log family, and Memory: schema and dataYes
Views, materialized views, dictionaries: definitionsYes. The target table of a materialized view is backed up only if it is in the scope.
Tables of external engines (S3, URL, Kafka, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and similar): definitionsYes; their data is stored elsewhere and is not backed up. The review step lists them.
Users, roles, settings profiles, quotas, row policies created with SQLOnly when chosen as a separate scope item
SQL user-defined functions, workloads, and resourcesOnly when chosen as a separate scope item
The console tables in the admin_databaseOnly when chosen (the wizard offers them by default to users who may back them up)
Server configuration (config.xml, config.d, users.xml, users.d) and the secrets in it, TLS certificates and keys, keys of encrypted disksNo. The backup worker can back them up as server bundles.
Executable UDF scripts, dictionary source files, format schemasNo. Server bundles can include them.
Named collections, including the S3 credentials of destinationsNo
Keeper's own stateNo: RESTORE rebuilds the Keeper metadata of replicated tables. Server bundles can include a Keeper snapshot.
The cluster agent's key and the secrets of the clusters it createdNo. Server bundles can include its state directory.
Point-in-time recoveryNo. A backup is a snapshot of when each table was copied; changes between backups are lost.

Each table is backed up from the data parts it has when its own backup starts. A backup of several tables is therefore not a transactionally consistent snapshot: rows inserted during the backup may be in one table and missing from another. The review step of the wizard says so, and lists unfinished mutations and running schema changes.

A backup is made by the server the console is connected to. In a cluster, it contains this server's data only.

Destinations

Backups go only to destinations that an administrator added on the Destinations tab with Add destination. Users choose a destination by name; they never type a path or a URL.

FieldMeaning
TypeServer backup disk or S3-compatible bucket. Cannot be changed later.
Name, DescriptionThe name users choose. Names are unique.
DiskFor a disk destination: a disk of the server allowed in backups.allowed_disk of the server configuration.
Endpoint, BucketFor S3: the S3-compatible server, typed as https://host[:port], which must be an allowed endpoint, and the bucket.
Access key ID, Secret access keyFor S3: the credentials the server uses. They are stored in a named collection console_backup_<id>, created with CREATE NAMED COLLECTION by the review of the form, never in the console tables or the browser, and never shown again. The server masks them in system.query_log and its logs. When editing, leave them empty to keep the stored credentials.
Worker credential referenceFor S3: the prefix of the environment variables with the credentials the backup worker uses to list and delete artifacts: <REF>_ACCESS_KEY_ID, <REF>_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. Uppercase letters, digits, and underscores.
PrefixAll artifacts of the destination are stored under this path (default console), and the worker deletes only under it. It may not contain .. or start with /.
Allowed databasesComma-separated. Backups of other databases cannot use this destination in the console. Empty: any database.

The server, not the browser, connects to an S3 endpoint, and verifies HTTPS certificates with its usual certificate checks. The endpoint must be reachable from the server, and from every server of a cluster that runs backups. The backup worker reaches it too, to list and delete backups. An endpoint with plain HTTP is accepted with a warning: data and credentials then travel in clear text.

Warning

The server checks remote_url_allow_hosts only for redirects of BACKUP TO S3, not for the endpoint itself. A user with WRITE ON S3 can therefore make the server send requests to any address it can reach, including internal and cloud metadata addresses. The console allows only the allowed endpoints. Do not grant READ ON S3 or WRITE ON S3 to users who should not have that ability outside the console.

Testing and enabling a destination

A new destination is recorded Disabled until it is tested. Test writes a small backup of the destinations table from the server to <prefix>/_console_test/<uuid> and opens it; Record result stores the result with the destination. Listing and deleting at the destination are tested by the backup worker with its own credentials when it next runs, which also removes the test backup. After a passed test, select Enable. A failed test leaves the destination disabled.

The test runs on the server the console is connected to. In a cluster, every server that runs backups needs the same access.

The Protection column shows what protects each destination: encryption at rest, Object Lock, and whether it is off-site. For S3, the backup worker reads these bucket settings after every destination test and every 6 hours; a setting it cannot read is shown as unknown. Recommended S3 permissions and bucket settings has the policies for separate server and worker keys. See Protect backups.

Remove deletes neither the backups of a destination nor its named collection; it is refused while a schedule uses the destination. When the credentials are no longer needed, drop the collection with DROP NAMED COLLECTION.

Allowed S3 endpoints

S3 destinations can use only allowed endpoints. Since the server does not restrict the endpoint of BACKUP TO S3 itself, this list keeps the console from sending backups, and their credentials, to an unintended server. The endpoints come from two places, both listed under Allowed endpoints on the Destinations tab:

  • The console. Allow endpoint adds an exact endpoint, such as http://10.0.4.20:9000, or a domain pattern, such as https://*.example.com, with a Note. When you add a destination at an endpoint that is not allowed yet, the review of the destination includes the step that allows it, with a warning. Remove takes an endpoint off the list; destinations that already use it keep working. This needs SELECT and INSERT on the backup_endpoints table, and every change is in the audit log. Installations set up before this table existed show Set up in the section.
  • The server configuration. backup_s3_endpoints in the web_console section (see Configuration). These entries are shown in the console but changed only in the configuration. Patterns for any host (https://*, *) and link-local or metadata addresses can be allowed only here. A configuration reload applies a change.
EntryAllows
https://minio.example.com:9000Exactly this endpoint.
https://*.example.comAny subdomain of example.com, on the default port. Add :port to allow another port.
https://* or http://*:9000Any host with this scheme (and port).
*Any HTTP or HTTPS endpoint.

Patterns never match internal addresses: localhost, loopback and private network addresses, link-local addresses including the cloud metadata service 169.254.169.254, and names ending in .internal or .local. To use such an endpoint, allow it exactly. Link-local and metadata addresses (169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10, metadata.google.internal, instance-data) can be allowed only in the server configuration. The console checks the address as typed: it cannot detect a public name that resolves to an internal address, so use patterns only for domains you trust.

For example, to allow a MinIO server on the internal network and the buckets of AWS S3:

xml
<clickhouse>
    <web_console>
        <backup_s3_endpoints>http://10.0.4.20:9000, https://*.amazonaws.com</backup_s3_endpoints>
    </web_console>
</clickhouse>

Manual backups

New backup on the Backups tab opens a wizard with four steps:

  1. Scope: What to back up is Whole databases or Tables of one database, optionally with Partitions (optional) for a single table. Structure only backs up the CREATE statements without data. Under Server objects, the access entities (users, roles, settings profiles, row policies, quotas), the SQL user-defined functions, workloads, and resources, and the console's tables are separate choices.
  2. Destination: only enabled destinations whose Allowed databases allow the whole scope are listed.
  3. Type: Full backup, or Incremental on a Base backup: an earlier backup of exactly the same scope at the same destination, which must open. Restoring an incremental backup needs its whole chain. The option to capture validation values records the row count and a fingerprint (groupBitXor(cityHash64(*))) of each table before and after the backup, to compare restores with. It reads every table twice. When the source changed during the backup, the result says so and the values are not used for checks.
  4. Review: the objects with their engines, rows, and sizes; the tables of external engines, whose data is not backed up; the views that read from databases outside the scope; unfinished mutations and running schema changes; and the consistency statement. Start backup submits it.

Each operation has an ID that is also the id setting of the native operation in system.backups, the log_comment of its statements, and the correlation ID of its audit records. Before submitting, the console records the operation (queued), then submits BACKUP ... ASYNC and records the outcome of the submission:

StateMeaning
queuedRecorded, not yet accepted by the server.
runningAccepted by the server.
succeeded, failed, cancelledReported by the server (system.backups, then system.backup_log).
