unknownThe console could not determine the outcome: the answer to the submission was lost, or the server has no record and the artifact could not be checked. Check the target before running the operation again.

Operations run in the server. Closing the browser neither cancels nor loses them: the next visit to the page, and every cycle of the backup worker, reconciles unfinished operations. When the server no longer lists an operation, for example after a restart, the console opens the artifact: a complete backup is recorded as succeeded, a missing one as failed with the explanation that it was interrupted. An operation is never submitted twice: the server refuses a second backup with the same ID or location.

Cancel on the Operations tab runs KILL QUERY for the server operation. The server removes a partial backup. Rows restored before a restore was cancelled stay in its target.

The server shows no progress of a running backup in percent, and the console does not estimate one: it shows the elapsed time, and the files and bytes written when the server reports them. When an S3 destination becomes unreachable, the server retries each request for about an hour (backup_restore_s3_retry_attempts), and the operation stays running until you cancel it. The destination test and the artifact checks use two attempts and fail in seconds.

In the inventory, each backup shows its status levels: the operation state, Artifact opened (or Artifact not checked), Restore test passed (or Never test-restored), and Recovery rehearsed after a recovery rehearsal. Check opens the backup read-only with the Backup database engine and reads every table. Delete requests the deletion of a backup, confirmed by typing its short ID; the worker executes it, since SQL cannot delete a backup.

Restores

Restore… on the Restore tab, or Restore on a row of the inventory, opens the restore wizard:

  1. Backup and chain: what the backup contains and does not contain; the chain of an incremental backup, every base of which must open.
  2. Target: the server and its version (a warning when the backup was made with another version), the privileges, checked with CHECK GRANT before starting, and the free space of the default disk next to the size of the backup.
  3. Names and options: a target database for each database of the backup, by default a new database restore_<database>_<time>. Structure only creates the tables without data. Access entities, and functions, workloads, and resources, are restored only when chosen, as separate choices.
  4. Conflicts: whether the target databases exist.
  5. Confirm: type the name of the first target database, then Start restore.

A restore never touches existing data:

  • RESTORE DATABASE ... AS restores each database into its new name, and rewrites the references of views and materialized views to it.
  • The console uses create_table = 'create' and create_database = 'create' and never allow_non_empty_tables, so the server refuses to restore over an existing object instead of appending to it. When a target exists, the wizard stops and offers a Drop … button for each existing target: a separate dialog with a typed confirmation and its own audit record.
  • Access entities are restored with create_access = create: existing entities with the same names make the restore fail.

After a restore, the console compares the target with the backup: the tables and their engines, the row counts, and, when the backup captured them, the fingerprints. Each check is recorded with the operation.

Schedules and retention

Add schedule on the Schedules tab creates a schedule that backs up chosen databases Hourly, Daily, or Weekly, at a Weekday, Hour, and Minute in a Time zone (an IANA name such as Europe/Berlin or UTC). The Strategy is Full backup each time, or Incremental, with a full backup every N runs; for an incremental schedule, When the base is missing chooses between failing the run and making a full backup. Other fields:

FieldMeaning
DestinationWhere the backups go.
Second copy toOptional: after each full backup, the worker makes a new, independent full backup of the same databases at this destination. Retention keeps the same number there.
KeepThe number of most recent backups the worker keeps; for an incremental schedule, full backups with their incremental chains. Older ones are deleted, except bases of kept backups.
Test-restore each backupA restore test after each backup, in an isolated database on this server.
Failure notificationOptional: the name of an environment variable of the backup worker that holds a webhook URL, called when a run fails.

Schedules are run by the backup worker, not by the browser or the server. Each run has an operation ID and an artifact name derived from the schedule and the local time of the run, so two workers that see the same run submit it only once. A run is postponed while another operation of the same schedule, destination, or databases is running.

Daylight saving time changes are handled as follows. A run is due at the first minute, on or after the scheduled local time, of each local day (or hour). When the clock is set back and a local time occurs twice, the schedule runs at the first occurrence. When the clock is set forward and the local time does not exist, it runs at the first minute after the gap. A run missed because no worker was running is made once, when a worker starts within the same period; older missed runs are not made up.

Retention keeps the last N chains: a full backup and the incremental backups based on it. Retention preview shows, for each destination of the schedule, which backups retention would delete and why the others are kept. A backup that is the base of another backup that is kept is never deleted, by retention or by hand: the inventory marks it Protected, the deletion dialog refuses it, and the worker checks it again before deleting. Remove keeps the backups of a schedule, but the worker no longer deletes them by retention.

Warning

Do not configure bucket lifecycle rules that expire objects of a backup prefix: they can delete a base and break the chains that depend on it.

Recovery verification

Test restore on a row of the inventory, then Run restore test, restores a backup into new databases named console_verify_<id>_<database> on the server the console is connected to, compares them with the backup and with the values captured when it was made, and drops them. Access entities are never restored by a test. The result is recorded with its checks, shown in the inventory and on the Recovery verification tab, and audited; a failed test stays visible until a later one passes.

A restore test shows that the backup opens and that its data matches, on this server. It does not test a restore on another server or of another version, nor the recovery of what the backup does not cover. The measured restore duration is not a recovery time objective: it depends on the load, the size, and the target. To rehearse the recovery of a whole server on an isolated server, see Recover a whole server.

The Resilience (3-2-1-1) check on the Overview evaluates the backups of the last 7 days: Two copies, One off-site, One immutable, Encrypted at rest, and Restores tested (a restore test passed in the last 30 days). Each line says whether it is Met and why.

Server bundles

BACKUP copies databases, tables, and access entities, but not the server's configuration files, the secrets in them, TLS keys, scripts, or Keeper's own state. The backup worker backs those up as server bundles: it reads the files on the server host, encrypts them, and stores the ciphertext at a destination. They are on the Server state tab.

Encryption and key providers

Each bundle has its own random 256-bit data key (AES-256-GCM), wrapped by the master key of the worker. The master key is never stored with a bundle, and never included in one, even when it lies under one of the included paths. The destination and the server only ever hold ciphertext: the worker stores the bundle in a table of its own in the admin_database, backs it up with BACKUP TABLE to the destination, and drops the table. The clear header of a bundle names the cipher and the key provider and holds the wrapped data key, but no file names, sizes, or checksums.

The worker's BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER chooses where the master key lives:

ProviderShown asWhere the master key isBundles from the console and on a schedule
fileKey file on the worker hostA 256-bit key in a file readable by its owner only (BUNDLE_KEY_FILE), made with bundle-key-init. Keep a copy out of band, with its fingerprint: without it, no bundle can be decrypted.Yes
vaultHashiCorp Vault TransitThe Transit secrets engine of HashiCorp Vault wraps the data key; the master key never leaves Vault. Vault must be reachable to restore.Yes
passphrasePassphraseNowhere: derived from a passphrase of at least 12 characters with scrypt, entered on the worker host for each bundle and each restore.No: a person makes and restores bundles on the worker host with the bundle and bundle-restore commands.

The Backup worker box of the tab shows the worker that makes bundles, the master key with its fingerprint (for example sha256:… for a key file, or vault:<mount>/<key>), the included paths, whether a Keeper snapshot is included, the staging directory, and the automatic bundles. A bundle records the key it was encrypted with, shown in its Key column: a worker refuses to decrypt a bundle made with another key. To choose and set up a provider, see Protect backups.

Contents

Variable of the workerMeaning
BUNDLE_PATHSFiles and directories to include, comma-separated (default /etc/clickhouse-server). Add TLS keys, user_scripts, format schemas, dictionary files, the named collections directory, and the cluster agent's state directory where they are on this host. A file the worker cannot read fails the bundle.
BUNDLE_KEEPER, BUNDLE_KEEPER_SNAPSHOTShost:port of Keeper and its snapshot directory: the worker asks Keeper for a new snapshot (csnp, allowed by default in four_letter_word_white_list) and includes it.
BUNDLE_DESTINATION, BUNDLE_EVERY_HOURSAutomatic bundles to that destination every so many hours (not with a passphrase).
BUNDLE_STAGING_DIRWhere restores put files (default /var/lib/clickhouse-console/restore-staging).

Making and restoring bundles

Back up the server state… asks for a Destination; Request the bundle records the request, and the worker makes the bundle when it next runs. Bundles appear in the Server bundles table with their files, size, and key.

A restore never writes into the server:

  • Compare, then Request the comparison: the worker decrypts the bundle and reports, by checksum, which files on the worker host are the same, changed, missing, or not in the bundle. Only names and results are recorded, never contents.
  • Stage…, confirmed by typing the short ID of the bundle, then Request staging: the worker writes the files, readable by their owner only, into a new directory under BUNDLE_STAGING_DIR, with a RESTORE.txt. The files hold secrets in clear: apply what you need, then delete the directory.

To apply staged files: stop the server, compare and copy the files you need, restore their owners and modes, and start the server. For Keeper, put the snapshot into its snapshot directory with Keeper stopped and its newer snapshots and logs moved aside.

Compare the latest bundle with the host regularly, for example after every change of the configuration: it proves that the master key, the bundle, and the destination all still work.

Backup worker

utils/web-console/backup_worker.mjs is a long-running process next to the server. It needs Node.js 18 or later and no packages; the tools image runs it as backup-worker. Each cycle (every 30 seconds by default, INTERVAL_SECONDS) it:

  • records a heartbeat, shown on the Overview;
  • reconciles unfinished operations;
  • submits due scheduled backups, the second copies, and restore tests of schedules that ask for them;
  • applies retention and executes requested deletions;
  • tests listing and deleting at destinations, removes destination test artifacts, and reads the protection settings of S3 buckets;
  • makes and restores server bundles, when BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER is set;
  • calls a webhook when a scheduled operation fails.
bash
CLICKHOUSE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8123 CLICKHOUSE_USER=backup_worker CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=... \
PROD_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... PROD_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=... \
node utils/web-console/backup_worker.mjs

--once runs one cycle and exits. Run the worker as a service on the server host: deleting from a disk destination needs access to the disk's directory, and server bundles read the files of the host. Several workers may run at the same time. The worker reads S3 credentials from environment variables named after the destination's credential reference (<REF>_ACCESS_KEY_ID, <REF>_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, <REF>_REGION), and a schedule's webhook URL from the variable named in the schedule. It writes only to the console tables, and logs JSON lines without credentials. The Overview warns when the worker has not reported for more than 5 minutes.

All its variables, arguments, and commands are listed in Helper processes. Its service account needs the privileges of a Backup Administrator for the databases of the schedules, SELECT on them for fingerprints, and INSERT on the backup tables and the audit log; for server bundles, also CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, INSERT, SELECT, and BACKUP on console_admin.server_bundle*. See Create service accounts.

Privileges

As everywhere in the console, every action is a statement run as you and authorized by the server (see Security model). These are the privileges each action needs:

ActionPrivileges
See the pageSELECT on the backup tables
Back upBACKUP on the scope; READ, WRITE ON DISK, or NAMED COLLECTION on the destination's collection and READ, WRITE ON S3; INSERT on backup_operations, backup_events, and audit_log
RestoreREAD ON DISK, or READ ON S3 and the collection; CREATE DATABASE, CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW, CREATE DICTIONARY, INSERT on the target; for access entities, the access management privileges
Test restoreAs restore, on console_verify_*, and DROP DATABASE on it
Check an artifactCREATE DATABASE, DROP DATABASE ON console_inspect_*.* (the artifact is opened with the Backup database engine)
Manage destinationsINSERT on backup_destinations; for S3, CREATE NAMED COLLECTION, ALTER NAMED COLLECTION, DROP NAMED COLLECTION on console_backup_*
Allow S3 endpointsSELECT and INSERT on backup_endpoints
Manage schedulesINSERT on backup_schedules
Request a server bundle, a comparison, or stagingINSERT on backup_operations and backup_events
CancelKILL QUERY

The role templates bundle them:

TemplateGrants
Backup ViewerSELECT on the backup tables, the audit log, system.backups, system.backup_log, and system.disks; SHOW DATABASES.
Backup OperatorThe viewer's, plus backing up the chosen databases to disks (optionally S3), checking artifacts, and requesting deletions; optionally KILL QUERY.
Restore OperatorThe viewer's, plus restoring into new databases named restore_* and restore tests. It cannot drop databases other than its restore tests, or restore access entities.
Backup AdministratorAll of the above for the chosen databases, plus destinations, allowed S3 endpoints, schedules, and KILL QUERY.

Note

READ ON S3 and WRITE ON S3 apply to every S3 URL, not only to the configured destinations, and READ ON DISK and WRITE ON DISK to every disk: grant them only to users trusted with that.

Troubleshooting

  • An operation is unknown. On Operations, look at the source of the state and the error. For a backup, select Check in the inventory: if the backup opens, it is usable. For a restore, inspect the target databases before restoring again into new ones.
  • A backup was interrupted. A backup interrupted by a server failure is recorded as failed, and its partial files stay at the destination: select Delete on its row to have the worker remove them.
  • An operation stays running. system.backups shows the server's view. For S3, check that the endpoint is reachable from the server, then cancel the operation.
  • A scheduled backup did not run. On the Overview, check the worker heartbeat, then the worker's log. A run is postponed while an operation on the same databases or destination is running, and missed runs are not made up after the period.
  • A deletion failed. The operation shows the reason, for example that the backup is the base of another one, that Object Lock prevents it, or that the worker has no credentials or no access to the disk directory. Partial deletions on S3 list the keys that remain.
  • A restore test failed. The checks list the tables whose counts or fingerprints differ. A fingerprint difference with equal counts usually means the source changed during the backup without the console capturing it; test the next backup before relying on this one.
  • The worker cannot make bundles. The Backup worker box of Server state shows the reason, for example that BUNDLE_KEY_FILE is not set, or that the key file is readable by other users.
  • Recovering the console tables. They are ordinary tables and can be in a backup's scope. Restore them into a new database and set admin_database to it, or copy their rows back.

guides/clusters.title: Cluster Management
guides/clusters.description: How the Clusters page of the ClickHouse web console manages the lifecycle of ClickHouse deployments through the cluster agent and its docker-compose and kubernetes providers.
guides/clusters.html:
The Clusters page of the Administration category manages the lifecycle of ClickHouse deployments: planning, provisioning, registration, configuration, scaling, maintenance, upgrades, recovery, decommissioning, and retirement.

ClickHouse has no SQL statement that creates servers, provisions infrastructure, or redistributes data, so the console does not pretend to. It records plans, versioned desired configurations, and operations in the console tables. The cluster agent, a process on the infrastructure host, executes them through a provider, checks every result, and records what it observes. The console never connects to the managed clusters and never handles their credentials: what it shows comes from the agent's observations, with the time they were made.

Views

The page has three tabs: Cluster Inventory, Create Cluster, and Register Existing. Each cluster of the inventory has its own tabs.

ViewWhat it shows
Cluster InventoryRegistered clusters with their environment, owner, provider, mode, lifecycle state, health, versions, the age of the last observation, drift, and operations that need attention; the state of the cluster agent. Filters: a search on name, identifier, owner, and workload; environment, provider, mode, and lifecycle; and Needs attention (drift, failed or blocked operations, or a cluster that is not healthy).
Create ClusterThe creation wizard.
Register ExistingRead-only registration of an existing deployment.
OverviewIdentity, endpoints, secret references, health, recovery targets and measured evidence, recent operations.
Nodes & TopologyShards, replicas, and their observed state, version, replication, background work, disk, and memory; Restart and Decommission. For registered deployments: the discovered topology with its provenance and conflicts.
KeeperMembers, roles, quorum, versions, and latency.
ConfigurationDesired settings, observed differences, drift, and the revision history.
Capacity & ScalingCapacity per node; resize, add replicas, add or remove a shard.
Maintenance & UpgradesRolling restarts and version upgrades.
Protection & RecoveryVerified backups of the cluster and the recovery procedures.
OperationsEvery lifecycle operation with its steps, evidence, and state; Cancel and Retry.
RetirementResources with their disposition; retirement and resource deletion.

The page needs the console tables. When they are missing, it shows Set up Cluster Management: Set up creates the cluster tables in the admin_database. It creates or changes no deployment. Setting up needs CREATE TABLE on the admin_database.

Modes and states

A cluster in the inventory is a platform-managed deployment. It is not the same as a named cluster in remote_servers: a deployment can define several, and an entry in system.clusters does not prove infrastructure ownership.

ModeMeaning
ObserveInventory and monitoring only. Registered deployments start here.
ManageConfiguration and lifecycle operations through the provider. Clusters created in the console start here.
RetiredA historical record: observation and operations stop; the remaining resources are listed with their disposition.

The lifecycle state (planned, provisioning, validating, ready, degraded, unreachable, maintenance, failed, retiring, retired) is separate from the state of each operation. A node is unreachable when it does not answer the agent; it is failed only when the provider confirms it, for example a container that is not running. An unreachable node is never taken as permission to delete its data or its replica metadata.

Cluster agent

utils/web-console/cluster_agent.mjs is a long-running process on the infrastructure host. It needs Node.js 18 or later and no packages; the tools image runs it as cluster-agent. It:

  • executes queued lifecycle operations with checkpoints, one at a time per cluster, after checking on the server that the requester holds the capability (EXECUTE AS <requester> CHECK GRANT);
  • provisions and changes clusters through a provider;
  • observes every registered cluster (nodes, replication, Keeper, configuration drift) and records what it saw, so the console shows the last observation even when a cluster is unreachable;
  • records a heartbeat with its providers and the environments it may change, shown in the Cluster agent box of the inventory. The box warns when the agent has not reported for more than 2 minutes: observations are then stale and operations wait.
bash
CLICKHOUSE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8123 CLICKHOUSE_USER=cluster_agent CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=... \
CLUSTER_AGENT_STATE_DIR=/var/lib/clickhouse-console/clusters CLUSTER_AGENT_ENVIRONMENTS=lab,development \
node utils/web-console/cluster_agent.mjs
VariableMeaning
CLUSTER_AGENT_STATE_DIRDirectory of the generated deployments and their secrets, and of the agent's key pair agent-key.pem (readable by its owner), whose public key the agent publishes for encrypting administrator passwords. Required for docker-compose. Back it up, for example in a server bundle.
CLUSTER_AGENT_ENVIRONMENTSEnvironments the agent may change (default lab,development). Operations on clusters in other environments are rejected.
CLUSTER_AGENT_PORT_RANGEHost ports for lab endpoints, bound to 127.0.0.1 (default 31000-31999).
CLUSTER_AGENT_IMAGESImage repositories allowed for nodes (default clickhouse/clickhouse-server,clickhouse/clickhouse-keeper,contentsquareplatform/chproxy).
CLUSTER_AGENT_HOST_ALIASName of the Docker host as seen from the containers, used to reach S3 endpoints published on it (default host.docker.internal).
<REF>_USER, <REF>_PASSWORDCredentials of a registered deployment whose credential reference is <REF>.
<REF>_ACCESS_KEY_ID, <REF>_SECRET_ACCESS_KEYCredentials of an S3 backup destination, as for the backup worker.

--once runs one cycle and exits. All variables, including INTERVAL_SECONDS and OBSERVE_SECONDS, are listed in Helper processes.

The agent runs only docker and kubectl with fixed argument lists, never a shell, and never text from the browser as a command; Secrets reach kubectl on its standard input, never in its arguments. Docker objects carry the labels io.clickhouse.console.cluster and io.clickhouse.console.managed-by; the agent stops or deletes only objects with the labels of the cluster it works on.

The account of the agent on the server that holds the console tables needs SELECT and INSERT on the cluster tables, SELECT on backup_destinations, INSERT on audit_log, and IMPERSONATE on the users who request operations, so that it can check their capabilities with EXECUTE AS <user> CHECK GRANT. See Create service accounts.

Warning

On a Docker host, the agent uses the Docker socket. Access to the socket is equivalent to root on the host: run the agent only where that is acceptable. See Deploy with Docker Compose.

Providers

ProviderStatusNotes
Docker Compose (local lab) (docker-compose)ImplementedContainers on the agent's Docker host, bound to 127.0.0.1. All nodes share one host: they are not independent failure domains. For development and tests, not for high availability. Needs the docker CLI with Compose v2, and the images on the host: the agent does not pull images.
Kubernetes (ClickHouse operator) (kubernetes)ImplementedSee Kubernetes provider.
Linux servers (agent)Not availableNot implemented: no verified host automation integration.

Kubernetes provider

The kubernetes provider deploys clusters with the ClickHouse operator of ClickHouse Inc. A cluster of the console is one KeeperCluster and one ClickHouseCluster (clickhouse.com/v1alpha1) named chc-<id>, in a namespace of the agent's Kubernetes cluster, with a Secret chc-<id>-console and, when chosen, a client Service chc-<id>-client. The operator creates the StatefulSets, pods, Services, ConfigMaps, and a volume claim per pod. The agent uses kubectl with fixed argument lists, and reaches the pods with kubectl port-forward: nothing is exposed for it outside the cluster.

It was verified with operator v0.0.8 (2026-09-25), cert-manager v1.16.2, and k3s v1.31.5 in k3d. The agent refuses an operator version it was not verified with (CLUSTER_AGENT_OPERATOR_VERSIONS). Behavior of that operator that the provider relies on:

  • replicas is the number of replicas of every shard: all shards have the same size, and the operator adds or removes the replica or the shard with the highest index. The console therefore adds or removes one replica in every shard, and removes only the last shard.
  • The cluster in remote_servers is named default, with an interserver secret; the macros shard and replica are indexes from 0; the default database is Replicated.
  • Deleting the resources deletes the pods and Services, but not the volume claims: the StatefulSets retain them when deleted or scaled down.
  • A larger data volume in the resource is applied by the operator to every claim; it fails on a storage class that does not allow expansion.
  • Settings, resources, and the image are rolled out one replica at a time; the operator reports the result with conditions (Ready, Healthy, ConfigurationInSync, ClusterSizeAligned, VersionInSync), which the agent waits for before its own checks in ClickHouse.

Choices in the wizard

The agent publishes what it finds in its Kubernetes cluster (version, operator, storage classes with their provisioner, reclaim policy, expansion, and binding mode, and the namespaces it may use), and the wizard offers these as choices:

ChoiceOptionsEffect
NamespaceA new namespace (default chc-<name>), or an existing oneOnly namespaces matching CLUSTER_AGENT_K8S_NAMESPACES. A new namespace is labeled as the cluster's and can be deleted with it; an existing one is never deleted.
Storage classThe classes of the clusterThe volumes of the nodes and of the Keeper members. The wizard shows whether the class allows expansion.
Volume reclaim policyRetain (default), DeleteSet by the agent on every volume of the cluster, whatever the class says. With Retain, a volume and its data stay when its claim is deleted, until the volume is deleted too. With Delete, the provisioner deletes the volume with its claim.
Volume sizesData volume per node, Keeper volume per member, in GiBThe claims of the operator.
Client ServiceNone, ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancerA Service in front of all ClickHouse pods, ports 8123 and 9000.
ImagesClickHouse server, ClickHouse KeeperPinned versions from the allowed repositories; the nodes pull them.
CPU and memoryPer nodeRequests and limits of the ClickHouse containers.

chproxy is not offered on Kubernetes: use the client Service.

Operations on Kubernetes

OperationImplementationVerified in the lab
ProvisionPreflight (Kubernetes, operator and its version, storage class, namespace, images), the Secret, the two resources, readiness reported by the operator, the reclaim policy of the volumes, the Keeper quorum, topology and administrator sign-in on every node, and a write, replicate, and read testYes
ConfigurationSettings in extraConfig and the default profile; rollout reported by the operator; values checked on every node; drift between the applied resources and the cluster, and between the settings and the nodesYes
Expand storageA larger data volume, refused on a class without expansion and for a smaller size; capacity checked on every claimYes (lab driver: the size is recorded but not enforced)
Add replicasOne replica in every shard; schema of a peer, catch-up, and row countsYes
Remove replicasThe last replica of every shard, after the remaining replicas are caught up and the Keeper quorum is healthy; replica metadata dropped from Keeper; claims keptYes
Add or remove a shardA shard with the schema of shard 1; only the last shard, only when emptyYes
Restart a nodeThe pod is deleted and recreated by its StatefulSet, one at a time, after peer checksYes
Resize CPU and memoryRequests and limits; rollout reported by the operatorImplemented; not run in the lab suite
UpgradeThe image of the resource; the operator replaces the pods one replica at a time; version and errors checked on every nodeImplemented; not run in the lab suite
BackupAs for Docker; the pods reach an S3 endpoint on the agent host through CLUSTER_AGENT_K8S_HOST_ALIASYes, to MinIO through host.k3d.internal
RetireThe two resources and the client Service are deleted; the claims, volumes, Secret, and namespace are kept and recordedYes
Delete resourcesOnly the approved resources of the cluster: resources, Secret, Service, claims, volumes, and the namespace when it was created for the cluster and is emptyYes
Keeper membershipNot implemented

Deleting the volume object of a Retain volume does not delete the storage behind it: Kubernetes leaves it to the storage system. Check it there before reusing the space.

Agent setup for Kubernetes

The provider is enabled when the agent has a kubeconfig:

bash
CLUSTER_AGENT_KUBECONFIG=/etc/clickhouse-console/kubeconfig CLUSTER_AGENT_K8S_NAMESPACES='chc-*' \
CLICKHOUSE_URL=... CLICKHOUSE_USER=cluster_agent CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=... CLUSTER_AGENT_STATE_DIR=... \
node utils/web-console/cluster_agent.mjs
VariableMeaning
CLUSTER_AGENT_KUBECONFIGThe kubeconfig of the agent; enables the provider.
CLUSTER_AGENT_KUBE_CONTEXTA context of the kubeconfig (default: its current context).
CLUSTER_AGENT_K8S_NAMESPACESNamespaces the agent may use: names, or prefixes followed by * (default chc-*).
CLUSTER_AGENT_OPERATOR_NAMESPACENamespace of the operator (default clickhouse-operator-system).
CLUSTER_AGENT_OPERATOR_VERSIONSOperator versions the agent accepts (default v0.0.8).
CLUSTER_AGENT_K8S_HOST_ALIASName of the agent host as seen from the pods, for S3 endpoints published on it (default host.k3d.internal).

The account of the kubeconfig needs, in the namespaces it may use: get, list, create, patch, and delete on clickhouseclusters and keeperclusters (clickhouse.com), Secrets, and Services; get, list, and delete on pods and persistent volume claims; create on pods/portforward. Cluster-wide: get and list on namespaces, storage classes, and persistent volumes; patch and delete on persistent volumes (reclaim policy and deletion); create and delete on namespaces when it creates them; get on the operator's Deployments. It needs no right on other namespaces, and never cluster-admin. Anyone who can read Secrets in a cluster's namespace can read its passwords.

kubernetes.yaml of the deployment runs the agent with this provider for the same Kubernetes cluster: see Deploy on Kubernetes.

Capabilities of the docker-compose provider

CapabilityNative ClickHouse supportInfrastructure dependencyImplementationVerified limitations
Provision a clusterNone (no SQL creates servers)Docker with Compose v2, the image on the hostAgent generates compose and node configuration; checkpointed operation; readiness checksOne host; no TLS; the agent does not pull images
Register an existing deploymentsystem.clusters, system.macros, system.zookeeper_connection, system.disksNetwork access from the agent; credentials in its environmentRead-only discovery with provenanceA system.clusters entry is not proof of membership; external Keeper members are not contacted
MonitoringSystem tables, Keeper mntrAgent reaches the nodes and Keeper portsObservation every 30 seconds, kept 7 daysMemory is the host's, not the container limit; no certificate expiry (no TLS)
ConfigurationSYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG, system.server_settings.changeable_without_restartManaged files on the agent hostRevisions, reload or rolling restart, verification, driftA catalog of server settings and three profile settings
Add or remove a replicaReplicatedMergeTree, SYSTEM SYNC REPLICA, SYSTEM DROP REPLICAProvider creates and removes containersSchema copy, catch-up, count comparison; safety checks before removalTables whose replica name is not {replica} are skipped; non-replicated tables are created empty
Add a shardDistributed tables route new rowsProviderNew nodes with the schema of shard 1, emptyExisting data is never redistributed
Remove a shardNoneProviderOnly an empty shardData migration is not automated
Resize CPU and memoryNoneDocker limitsRolling recreationStorage cannot be resized: Docker volumes have no size
Restart and upgradeNoneProviderRolling, with peer checks; upgrade gates and stop on failureNo downgrade; no automatic rollback
Client routingNone (HTTP clients choose a node)chproxy image on the hostOptional chproxy container; its node list follows the topology and maintenanceOne chproxy container: a single point of failure; HTTP only
Keeper membershipKeeper reconfigurationProviderNot implemented: observed onlyThe ensemble is fixed at provisioning
Backup and verificationBACKUP, the Backup database engineAn S3 destination of Backup & RestoreOne verified backup per shardDisk destinations are unreachable from lab nodes
Restore into a replacement clusterRESTOREProviderNot automated: documented procedure
Decommission a nodeSYSTEM DROP REPLICAProviderTen-step workflow with checksNo load balancer: clients of the node are not moved
Retire and deleteNoneProviderDependency review, protection gate, scoped deletionBackups are deleted in Backup & Restore only

Creating a cluster

The Create Cluster wizard has seven steps in the browser, and an eighth done by the agent:

  1. Purpose and ownership: name, environment (lab, development, staging, production), owner, workload, expected data and growth, concurrent queries, ingestion, availability goal, and RPO and RTO targets. Sizing from these numbers is an estimate.
  2. Infrastructure provider: only implemented providers can be chosen, and only when an agent offers them for the environment. With kubernetes, the step offers the namespace, storage class, volume reclaim policy, and client Service (see Choices in the wizard), and the later steps the volume sizes and the Keeper image; the cluster name is default, and chproxy is not offered.
  3. Topology: shards, replicas per shard, Keeper members (1, 3, or 5), the cluster name, and the client routing: none, or chproxy. The wizard explains what failures the topology tolerates, separately for replicas, the Keeper quorum, and the routing, and that a lab on one host is one failure domain.
  4. Storage and resources: CPU and memory per node, the image, and the storage model (a local volume per node and per Keeper member).
  5. Security: the administrator user of the cluster and its password (at least 12 characters, without spaces, quotes, $, #, or backslashes, typed twice). The browser encrypts the password with the public key that the cluster agent publishes (RSA-OAEP with SHA-256): the plan and the console tables contain only the ciphertext, which only that agent can decrypt. The agent writes the password to the secrets file of the deployment on its host, and the nodes read it from the environment; it appears in no plan, URL, log, or console table. The agent and chproxy use a separate user, console_service, with a password the agent generates, as it does the cluster secret and the interserver credentials.
  6. Operational policies: backup destination, maintenance window, and an optional notification reference.
  7. Plan: the containers, volumes, network, endpoints, configuration, expected disruption, preconditions, readiness checks, and what happens if provisioning fails. Review shows the statements that record the cluster, its desired configuration (revision 1), and the operation; the plan contains no credentials.
  8. Readiness, done by the agent after submission: every node answers and authenticates with the administrator user, Keeper has a leader and a quorum, every node lists the topology, and a test database is written, replicated, read through the cluster, and dropped. The cluster is ready only after these checks, not when its containers run.

Provisioning is one durable operation. Submitting the same plan twice provisions once: the second operation is rejected. Every created resource is recorded with its owner operation. When provisioning fails, the resources created so far are listed under Retirement; submitting again reuses them, and Delete resources removes them.

Registering an existing deployment

Register Existing records a Name, Environment, Owner, Description, the HTTP Endpoints of the nodes, and a Credential reference: the agent reads <REF>_USER and <REF>_PASSWORD from its environment, so the browser never sees the credentials. Use a read-only account. Register deployment records it.

The agent connects to each endpoint and records the version, host name, macros, disks, Keeper sessions, users, and replicated tables of each node, and the named clusters each node reports. It records conflicting observations, such as different versions or different members for the same shard, and the provenance and confidence of every part. It changes, recreates, and rotates nothing. Endpoints that do not answer are recorded as unreachable.

A registered deployment stays in Observe mode. Adoption is accepted only for providers that implement management; no provider integration exists for external deployments, so their adoption is rejected with that reason.

Operations

Every change is an operation with an identifier, the requester (filled in by the server), the revision of the desired configuration, its parameters, and events for every step with its evidence. The agent:

  • runs operations one at a time per cluster, in the order they were requested;
  • checks the requester's capability on the server before starting (EXECUTE AS), the environment, the mode, and whether the provider implements the operation; a refusal is recorded as Rejected;
  • records each step when it starts and when it is done; a restarted agent continues after the last completed step, and steps are written to be safe to repeat;
  • tries a failing step at most 3 times, then marks the operation Needs an operator: Retry runs it again, Cancel stops it;
  • marks an operation Outcome unknown when the provider does not answer in time, and checks again;
  • when several agents run, lets the earliest claim of an operation win; an operation without progress for 10 minutes is taken over.

Cancel stops a running operation at its next step, until it passes its irreversible boundary (for example, stopping a node during decommissioning). Steps already done are not undone: infrastructure and database changes are not rolled back atomically. Each operation describes its recovery when it fails.

Monitoring

Every 30 seconds, the agent queries each node once (version, uptime, replication queue and delay, read-only replicas, merges, mutations, distributed queues, disk, memory, load, running and failed queries, Keeper sessions) and asks each Keeper member for mntr. Every value carries the time it was collected; the console marks observations older than two minutes as stale. The health of a cluster is derived from all its members, never from one node. Values the agent could not collect are shown as such. Observations are kept 7 days.

Configuration and drift

The desired configuration is versioned: every change is a new revision, with secrets referenced and never stored. Change settings edits a catalog of server settings (max_concurrent_queries, max_connections, keep_alive_timeout, max_table_size_to_drop, background_pool_size, max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio) and settings of the default profile (max_memory_usage, max_execution_time, max_threads). The agent writes them to managed files on each node, reloads the configuration, and restarts the nodes, one at a time, only for settings that the server reports it cannot change without a restart (changeable_without_restart). It then checks the values on every node.

For managed clusters, the agent compares the desired values with what the nodes report, and the managed files with what it wrote. Differences are shown as drift, with two explicit choices: Apply the desired configuration writes the files again, and Adopt the observed values makes them the desired ones. Nothing is overwritten silently. Settings outside the catalog are not managed.

Scaling

  • Resize changes CPU and memory per node and recreates the nodes one at a time, after their peers have caught up. Storage cannot be resized by the docker-compose provider; on Kubernetes, Expand enlarges the data volumes when the storage class allows it.
  • Add replica creates a node, copies the schema of a peer, waits until every replicated table has caught up and its row count matches, then updates the topology. The new replica is ready only after that. On Kubernetes, Add replicas and Remove replicas add or remove one replica in every shard.
  • Decommission (on Nodes & Topology) removes a replica. It is refused for the last replica of a shard, for a Keeper member, and when the remaining replicas are not caught up or the Keeper quorum is uncertain.
  • Add shard creates the nodes of a new shard with the schema of shard 1, empty. Existing rows stay where they are; Distributed tables route new rows by their sharding key over all shards from then on, which changes the shard of a key. The dialog requires an acknowledgement of this.
  • Remove shard is accepted only for a shard without rows. Moving data between shards (source and target mappings, a sharding expression, backfill and catch-up, duplicate and missing-row checks, cutover) is not automated.

Client routing with chproxy

A cluster of the docker-compose provider can be created with chproxy, an HTTP proxy for ClickHouse, in front of its nodes. Choose chproxy as the client routing on the topology step, with:

  • the image (contentsquareplatform/chproxy:<version>, already on the Docker host; the agent does not pull images);
  • the proxy user that clients authenticate with, mapped to the administrative user of the nodes;
  • the limits of that user: concurrent queries and the maximum time of a query.

The agent creates a chproxy container with an endpoint on 127.0.0.1 and a generated configuration. The configuration takes both passwords from the environment, so the file contains no secret. The password of the proxy user is CH_PROXY_PASSWORD in the secrets file of the deployment on the agent host; give it to applications through your secret management. chproxy checks every node every 5 seconds and sends queries only to healthy nodes.

The cluster is ready only after chproxy finds every node healthy, sends queries to them, and refuses a wrong password. The agent keeps chproxy in step with the cluster, reloading its configuration without restarting it:

  • it adds new replicas and shards to the routing once they are ready;
  • before stopping a node (decommissioning, restart, resize, upgrade), it takes the node out of the routing, and puts it back when the node has caught up;
  • it removes decommissioned nodes and removed shards.

Nodes & Topology shows the endpoint, the proxy user and its limits, and the routed nodes with their health; the cluster is degraded when chproxy does not answer. chproxy routes HTTP only: clients of the native protocol connect to the nodes directly. chproxy itself is one container: when it stops, its clients lose access while direct connections keep working.

Keeper

Keeper is a separate ensemble, created at provisioning with 1, 3, or 5 members. The Keeper view shows each member's role, version, znode count, and latency, and whether a quorum exists. Changing the ClickHouse replicas never resizes Keeper, and membership changes are not implemented. Operations that remove nodes stop when the quorum is uncertain.

Keeper keeps its log and snapshots in its own volumes. Table backups contain the data and metadata to recreate replicated tables, not the coordination state; after the loss of Keeper data, replicated tables are recovered with SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA.

Maintenance and upgrades

Restart (one node, on Nodes & Topology) and Restart all nodes restart nodes one at a time. Before each node, the other replicas of its shard must be caught up; after it, the node must answer and catch up. ClickHouse has no drain command. With chproxy, the agent takes the node out of its routing before stopping it and puts it back once the node has caught up, so clients of chproxy are not sent to it; queries already running on the node fail. Without chproxy, clients connected to the node reconnect. Inserts queued for distribution are sent after the restart.

Upgrade changes the image of the nodes:

  1. the agent refuses a downgrade, a jump of more than a year of releases, and an image that is not on the host;
  2. it requires a verified backup of the cluster from the last 24 hours, or a recorded reason to waive it;
  3. it upgrades the other replicas of each shard before the first one, one node at a time;
  4. after each node, it checks that the node answers, reports the target version, catches up, and shows no load or data errors;
  5. a failed check stops the rollout, and the remaining nodes keep the previous version;
  6. after the last node, it checks the topology and replication.

Changing the image back does not downgrade data that the new version may have written. The recovery path is a restore of the pre-upgrade backup into a new cluster of the old version. Validate a target version in a lab cluster first.

Protection and recovery

Back up now backs up every shard from a caught-up replica, without ON CLUSTER, to an S3 destination of Backup & Restore, then opens each shard's backup with the Backup database engine and reads back the row count of every table. Only a backup with that verification counts for upgrades and retirement. The Overview shows the recovery targets next to the measured evidence: the time of the last verified backup.

SituationProcedure
A replica failed, others are healthyDecommission the failed node, then add a replica: it copies the schema and fetches the data from the healthy replicas.
Data lost on all replicasRestore a verified backup into a new cluster, check it, then switch clients (not automated).
Infrastructure replacedCreate a cluster with the same topology, then restore its backup (restore not automated).
Keeper data lostRecreate the ensemble, then run SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA on each replicated table (not automated).
Switch to a recovery siteFence the old deployment first, switch client routing, measure data freshness, plan failback (not automated; no cross-site provider).

The console never creates a second authoritative deployment on its own: switching clients to a recovered cluster is an operator's decision.

Retirement and deletion

Decommissioning a node: identify its roles; check the remaining replicas and the Keeper quorum; compare row counts when the node answers; check running queries and queued distributed inserts; take it out of the routing of chproxy, if the cluster has one; stop it (the irreversible boundary); remove it from the cluster definition; remove its replica metadata from Keeper with SYSTEM DROP REPLICA (justified because the agent stopped and removed the node); check the remaining cluster; remove the container; keep or delete its volume as chosen.

Retirement (Start retirement on Retirement) is separate from deletion:

  1. Dependency review: applications and connections, ingestion pipelines, scheduled jobs, users and integrations, dashboards, backup schedules, and other dependencies each need a recorded disposition. Unknown is not accepted.
  2. Protection: a verified final backup, or a recorded reason why none is needed (refused when the cluster holds data); the retention deadline of the retained resources; legal or operational holds.
  3. Execution: the agent checks the dependencies, that no other operation is in progress, and the protection gate; then stops the containers, records every resource with its disposition and deadline, and sets the mode to Retired.
  4. Deletion (Delete resources), a separate operation that needs the capability destroy: only the resources selected (Select all selects every remaining resource), only when Docker labels them as the cluster's, and not before their retention deadline. The result lists every resource as retained, stopped, or deleted, with its owner and evidence.

Backups made through Backup & Restore, the configuration history, the operations, and the audit records remain after retirement and deletion. A registered deployment is only removed from the inventory, with Retire from the inventory: the console has no access to its infrastructure.

Capabilities and audit

Each capability is a column of the cluster_capabilities table, granted as INSERT(<column>): view_clusters, register, create_cluster, adopt, configure, scale, keeper, maintain, upgrade, recover, decommission, retire, and destroy. The console checks them with CHECK GRANT to offer actions; the agent checks them again with EXECUTE AS <requester> CHECK GRANT before it executes an operation. Requesting an operation also needs INSERT on cluster_operations, cluster_events, and cluster_revisions.

For example, to let the role cluster_operators change configurations:

sql
GRANT INSERT(configure) ON console_admin.cluster_capabilities TO cluster_operators;

The role templates bundle them:

TemplateGrants
Cluster ViewerSELECT on the cluster tables and backup_destinations; view_clusters.
Cluster OperatorThe viewer's, plus requesting operations, and register, configure, maintain, scale, decommission.
Cluster AdministratorEvery capability, optionally including destroy, and INSERT on clusters.

Plans, submissions, cancellations, and retries are audited by the console with the operation ID as correlation ID; the agent audits each result, failure, and rejection. See Audit activity.

Troubleshooting

  • Operations stay queued. The inventory shows the agent's last heartbeat. Start the agent, and check that it serves the cluster's environment.
  • An operation is rejected. The message names the missing capability, the environment, the mode, or the unsafe condition.
  • An operation needs an operator. The failing step shows its message and evidence. Fix the cause (for example, put a missing image on the host), then select Retry, or Cancel.
  • Provisioning failed. The resources created so far are listed under Retirement. Submit the creation again from the plan, or delete the resources.
  • A cluster is degraded. Nodes & Topology shows which nodes do not answer, and whether the provider confirms them failed. Keeper shows the quorum.
  • Drift. Configuration lists the differences; apply the desired configuration or adopt the observed values.
  • An upgrade stopped. The operation lists the upgraded nodes. Find the cause before continuing; to return, restore the pre-upgrade backup into a new cluster.

guides/identity-providers.title: Identity providers
guides/identity-providers.description: How the Identity Providers pages of the web console work: LDAP and Active Directory user directories, single sign-on with Keycloak, and how the ClickHouse server accepts each kind of sign-in.

headings.text: How the server accepts directory users
Directory users seen since the start

guides/identity-providers.html:
Besides the users and passwords managed on the Users page, people can sign in to the console, and to ClickHouse, through an external identity provider: an LDAP directory (OpenLDAP or Active Directory), or single sign-on with Keycloak over OpenID Connect. The Identity Providers group of the sidebar has a page for each: LDAP and SSO (Keycloak).

This guide explains what each page shows and does, and the model behind it. For the procedures, see Configure an LDAP user directory and Configure single sign-on with Keycloak. To try single sign-on on a test machine first, follow the single sign-on tutorial.

What the server can check

The console has no session of its own on the server. Every query reaches the server with credentials, and the server authenticates each one (see Security model). So whatever identity provider is used, the server must accept what the console sends.

MethodIn this buildNotes
Password (SQL users, users.xml)YesThe default.
LDAP authenticator (ldap_servers, users IDENTIFIED WITH ldap)YesThe user exists in ClickHouse; the directory checks the password.
LDAP user directory (user_directories.ldap)YesUsers and roles come from the directory, with role_mapping. Works with OpenLDAP and Active Directory.
Kerberos (users IDENTIFIED WITH kerberos)YesHTTP Negotiate.
X.509 certificates, SSH keysYesFor services and the command-line client, not for people in a browser.
HTTP authenticator (http_authentication_servers, users IDENTIFIED WITH http)YesThe server sends the user name and the password (HTTP Basic) to an HTTP service, which answers yes or no.
JWT (IDENTIFIED WITH jwt)Parsed onlyThe type exists, but the server does not verify tokens.

LDAP and Active Directory are native to the server. OpenID Connect (Keycloak and other providers) is not: the server cannot check its tokens. The console therefore uses the HTTP authenticator for single sign-on, with a small service, the token authenticator, that checks the tokens for the server (see Why a token authenticator).

LDAP

The LDAP page (/console/idp-ldap) shows the LDAP user directories of the server. Users of such a directory sign in with their directory password and get their roles from their LDAP groups. They are not created in ClickHouse. The users of users.xml and those created with SQL keep working next to them, and the console is the same for both.

A user directory is part of the server configuration. The console shows it, tests a sign-in through it, and generates its configuration, but it does not change the server configuration.

To open the page, your user needs SELECT on system.user_directories. Without it, the page says that the console cannot tell whether an LDAP directory is configured.

Directory sign-in

The Directory sign-in (LDAP) box lists the LDAP user directories that system.user_directories reports. Its buttons are:

  • Configure LDAP…, when no directory exists, or Add a directory…, when one does: opens the configuration generator (see Generated configuration).
  • Test sign-in…, when a directory exists: see Test a directory sign-in.

Each directory has a Configuration… button, which opens the generator with the fields filled from the directory (except the connection settings, which the server does not report), and shows:

FieldContent
DirectoryThe name of the user directory and its precedence.
LDAP serverThe entry of ldap_servers it uses.
Default rolesThe roles every directory user gets. A role that does not exist on the server is marked: create it, or the users get nothing from it.
Roles from groupsThe group search of role_mapping: the attribute, the base DN, the scope, the filter, and the prefix.
PrecedenceWhether a user of the same name in an earlier directory signs in there instead.

When the groups map to roles but no role exists yet, the box warns that roles are mapped by name, and that you must create the roles the groups stand for.

How the server accepts directory users

The server checks the password of a directory user by binding to the LDAP server as the bind DN of ldap_servers, in which {user_name} is replaced by the name the user signs in with. It then finds the user's groups with the search of role_mapping: a group whose attribute is <prefix><role> gives the role <role>, if that role exists. Groups without the prefix are ignored. The roles of <roles> are given to every directory user. See LDAP for every setting.

AspectBehavior
Verification cooldownThe server checks a password with the directory on every request, unless a check succeeded within verification_cooldown seconds. The console sends a request for every action, about 80 when signing in, so the generated configuration uses 300 seconds. A user disabled in the directory keeps access for at most this long.
PrecedenceThe directories are tried in order: users.xml, then the users created with SQL, then LDAP. A local user with the same name as a directory user comes first.
ChangesA new user directory is created only when the server starts. Later changes of the LDAP server settings take effect with SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG.
OffboardingDisable the user, or remove them from the groups, in the directory: it takes effect after the cooldown. Directory users cannot be suspended or deleted in the console.
Access reviewsClickHouse cannot list the directory: review group membership in LDAP.
TransportPasswords travel with every request: serve the console over HTTPS, and never use LDAP without TLS.

Directory users appear on the Users page, read-only, once they have signed in. See Users and roles.

Generated configuration

Configure LDAP… (or Add a directory…) opens a form that generates the XML of an LDAP server and an LDAP user directory, to save as a file in config.d of the server. The fields are Server name, Host, Port, Encryption (LDAPS or StartTLS), CA certificate file, Bind DN, Verification cooldown (seconds), Default roles, and, under Roles from LDAP groups, Base DN of the groups, Search filter, Attribute, and Prefix. Copy copies the result.

The configuration is secure by default:

  • LDAPS (port 636) or StartTLS (port 389), never plain LDAP;
  • tls_minimum_protocol_version tls1.2;
  • the certificate of the LDAP server always checked (tls_require_cert demand), with your certificate authority in tls_ca_cert_file;
  • a verification_cooldown, 300 seconds by default.

The form checks that the bind DN contains {user_name}, and that the search filter contains {bind_dn} or {user_name}, so that it finds the groups of the user. Leave the base DN of the groups empty for no group mapping: the users then get only the default roles.

For Active Directory, bind as {user_name}@<domain> and find nested groups; see Active Directory.

Test a directory sign-in

Test sign-in… signs in once with a user name and a password, with a query that reads the user's name and enabled roles. It shows Signed in as, Through (the directory that accepted the user), and Roles, or the reason the server refused the sign-in. The password is used for this request only: it is not stored, shown again, or written to the audit log. The test is recorded in the audit log (action test_directory_sign_in) when your user can write it.

Because of verification_cooldown, the server may reuse a successful check for that many seconds, so a change in the directory shows only after it.

Directory users seen since the start

ClickHouse knows a directory user from their first sign-in after the server started. This box lists those users, with their directory, and links to each on the Users page. It needs SELECT on system.users. After a restart, the list starts empty again.

Attributes from the directory

Data Access Policies can take user attributes, such as the department, from the same directory. Define the attribute with the source ldap on the Attributes tab of Data Access Policies, and run the access policy worker with LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_URL (LDAPS or StartTLS). The worker reads the values; the console does not connect to the directory. See Attributes and Import user attributes.

SSO (Keycloak)

The SSO (Keycloak) page (/console/idp-sso) keeps the settings of a Keycloak provider, tests the connection to it, and tries a sign-in. It also shows how the server accepts these sign-ins, and the users of single sign-on.

The console signs users in with the Authorization Code flow and PKCE, as a public client, so no client secret is kept in the browser. The tokens of a test are checked and then dropped, never stored.

Provider settings

The settings are kept in the table idp_providers of the console database (console_admin by default). Until it exists, the page shows Set up single sign-on: Set up creates the table (it needs CREATE TABLE on the console database), and does not add a provider. See Identity provider tables.

Add Keycloak… (and Edit… on a provider) has these fields:

FieldDefaultMeaning
NameKeycloakThe name of the provider in the console.
Client IDclickhouse-consoleThe client of the console in the realm.
Keycloak URL—The address of the Keycloak server, without /realms. HTTPS; plain HTTP only on localhost.
Realm—The realm. The issuer is built as <Keycloak URL>/realms/<realm> and shown below the field.
Scopesopenid profile emailMust include openid.
User name claimpreferred_usernameThe claim that is the ClickHouse user name.
Group claimgroupsEmpty for none.
Role prefixclickhouse-A group <prefix><role> gives the role <role>; other groups are ignored.
Default roles—Roles every SSO user gets, comma-separated.
EnabledOn

Every change is a statement that you review before it runs, and it is recorded in the audit log, like the other settings of the console. A changed provider loses its last connection test: the test describes the settings it ran with. Remove… removes only the settings in the console; the realm and the client in Keycloak are not changed.

Reading the page needs SELECT on idp_providers; changing the providers and storing connection tests needs INSERT on it.

The form and the empty page show what the client of the console in Keycloak needs, with the values of this console:

SettingValue
Client authenticationOff (a public client).
Authentication flowStandard flow only; no implicit flow, no direct access grants.
PKCE methodS256 (Advanced → Proof Key for Code Exchange).
Valid redirect URI<console origin>/console/oidc-callback
Valid post logout redirect URI<console origin>/console/login
Web origin<console origin>
Group claimA Group Membership mapper, without the full path, named after the group claim (groups).
AudienceAn Audience mapper that adds the client to the access token, for the server to check.

Test connection

Test connection checks the provider from the browser, as the console will use it:

CheckPasses when
Discovery document<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration answers. A wrong realm is told apart from an unreachable server: if the realm master answers, the page says that the realm does not exist (realm names are case-sensitive).
IssuerThe issuer of the document is the configured issuer. Otherwise tokens would be refused: check the hostname setting of Keycloak (KC_HOSTNAME).
Authorization Code flowThe provider offers the response type code.
PKCEThe provider reports PKCE with S256.
EndpointsThe authorization, token, keys, and end-session endpoints use HTTPS (plain HTTP only on localhost).
Signing keysThe provider has a signing key the console can verify: RS256, ES256, or PS256.
Default rolesThe default roles exist on the server.
Roles for groupsSome role exists for the groups to map to.

The result is stored with the provider (with INSERT on idp_providers), shown as Last connection test with its time, and recorded in the audit log. The client itself (redirect URI, web origin, PKCE) is checked by a test sign-in.

Test sign-in

Test sign-in… opens the Keycloak sign-in page in a separate window, where you sign in as the user to test. The sign-in is a real one: Authorization Code with PKCE (S256), state, nonce, and prompt=login, so that Keycloak asks for the password every time, even when the browser already has a session with it. The console checks that the answer comes from the expected issuer (RFC 9207), exchanges the code for tokens, and verifies:

  • the signature of the ID token and of the access token, with the provider's keys (RS256, PS256, ES256 only);
  • the issuer, the audience, the client it was issued to, the expiry, and the nonce of the ID token;
  • that the audience of the access token names the client of the console, so that the server can use it.

It then shows Signed in as, Name and e-mail, Groups, Roles it would get (with the roles that do not exist marked), ClickHouse user (whether a user of that name exists, where, and with which authentication), and Access token (how long it is valid and its audience, or why the server cannot use it). The tokens are dropped afterwards: they are not stored, shown, or recorded. The test is recorded in the audit log.

The browser must allow pop-ups for the console: the window is opened directly in the click.

Signing in to ClickHouse

The Signing in to ClickHouse box explains how the server accepts the sign-ins, and shows:

  • Sign-in page: whether the sign-in page offers single sign-on, with its issuer and client, from the server configuration (web_console.sso_*). The providers of this page are for the tests: the sign-in page reads the server configuration, which it can read before anyone is signed in.
  • Users of single sign-on: the users identified with an HTTP authentication server, with their default roles. It needs SELECT on system.users.

How single sign-on works

Sign in with Keycloak

With web_console.sso_issuer and web_console.sso_client_id set in the server configuration, the sign-in page offers Sign in with Keycloak (the text follows web_console.sso_name). The values are served in /console/config.json. They are public: the client of the console has no secret. See undefined.

  1. The console opens the provider's sign-in page in a separate window, with Authorization Code and PKCE.
  2. The window returns to /console/oidc-callback, which passes the answer to the console page and closes. Without the PKCE verifier, which stays in the console page, the code cannot be exchanged for a token.
  3. The console verifies the ID token, takes the user name from its claim (sso_username_claim, default preferred_username), and signs in to the server with that user name and the access token as the password.

The access token is the password of the session, kept in memory only, like a password. The console refreshes it at 70% of its lifespan, and posts each new token to the native panels (console-credentials messages, from the console to its own frames). When the provider refuses a refresh, because the session ended there or the user was disabled, the console signs out and closes every panel. Signing out also ends the session with the provider (its end_session_endpoint), and returns to the sign-in page.

If the provider signs the user in but the server refuses the token, the sign-in page says that the user must exist on the server, identified with the token authenticator, and that the authenticator must be running.

The token authenticator

The token authenticator (sso_authenticator.mjs, the sso-authenticator command of the tools image) is the HTTP authentication server sso of the server. For the users IDENTIFIED WITH http SERVER 'sso', the server sends it the user name and the password (the access token) as HTTP Basic credentials, and accepts the sign-in when the answer is 200. The authenticator checks:

  • the signature, with the provider's keys, cached and fetched again for an unknown key ID at most every 30 seconds; only RS256, PS256, and ES256, so a token signed with none or a shared secret is refused;
  • the issuer;
  • the type: an access token, not an ID token (typ Bearer);
  • the client it was issued to (azp) and the audience;
  • the expiry and the time it becomes valid, with 30 seconds for clock skew;
  • that the user name claim is the user name of the sign-in.

Whatever it cannot check is refused, including when the provider's keys are unavailable: it fails closed. It logs the reason of each refusal, never the token. See Token authenticator API and Helper processes.

The authenticator is on the path of every query of an SSO user: run it next to the server, reachable only from it, with short timeouts.

User sync

Users must exist in ClickHouse before they sign in. The authenticator can keep them in line with the provider. With a confidential client of the provider that can read users and groups, every interval (60 seconds by default) it:

  • creates a user IDENTIFIED WITH http SERVER 'sso' for each enabled member of the groups clickhouse-<role> (the prefix is SSO_ROLE_PREFIX);
  • grants the roles of their groups and the default roles, and revokes the roles they no longer get; a role that does not exist is skipped;
  • drops the users who left every such group, or were disabled or deleted.

It changes only the users identified with this authentication server, never a user with a password or another method, and skips a name that already exists with another method. When the provider shows no group with the prefix while such users exist, it refuses to apply the result, so that a wrong setting or a failure of the provider cannot remove every user at once. Each change is recorded in the audit log. See User sync.

Without the sync, an administrator creates the users:

sql
CREATE USER alice IDENTIFIED WITH http SERVER 'sso' SCHEME 'BASIC';
GRANT analysts TO alice;

Why a token authenticator

There are several ways to accept OpenID Connect sign-ins with this server:

OptionAssessment
A token authenticator, through the HTTP authenticatorUsed. No change to the server; works with any OpenID Connect provider; the token is checked on every request. The users must exist in ClickHouse, which the sync takes care of, and the service is on the path of every query.
Keycloak with LDAP federation, and the server on the same directoryOne identity, but not single sign-on: the console signs in with directory passwords.
Token validation in the serverThe type jwt exists, but its validation would have to be written and maintained in the server.
A proxy that signs users in and passes a headerNot suitable: the server has no trusted-header authentication, so the proxy would have to hold a password for every user.

SAML providers and social sign-in are reached through Keycloak, which brokers them: the console only speaks OpenID Connect to Keycloak.

Limits

  • Panels that keep their token. The SQL Console, the Web Terminal, and ClickStack keep the token they started with, because their embedding cannot receive new credentials. Reload them after the token expires.
  • Revocation latency. A token is accepted until it expires, as for any bearer token. A user disabled in Keycloak cannot refresh, so the console signs out at the next refresh, and the sync drops the user within its interval: access ends within the lifespan of an access token, 5 minutes by default in Keycloak.
  • Users must exist. The sync creates them, or an administrator does.
  • Names. A user created with a password or another method is never changed by the sync: give SSO users their own names.
  • Transport. Serve the console and Keycloak over HTTPS: the authenticator and the console accept plain HTTP only for a provider on localhost.
  • Other providers. The checks and the sign-in are generic OpenID Connect, but the issuer of the SSO page is built from a Keycloak URL and realm, and the sync uses the admin API of Keycloak.

how-to/deploy-with-docker-compose.title: Deploy with Docker Compose
how-to/deploy-with-docker-compose.description: Deploy the ClickHouse server with the web console and its helper processes on one Docker host with Docker Compose, then upgrade or roll back.

headings.text: Cluster agent on a Docker host

how-to/deploy-with-docker-compose.html:
Use this guide to deploy the ClickHouse server with the web console, and its helper processes, on one Docker host, from the image archives and the deploy/ directory of a release of the console. Every environment gets the same images; what differs is in .env and config.d/.

For Kubernetes, see Deploy on Kubernetes. For the components and how they fit together, see Architecture.

Before you begin

  • Docker with Compose v2 (docker compose).
  • The release of the console, made by package_images.sh (see Build and package the images):
    FileContent
    clickhouse-server-console-<version>-amd64.tar.gzThe image clickhouse-server-console:<version>: the official clickhouse/clickhouse-server image of the same release, with the server binary of this build, which serves the console at /console. Every setting and environment variable of the official image applies.
    clickhouse-console-tools-<version>-amd64.tar.gzThe image clickhouse-console-tools:<version>: Node.js with the helper processes. The first argument chooses the process: backup-worker, cluster-agent, access-policy-worker, or sso-authenticator.
    MANIFEST.txtThe commit, the base image digest, and the image IDs.
    SHA256SUMSThe checksums of the archives.
    deploy/compose.yaml and its overrides, kubernetes.yaml, .env.example, config.d/, service-accounts.sql, and README.md.

    The version is <ClickHouse release>-console.<commit>.

Load and verify the images

In the directory of the release:

bash
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
docker load -i clickhouse-server-console-<version>-amd64.tar.gz
docker load -i clickhouse-console-tools-<version>-amd64.tar.gz

sha256sum prints OK for each archive, and docker load prints the name of each image. Compare the image IDs with MANIFEST.txt:

bash
docker image inspect clickhouse-server-console:<version> clickhouse-console-tools:<version> --format '{{.Id}}'

To use a registry instead, tag and push both images, then use the registry names in compose.yaml:

bash
docker tag clickhouse-server-console:<version> registry.example.com/clickhouse/clickhouse-server-console:<version>
docker push registry.example.com/clickhouse/clickhouse-server-console:<version>

Configure the environment

Work in the deploy/ directory.

  1. Create .env, readable by its owner only, and fill it in:

    bash
    cp .env.example .env && chmod 600 .env
    VariableMeaning
    CONSOLE_VERSIONThe version of the images, already set by package_images.sh.
    CONSOLE_BIND, CONSOLE_HTTP_PORT, CONSOLE_NATIVE_PORTThe address and ports the server publishes on the host (default 127.0.0.1, 8123, 9000). Use the host's address, or 0.0.0.0, only behind a firewall or a TLS-terminating proxy: otherwise the console sends passwords over plain HTTP.
    CLICKHOUSE_ADMIN_PASSWORDThe password of default, the first administrator (with access management).
    BACKUP_WORKER_PASSWORD, ACCESS_POLICY_WORKER_PASSWORD, CLUSTER_AGENT_PASSWORDThe passwords of the service accounts of the helpers.
    ACCESS_POLICY_INTERVAL_SECONDS, ATTRIBUTE_FEED, ATTRIBUTE_FEED_SOURCE, ATTRIBUTE_FEED_TOKENThe access policy worker: its interval, and an optional attribute feed.
    DOCKER_GID, CLUSTER_AGENT_UID, CLUSTER_AGENT_STATE_DIR, CLUSTER_AGENT_ENVIRONMENTS, CLUSTER_AGENT_KUBECONFIG, CLUSTER_AGENT_K8S_NAMESPACESThe cluster agent (compose.cluster-agent.yaml).
    BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER, VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_TRANSIT_KEY, BUNDLE_DESTINATION, BUNDLE_EVERY_HOURSServer bundles (compose.bundles.yaml).
    SSO_NAME, SSO_ISSUER, SSO_CLIENT_ID, SSO_SYNC_CLIENT_ID, SSO_SYNC_PASSWORD, SSO_ROLE_PREFIX, SSO_DEFAULT_ROLESSingle sign-on (compose.sso.yaml).

    Every variable is described in Configuration.

  2. Edit config.d/web-console.xml: the links of the Resources group (internal mirrors, or empty on a network without Internet access), the database of the console tables (admin_database, default console_admin), and the S3 endpoints allowed for backups (backup_s3_endpoints). A configuration reload applies changes without a restart. See undefined.

  3. Optionally, create backup-destinations.env with the S3 credentials of the backup destinations, named after their credential reference: <REF>_ACCESS_KEY_ID and <REF>_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. Keep it readable by its owner only.

Further server configuration goes into more files mounted into /etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/ and /etc/clickhouse-server/users.d/, as for the official image: add a line to the volumes of the clickhouse service for each.

Start the server

bash
docker compose up -d clickhouse
docker compose ps clickhouse

The service becomes healthy when /ping answers. It keeps its data and logs in the volumes clickhouse-data and clickhouse-logs.

Sign in and set up

  1. Open http://<host>:<CONSOLE_HTTP_PORT>/console, and sign in as default with CLICKHOUSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD.
  2. Under Administration, select Set up on Component Access, Backup & Restore, Clusters, and the tabs of Data Access Policies that you use. This creates the console tables. See Setting up.
  3. Create the service accounts of the helpers, as described in Create the service accounts:
    bash
    set -a; . ./.env; set +a
docker compose exec -T clickhouse clickhouse-client --password "$CLICKHOUSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD" \
    --param_backup_pw="$BACKUP_WORKER_PASSWORD" --param_policy_pw="$ACCESS_POLICY_WORKER_PASSWORD" \
    --param_agent_pw="$CLUSTER_AGENT_PASSWORD" \
    --multiquery < service-accounts.sql

    Every password in the command must be set in .env. For a helper you do not deploy, for example the cluster agent, delete its section of service-accounts.sql and its --param_... argument instead of passing an empty password. The section of sso_sync is commented out: with single sign-on, uncomment it and add --param_sso_pw="$SSO_SYNC_PASSWORD".

Start the helpers

bash
docker compose up -d

This starts the backup worker and the access policy worker next to the server. Their heartbeats appear on the Backup & Restore Overview and on the Cluster Inventory.

Optional parts are override files, added with -f to compose.yaml. Use the same list of files in every later docker compose command:

FileAddsGuide
compose.cluster-agent.yamlThe cluster agent, which creates and operates clusters on this host.Cluster agent on a Docker host
compose.bundles.yamlServer bundles in the backup worker: the configuration of this deployment and its secrets, encrypted.Server bundles
compose.sso.yamlThe token authenticator, and config.d/sso.xml in the server, for single sign-on with Keycloak.Configure single sign-on with Keycloak

For example, with the cluster agent and single sign-on:

bash
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.cluster-agent.yaml -f compose.sso.yaml up -d

Cluster agent on a Docker host

The agent uses the host network and the Docker socket. Access to the socket is equivalent to root on the host: run the agent only where that is acceptable. Its state directory (CLUSTER_AGENT_STATE_DIR) is mounted at the same path as on the host, because the Docker daemon resolves the paths of the deployments it generates, and must be writable by CLUSTER_AGENT_UID:

bash
sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/clickhouse-console/clusters && sudo chown 1000 /var/lib/clickhouse-console/clusters
stat -c %g /var/run/docker.sock                    # the value of DOCKER_GID
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.cluster-agent.yaml up -d
