  • Back up the state directory: it holds the agent's key pair (agent-key.pem) and the secrets of the clusters it created.
  • The images of the clusters (clickhouse/clickhouse-server:<version>, and contentsquareplatform/chproxy:<version> for client routing) must be on the host: the agent does not pull images.
  • Set CLUSTER_AGENT_KUBECONFIG to a kubeconfig on the host to enable the kubernetes provider as well.
  • On Docker Desktop, the host network is that of Docker Desktop's virtual machine: enable host networking in its settings (Resources → Network). The agent then reaches the published ports of the server.

See Clusters.

Server bundles

With BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER=file (the default), create the master key once, keep a copy out of band with its fingerprint, then start the worker with the override:

bash
mkdir -p bundle-keys restore-staging && sudo chown 101:101 bundle-keys restore-staging && sudo chmod 700 bundle-keys restore-staging
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.bundles.yaml run --rm backup-worker backup-worker bundle-key-init --key-file /keys/bundle.key
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.bundles.yaml up -d backup-worker

Without the key, no bundle can be decrypted. See Server bundles for the other key providers.

Verify

  • docker compose ps shows every service running, and the server healthy.
  • docker compose logs backup-worker access-policy-worker shows no connection or authentication errors.
  • In the console, Backup & Restore → Overview shows the heartbeat of the backup worker.

Upgrade

  1. Load and verify the new archives, as in Load and verify the images.
  2. Set CONSOLE_VERSION in .env to the new version.
  3. Apply, with the same list of files as before:
    bash
    docker compose up -d

The data stays in the volumes.

Roll back

Set the previous version in CONSOLE_VERSION again, and run docker compose up -d.

Warning

Rolling back to a server older than the ClickHouse release of the data is not supported by ClickHouse. Keep the release of the base image when you roll back the console: a version with the same <ClickHouse release> part.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
set CONSOLE_VERSION in .env (or another set ... in .env)A required variable is empty in .env.
The helpers do not startThey wait until the server is healthy. Check docker compose logs clickhouse.
A helper logs an authentication errorIts service account does not exist, or its password differs from .env: run service-accounts.sql again with the same passwords.
The console cannot be reached from another machineCONSOLE_BIND is 127.0.0.1 by default. Put a TLS-terminating proxy in front, or bind to the host's address behind a firewall.

how-to/deploy-on-kubernetes.title: Deploy on Kubernetes
how-to/deploy-on-kubernetes.description: Deploy the ClickHouse server with the web console, the backup worker, the access policy worker, and the cluster agent on Kubernetes with kubernetes.yaml.
how-to/deploy-on-kubernetes.html:
Use this guide to deploy the ClickHouse server with the web console, and its helper processes, on Kubernetes, with the manifest kubernetes.yaml of the deploy/ directory of a release of the console.

For one Docker host, see Deploy with Docker Compose.

What the manifest creates

All objects are in the namespace clickhouse-console:

ObjectPurpose
ConfigMap web-console-configweb-console.xml, mounted into /etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/ of the server: the Resources links, admin_database, and backup_s3_endpoints.
StatefulSet clickhouseThe server with the console, one replica, with a 20 GiB volume data at /var/lib/clickhouse. It requests 1 CPU and 2 GiB of memory, with a limit of 4 GiB, and is ready when /ping answers.
Service clickhouseThe ports 8123 (HTTP, with the console) and 9000 (native).
Deployment backup-workerThe backup worker, as backup_worker.
Deployment access-policy-workerThe access policy worker, as access_policy_worker, every 60 seconds.
ServiceAccount, ClusterRole, and ClusterRoleBinding cluster-agentWhat the cluster agent does with kubectl, and nothing more.
ConfigMap cluster-agent-kubeconfigA kubeconfig that uses the service account of the pod.
PersistentVolumeClaim cluster-agent-state1 GiB for the state of the agent, including its key pair.
Deployment cluster-agentThe cluster agent with the kubernetes provider only, as cluster_agent.

The cluster agent manages clusters with the ClickHouse operator in the same Kubernetes cluster, in the namespaces that match CLUSTER_AGENT_K8S_NAMESPACES (chc-*). Kubernetes RBAC cannot express a namespace prefix, so the agent restricts the namespaces itself. The agent's key pair for administrator passwords is kept in its volume: losing it makes queued creations undecryptable. If you do not manage clusters, remove the part of the agent from the manifest. See Kubernetes provider.

Before you begin

  • A Kubernetes cluster and kubectl with the rights to create a namespace, cluster roles, and the objects above.
  • The image archives and the deploy/ directory of the release (see Deploy with Docker Compose). package_images.sh sets the version tags of the images in kubernetes.yaml.
  • For the cluster agent, the ClickHouse operator in the cluster.

Deploy

  1. Make the images available to the nodes

    Either push both images to your registry and change the image: lines of kubernetes.yaml to the registry names, or import the archives on every node: with k3d, k3d image import; with containerd, ctr -n k8s.io images import.

    The containers use imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent.

  2. Create the Secret with the passwords

    bash
    kubectl create namespace clickhouse-console
kubectl -n clickhouse-console create secret generic clickhouse-console-passwords \
    --from-literal=admin=... --from-literal=backup_worker=... --from-literal=access_policy_worker=... \
    --from-literal=cluster_agent=...

    admin is the password of default, the first administrator (with access management). The other keys are the passwords of the service accounts.

  3. Adjust the configuration

    Edit the ConfigMap web-console-config in kubernetes.yaml: the Resources links (internal mirrors, or empty on a network without Internet access), the admin database, and the S3 endpoints allowed for backups. See undefined.

    For S3 credentials of backup destinations, uncomment the envFrom of the backup worker, and create the Secret clickhouse-console-backup-destinations with the keys <REF>_ACCESS_KEY_ID and <REF>_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY.

  4. Apply the manifest

    bash
    kubectl apply -f kubernetes.yaml
kubectl -n clickhouse-console rollout status statefulset/clickhouse

  5. Open the console

    bash
    kubectl -n clickhouse-console port-forward svc/clickhouse 8123:8123

    Open http://localhost:8123/console, and sign in as default with the password of the key admin.

  6. Set up and create the service accounts

    Under Administration, select Set up on Component Access, Backup & Restore, Clusters, and the tabs of Data Access Policies that you use. Then create the service accounts with service-accounts.sql, running clickhouse-client with kubectl -n clickhouse-console exec -i clickhouse-0 --: see Create the service accounts.

    Once the accounts exist, the heartbeats of the workers appear on Backup & Restore → Overview and on the Cluster Inventory.

Expose the console

For access from outside the cluster, put an Ingress with TLS in front of the Service clickhouse: the console sends passwords in HTTP headers, so they must not travel over plain HTTP.

More configuration

Further server configuration, such as an LDAP user directory, goes into more keys of a ConfigMap, mounted into /etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/ like web-console.xml. A new user directory needs a restart of the server:

bash
kubectl -n clickhouse-console rollout restart statefulset/clickhouse

Upgrade and roll back

Make the new images available to the nodes, change the image tags in kubernetes.yaml, and run kubectl apply -f kubernetes.yaml. The data stays in the volumes. To roll back, set the previous tags again and apply.

Warning

Rolling back to a server older than the ClickHouse release of the data is not supported by ClickHouse. Keep the release of the base image when you roll back the console.

how-to/create-service-accounts.title: Create the service accounts
how-to/create-service-accounts.description: Create the ClickHouse accounts of the helper processes of the web console with service-accounts.sql, with the least privileges each one needs.
how-to/create-service-accounts.html:
Use this guide to create the ClickHouse accounts that the helper processes of the console sign in with: backup_worker, access_policy_worker, cluster_agent, and sso_sync. The file service-accounts.sql of the deploy/ directory creates them with the privileges each one needs, and nothing more.

For what each helper does, see Helper processes. For the full list of privileges, see Service accounts.

Before you begin

  • A running server, and an administrator with access management, for example default of the deployment.
  • The console tables created: select Set up on Component Access, Backup & Restore, Clusters, and the tabs of Data Access Policies that you use (see Setting up). The accounts are granted privileges on these tables, in console_admin (the admin_database setting).
  • A password for each account, in .env with Docker Compose, or in the Secret on Kubernetes.

The accounts

AccountHelperPrivileges
backup_workerBackup workerA role made with the Backup Administrator template, for the databases of the schedules. For server bundles: CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, INSERT, SELECT, and BACKUP on console_admin.server_bundle*.
access_policy_workerAccess policy workerSELECT on console_admin.*; INSERT on dap_owned, dap_deployments, audit_log, and, with an attribute feed, dap_user_attributes; SELECT on system.users, roles, role_grants, grants, and row_policies; SHOW USERS, SHOW ROLES, SHOW ROW POLICIES; IMPERSONATE on each rule author.
cluster_agentCluster agentSELECT and INSERT on clusters, cluster_revisions, cluster_operations, cluster_events, cluster_observations, and cluster_resources; SELECT on cluster_capabilities and backup_destinations; INSERT on audit_log; IMPERSONATE on each user who requests cluster operations.
sso_syncToken authenticator, for its user syncCREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER; SHOW USERS, SHOW ROLES; SELECT on system.users, roles, and role_grants; INSERT on audit_log; the roles of the groups WITH ADMIN OPTION.

Each account is created IDENTIFIED WITH sha256_password, with its password passed as a query parameter, so that the password is not written in the file.

Fill in the placeholders

The privileges that depend on your deployment are placeholders in angle brackets. The lines that contain one are commented out, so that nothing is granted by guess. Edit service-accounts.sql, and replace each with real names:

  1. The role of the backup worker. Create a role with the Backup Administrator template on Roles & Permissions (see Role templates), for the databases that the schedules back up. The template lists its exact privileges before it creates the role. Then:

    sql
    GRANT backup_admin TO backup_worker;

  2. The rule authors of the access policy worker. The worker acts as the author of each rule, with EXECUTE AS, so it needs no privilege to grant anything itself, only the right to impersonate the authors:

    sql
    GRANT IMPERSONATE ON alice TO access_policy_worker;

  3. The requesters of the cluster agent. The agent checks the capabilities of each requester with EXECUTE AS <user> CHECK GRANT:

    sql
    GRANT IMPERSONATE ON alice TO cluster_agent;

  4. The roles of the user sync. Grant the roles that the groups clickhouse-<role> stand for, and the default roles of the sync, with the admin option, so that the sync can grant those and no other role:

    sql
    GRANT analysts, console_admin_reader TO sso_sync WITH ADMIN OPTION;

    ROLE ADMIN would also work, but lets the account grant every role.

The section of sso_sync is commented out in the file: uncomment it only with single sign-on. Delete the sections of the other accounts you do not deploy, for example cluster_agent without the cluster agent, and leave out their parameters below. The names backup_admin and alice are examples.

Run the file

Run the file as the administrator, with one --param_ argument per account: backup_pw, policy_pw, agent_pw, and, with single sign-on, sso_pw. A parameter that a statement uses but the command does not pass stops the file at that statement.

In the deploy/ directory, with the passwords of .env:

bash
set -a; . ./.env; set +a
docker compose exec -T clickhouse clickhouse-client --password "$CLICKHOUSE_ADMIN_PASSWORD" \
    --param_backup_pw="$BACKUP_WORKER_PASSWORD" --param_policy_pw="$ACCESS_POLICY_WORKER_PASSWORD" \
    --param_agent_pw="$CLUSTER_AGENT_PASSWORD" \
    --multiquery < service-accounts.sql

With the section of sso_sync uncommented, add --param_sso_pw="$SSO_SYNC_PASSWORD".

With the passwords of the Secret clickhouse-console-passwords:

bash
secret() { kubectl -n clickhouse-console get secret clickhouse-console-passwords -o "jsonpath={.data.$1}" | base64 -d; }
kubectl -n clickhouse-console exec -i clickhouse-0 -- clickhouse-client --password "$(secret admin)" \
    --param_backup_pw="$(secret backup_worker)" --param_policy_pw="$(secret access_policy_worker)" \
    --param_agent_pw="$(secret cluster_agent)" \
    --multiquery < service-accounts.sql

The Secret of kubernetes.yaml has no password for sso_sync: to use single sign-on, add a key for it, uncomment the section of sso_sync, and add its --param_sso_pw.

The statements use CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS, and the grants can be repeated, so you can run the file again after changing it. An existing account keeps its password: to change one, use ALTER USER ... IDENTIFIED WITH sha256_password BY ..., then update the password of the helper and restart it.

Verify

sql
SHOW GRANTS FOR backup_worker;
SHOW GRANTS FOR access_policy_worker;
SHOW GRANTS FOR cluster_agent;
SHOW GRANTS FOR sso_sync;

Then start the helpers. Their heartbeats appear on Backup & Restore → Overview and on the Cluster Inventory, and the token authenticator logs users synced.

Least privilege

  • One account per helper. Do not share an account between helpers, and do not run a helper as default.
  • Impersonation, not grants. The access policy worker and the cluster agent act as the users they work for, with EXECUTE AS, so ClickHouse checks those users' privileges. Grant IMPERSONATE only on the users who author rules or request cluster operations.
  • Named roles for the sync. Grant sso_sync the roles of the groups WITH ADMIN OPTION rather than ROLE ADMIN. The sync changes only the users identified with its authentication server; checking tokens needs no account at all.
  • The backup role. Limit the role of the backup worker to the databases of the schedules. Grant the server bundle tables only when you use server bundles.
  • Protect the accounts. Mark the service accounts as protected accounts, so that the console does not delete or suspend them (see Protected accounts), and keep .env readable by its owner only (chmod 600).

how-to/configure-ldap.title: Configure an LDAP user directory
how-to/configure-ldap.description: Let the users of an LDAP directory or of Active Directory sign in to the web console and to ClickHouse with their directory password, with roles from their groups.

headings.text: Create the roles of the groups

how-to/configure-ldap.html:
Use this guide to let the users of an LDAP directory (OpenLDAP, Active Directory, or another LDAP server) sign in to the console and to ClickHouse with their directory password, with roles given by their LDAP groups. The users are not created in ClickHouse; the users of users.xml and those created with SQL keep working.

For how directory sign-in works, see LDAP. For every setting of the server, see LDAP.

Before you begin

  • A user of the console with SELECT on system.user_directories, to open Identity Providers → LDAP, and with access management, to create roles.
  • Access to the server configuration (config.d), and the right to restart the server.
  • The LDAP server reachable from the ClickHouse host over LDAPS (port 636) or StartTLS (port 389), and the certificate of its certificate authority (CA) as a PEM file.
  • For roles from groups: the base DN of the groups, and a naming convention for the groups that stand for ClickHouse roles. This guide uses the prefix clickhouse-: the group clickhouse-analysts gives the role analysts.

Generate the configuration

  1. In the console, under Identity Providers, select LDAP.

  2. Select Configure LDAP…, or Add a directory… when a directory already exists.

  3. Fill in the form:

    FieldExampleNotes
    Server namecorpThe name of the entry in ldap_servers: letters, digits, _, and -.
    Hostldap.example.comA name that is in the certificate of the LDAP server. See the host name localhost.
    PortemptyEmpty: 636 for LDAPS, 389 for StartTLS.
    EncryptionLDAPS (TLS from the start)Or StartTLS (on the plain port).
    CA certificate file/etc/clickhouse-server/ldap-ca.crtThe CA of the LDAP server, on the ClickHouse host.
    Bind DNuid={user_name},ou=users,dc=example,dc=org{user_name} is replaced by the name the user signs in with. For Active Directory, see Active Directory.
    Verification cooldown (seconds)300See Verification cooldown.
    Default rolesconsole_admin_readerRoles every directory user gets, comma-separated.
    Base DN of the groupsou=groups,dc=example,dc=orgEmpty: no roles from groups.
    Search filter(&(objectClass=groupOfNames)(member={bind_dn}))Must contain {bind_dn} or {user_name}.
    AttributecnThe attribute of a group that holds the role name.
    Prefixclickhouse-Groups without the prefix are ignored.

    The role console_admin_reader, created when you set up Component Access, lets the console apply its access policy to the users. Leave Default roles empty if you do not use it.

  4. Select Copy. The text is the configuration of an LDAP server and an LDAP user directory, for example:

    xml
    <clickhouse>
    <ldap_servers>
        <corp>
            <host>ldap.example.com</host>
            <port>636</port>
            <enable_tls>yes</enable_tls>
            <tls_minimum_protocol_version>tls1.2</tls_minimum_protocol_version>
            <tls_require_cert>demand</tls_require_cert>
            <tls_ca_cert_file>/etc/clickhouse-server/ldap-ca.crt</tls_ca_cert_file>
            <bind_dn>uid={user_name},ou=users,dc=example,dc=org</bind_dn>
            <verification_cooldown>300</verification_cooldown>
            <operation_timeout>40</operation_timeout>
            <network_timeout>30</network_timeout>
            <search_timeout>20</search_timeout>
        </corp>
    </ldap_servers>
    <user_directories>
        <ldap>
            <server>corp</server>
            <roles><console_admin_reader/></roles>
            <role_mapping>
                <base_dn>ou=groups,dc=example,dc=org</base_dn>
                <scope>subtree</scope>
                <search_filter>(&(objectClass=groupOfNames)(member={bind_dn}))</search_filter>
                <attribute>cn</attribute>
                <prefix>clickhouse-</prefix>
            </role_mapping>
        </ldap>
    </user_directories>
</clickhouse>

    The certificate of the LDAP server is always checked (tls_require_cert demand), with TLS 1.2 or later. Keep these settings.

Create the roles of the groups

A group gives a role only if the role exists. For each group that stands for a role, create the role, with Roles & Permissions in the console or with SQL:

sql
CREATE ROLE analysts;
GRANT SELECT ON sales.* TO analysts;

Create the default roles too, if they do not exist. See Users and roles.

Install the configuration

  1. Save the text as a file in config.d of the server, readable by the server, for example /etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/ldap.xml, and the CA certificate at the path of CA certificate file.

    With the Docker Compose deployment, put both files next to config.d/web-console.xml, and mount them in the clickhouse service of compose.yaml:

    yaml
        volumes:
      - ./config.d/web-console.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/web-console.xml:ro
      - ./config.d/ldap.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/ldap.xml:ro
      - ./config.d/ldap-ca.crt:/etc/clickhouse-server/ldap-ca.crt:ro

    On Kubernetes, add both as keys of the ConfigMap, and mount them like web-console.xml.

  2. Restart the server: a new user directory is created only when the server starts.

    bash
    docker compose up -d clickhouse        # recreates the container with the new volumes

    Later changes of the LDAP server settings (host, TLS, cooldown) take effect with SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG.

Note

Put all the LDAP user directories of a server in one file. A second <ldap> element in another file of config.d is merged into the first one instead of adding a directory. With several directories, give each a <name>, which is also the name the console and system.users show.

Verify

  1. Reload Identity Providers → LDAP. The Directory sign-in (LDAP) box lists the directory, its LDAP server, the default roles, and the group search. A default role that does not exist is marked.
  2. Select Test sign-in…, enter the name and the password of a directory user, and select Sign in. The result shows Signed in as, Through (the user directory), and Roles. The password is not stored or recorded.
  3. Sign in to the console as that user. They appear on the Users page, read-only, and under Directory users seen since the start on the LDAP page.

You can also check the server directly:

sql
SELECT name, type, precedence FROM system.user_directories;

Choose the verification cooldown

The server checks a password with the directory on every request, unless a check succeeded within verification_cooldown seconds. The console sends a request for every action, about 80 when signing in, so without a cooldown each one is a bind to the directory. The trade-off: a user disabled in the directory, or removed from a group, keeps access for at most this long. 300 seconds is the recommended value; 0 checks every request.

To offboard a directory user, disable them, or remove them from the groups, in the directory. Directory users cannot be suspended or deleted in the console.

Active Directory

Active Directory needs three differences from the form's defaults: users bind with their user principal name, the server finds the user's DN for the group search, and the group search follows nested groups. Edit the generated file as follows:

xml
<clickhouse>
    <ldap_servers>
        <corp_ad>
            <host>dc1.ad.example.org</host>
            <port>636</port>
            <enable_tls>yes</enable_tls>
            <tls_minimum_protocol_version>tls1.2</tls_minimum_protocol_version>
            <tls_require_cert>demand</tls_require_cert>
            <tls_ca_cert_file>/etc/clickhouse-server/ad-ca.crt</tls_ca_cert_file>
            <!-- Bind with the user principal name, then find the user's DN, for the group search. -->
            <bind_dn>{user_name}@ad.example.org</bind_dn>
            <user_dn_detection>
                <base_dn>CN=Users,DC=ad,DC=example,DC=org</base_dn>
                <search_filter>(&(objectClass=user)(sAMAccountName={user_name}))</search_filter>
            </user_dn_detection>
            <verification_cooldown>300</verification_cooldown>
        </corp_ad>
    </ldap_servers>
    <user_directories>
        <ldap>
            <name>active_directory</name>
            <server>corp_ad</server>
            <roles>
                <console_admin_reader/>
            </roles>
            <!-- LDAP_MATCHING_RULE_IN_CHAIN: the groups the user is in directly or through nested groups. -->
            <role_mapping>
                <base_dn>CN=Users,DC=ad,DC=example,DC=org</base_dn>
                <search_filter>(&(objectClass=group)(member:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:={user_dn}))</search_filter>
                <attribute>cn</attribute>
                <prefix>clickhouse-</prefix>
            </role_mapping>
        </ldap>
    </user_directories>
</clickhouse>
  • Bind DN. {user_name}@ad.example.org binds with the user principal name of the domain. Users sign in with their account name, for example sam.
  • User DN detection. After the bind, the server searches for the user with sAMAccountName={user_name} under base_dn, and uses the DN it finds as {user_dn} in the group search.
  • Nested groups. The matching rule 1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941 (LDAP_MATCHING_RULE_IN_CHAIN) makes member:1.2.840.113556.1.4.1941:={user_dn} match the groups that contain the user directly or through other groups. Set base_dn to where the groups are; the default scope is subtree.
  • LDAPS. Connect to the domain controllers on port 636, and set the certificate of the CA that signed their certificates, as a PEM file, in tls_ca_cert_file.

The group names are the cn of the groups: the group clickhouse-analysts gives the role analysts.

Troubleshooting

The host name localhost

With <host>localhost</host>, the TLS check fails although the certificate is for localhost. The OpenLDAP client library that the server uses replaces the host name localhost with the host name of the machine when it checks the certificate. Connect by IP address, for example 127.0.0.1, when the certificate has that address as a subject alternative name, or by a name that is in the certificate.

Other problems

SymptomCause and fix
Test sign-in… answers Refused with an authentication errorCheck the bind DN with the directory's own tools, and the password. For Active Directory, check the domain in the bind DN.
The TLS handshake failstls_ca_cert_file is not the CA that signed the server's certificate, or the host is not a name in the certificate (see above). Keep tls_require_cert demand.
The user signs in with no roleThe groups do not have the prefix, the search filter finds no group, or the roles do not exist. The LDAP page marks default roles that do not exist. For nested groups in Active Directory, use the matching rule above.
The directory is not listed after the changeA new user directory is created only when the server starts: restart it.
A change in the directory shows lateverification_cooldown: the server reuses a successful check for that many seconds.
The user signs in as a local user insteadA user of the same name in users.xml or created with SQL comes first: the directories are tried in that order.
A second directory replaces the firstBoth <ldap> elements must be in one file, each with its own <name>.

how-to/configure-keycloak-sso.title: Configure single sign-on with Keycloak
how-to/configure-keycloak-sso.description: Set up single sign-on with Keycloak for a Docker Compose deployment of the web console: the clients in Keycloak, the token authenticator, the user sync, verification, and troubleshooting.

headings.text: The token authenticator refused a sign-in
The sign-in window does not open

how-to/configure-keycloak-sso.html:
Use this guide to let users sign in to the console, and to ClickHouse, with Keycloak, in a deployment made with Docker Compose. The console signs users in as a public client, with the Authorization Code flow and PKCE, and sends the access token to the server as the password. The token authenticator (sso-authenticator in the tools image) checks it for the server, and its user sync creates the users from the groups clickhouse-<role>. Passwords and LDAP keep working next to it.

For the model and its limits, see SSO (Keycloak). To try it on a test machine first, follow the single sign-on tutorial.

Before you begin

  • A deployment from compose.yaml, running, with Component Access set up (it creates console_admin and the role console_admin_reader).
  • The console served over HTTPS at its final address, https://<console> below, for example through a reverse proxy that terminates TLS. The access token is a password: it must not travel over plain HTTP.
  • A Keycloak server reachable over HTTPS from the browsers and from the Docker host, with a realm for ClickHouse, for example clickhouse, and an administrator of that realm. Its issuer is https://<keycloak>/realms/clickhouse.

Configure Keycloak

  1. Create the client of the console

    In the realm, create an OpenID Connect client clickhouse-console:

    SettingValue
    Client authenticationOff (a public client: no secret in the browser).
    Authentication flowStandard flow only; no implicit flow, no direct access grants.
    Proof Key for Code Exchange method (Advanced settings)S256
    Valid redirect URIshttps://<console>/console/oidc-callback
    Valid post logout redirect URIshttps://<console>/console/login
    Web originshttps://<console>

    Add two mappers to the client (its dedicated client scope):

    • Group Membership, named groups, with the token claim name groups and Full group path off.
    • Audience, with the included client audience clickhouse-console, added to the access token.

    The access tokens last 5 minutes by default; the console refreshes them.

  2. Create the client of the user sync

    Create a second client, clickhouse-sso-sync: client authentication on (confidential), with only Service accounts roles as the flow. On its service account, assign the roles view-users and query-groups of the client realm-management. Copy its client secret.

    Skip this step if you create the users yourself; then leave SSO_SYNC_CLIENT_ID empty below.

  3. Create the groups

    Create a group clickhouse-<role> for each ClickHouse role that single sign-on gives, for example clickhouse-analysts for the role analysts, and add the users. Groups without the prefix are ignored.

Configure ClickHouse

  1. Create the roles

    Create the roles the groups stand for, on the server, with Roles & Permissions or with SQL:

    sql
    CREATE ROLE analysts;
GRANT SELECT ON sales.* TO analysts;

  2. Create the account of the sync

    The sync signs in to the server as sso_sync. Create it with service-accounts.sql: uncomment the section of sso_sync, put its password in .env (SSO_SYNC_PASSWORD), and pass --param_sso_pw="$SSO_SYNC_PASSWORD", as described in Create the service accounts. Then let it grant the roles of the groups and the default roles, and only those:

    sql
    GRANT analysts, console_admin_reader TO sso_sync WITH ADMIN OPTION;

    Checking tokens needs no account: only the sync does.

  3. Store the secret of the sync client

    In the deployment directory:

    bash
    mkdir -p sso
printf '%s' '<client secret of clickhouse-sso-sync>' > sso/sync-secret
chmod 600 sso/sync-secret && sudo chown 1000 sso/sync-secret

    The file must be readable by the user 1000 of the container.

  4. Set the variables in .env

    bash
    SSO_NAME=Keycloak
SSO_ISSUER=https://<keycloak>/realms/clickhouse
SSO_CLIENT_ID=clickhouse-console
SSO_SYNC_CLIENT_ID=clickhouse-sso-sync
SSO_SYNC_PASSWORD=<password of sso_sync>
SSO_ROLE_PREFIX=clickhouse-
SSO_DEFAULT_ROLES=console_admin_reader

    SSO_ISSUER must be exactly the issuer that Keycloak reports, without a trailing slash. An empty SSO_SYNC_CLIENT_ID turns the sync off. Further settings of the authenticator, such as SSO_USERNAME_CLAIM and SSO_SYNC_INTERVAL_SECONDS, are listed in Helper processes.

Start the token authenticator

compose.sso.yaml adds the service sso-authenticator and mounts config.d/sso.xml into the server. That file declares the authenticator as the HTTP authentication server sso, and sets what the sign-in page offers, from the environment of the server container:

xml
<clickhouse>
    <http_authentication_servers>
        <sso>
            <uri>http://sso-authenticator:29700/</uri>
            <connection_timeout_ms>1000</connection_timeout_ms>
            <receive_timeout_ms>2000</receive_timeout_ms>
            <send_timeout_ms>1000</send_timeout_ms>
            <max_tries>2</max_tries>
        </sso>
    </http_authentication_servers>
    <web_console>
        <sso_name from_env="SSO_NAME"/>
        <sso_issuer from_env="SSO_ISSUER"/>
        <sso_client_id from_env="SSO_CLIENT_ID"/>
    </web_console>
</clickhouse>

A refused token is an answer, not a failure: max_tries retries only connection errors, briefly.

  1. Check the configuration. The command loads the provider's keys and prints the settings:

    bash
    docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.sso.yaml run --rm sso-authenticator sso-authenticator --check-config

    It prints a JSON object with issuer, client_id, audience, username_claim, token_type, the number of keys, and sync (the sync client, the server name sso, the role prefix, and the default roles, or null without the sync). It fails when the issuer cannot be reached or reports another issuer.

  2. Start it, and restart the server with the new file:

    bash
    docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.sso.yaml up -d

  3. Read its log:

    bash
    docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.sso.yaml logs sso-authenticator

    It shows keys loaded, listening, and, every interval, users synced with the number of members and changes.

Use both files in every later docker compose command, or the next up -d removes single sign-on.

The authenticator listens on port 29700 of the Compose network only, and the port is not published: only the server should reach it.

Verify

  1. Check the users the sync created:

    sql
    SELECT name FROM system.users WHERE has(auth_type, 'http');

  2. Open https://<console>/console. The sign-in page shows Sign in with Keycloak below the password form. Select it and sign in as a member of a clickhouse-<role> group: the console opens its home page.

  3. As an administrator, open Identity Providers → SSO (Keycloak). Select Set up if the page asks for it, then Add Keycloak… with the Keycloak URL https://<keycloak>, the realm clickhouse, and the client ID clickhouse-console.

  4. Select Test connection: every check is OK.

  5. Select Test sign-in…, and sign in as a user in the window. The result shows the user, the groups, the roles they would get, the ClickHouse user, and an access token usable by the server.

  6. In the Signing in to ClickHouse box, Sign-in page shows the issuer and the client of .env, and Users of single sign-on lists the synced users.

Troubleshooting

The token authenticator refused a sign-in

The sign-in page says that Keycloak signed the user in, but that the server did not accept the sign-in. The authenticator logs a refused line with the user and the reason (never the token):

Reason in the logCause and fix
token type <type>, not an access tokenThe password is not an access token, for example an ID token. With another provider, set SSO_TOKEN_TYPE.
issued to <client>, not clickhouse-consoleThe token was issued to another client (azp). Check SSO_CLIENT_ID and the client the sign-in page uses.
audience does not include clickhouse-consoleThe client has no Audience mapper for itself on the access token. Add it (see Configure Keycloak).
expiredThe token expired, more than 30 seconds ago. Check the clocks of the hosts. A panel that keeps its first token (the SQL Console, the Web Terminal, ClickStack) needs a reload.
the claim preferred_username is not the user nameThe user signed in under another name than the claim. The console uses the claim of the ID token; check that SSO_USERNAME_CLAIM and web_console.sso_username_claim name the same claim.
unknown key <kid>The token is signed with a key the provider does not publish (any more). The keys are fetched again at most every 30 seconds: sign in again.
issuer <issuer>The token comes from another issuer than SSO_ISSUER. See Issuer mismatch.
invalid signature, algorithm <alg> is not acceptedThe token is not signed by the provider with RS256, PS256, or ES256.

A cannot check the token line means that the provider's keys could not be fetched: the authenticator refuses every sign-in until they can be.

The user does not exist

The sign-in page says: Keycloak signed you in as <user>, but the server did not accept the sign-in. The user <user> must exist on the server, identified with the token authenticator (IDENTIFIED WITH http), and the authenticator must be running. When the log has no refused line for the user, the user does not exist or is not identified with http:

  • the user is not an enabled member of a clickhouse-<role> group, or the sync has not run yet (60 seconds by default);
  • the log shows a user of that name exists with another authentication: skipped: a user with a password or another method has that name, and the sync never changes it; give SSO users their own names;
  • the log shows sync failed: for example the provider shows no group clickhouse-*, which means a wrong prefix, a wrong realm, or a service account that cannot see the groups (it needs query-groups and view-users);
  • roles that do not exist are skipped: create the roles, or the user gets nothing from them.

The sign-in window does not open

The page shows The browser blocked the sign-in window: allow pop-ups for this page, and try again. Allow pop-ups for the address of the console.

The token request is blocked

The token request was blocked. Add https://<console> (or +) to the web origins of the client clickhouse-console. The browser fetches the tokens from Keycloak directly, which Keycloak allows only for the client's web origins (CORS). Add the origin of the console, exactly as the browser shows it: scheme, host, and port. A discovery error that mentions CORS has the same cause, or Keycloak cannot be reached.

Issuer mismatch

Test connection reports The provider reports the issuer <A>, not <B>: tokens would be refused. Check the hostname setting of Keycloak (KC_HOSTNAME)., and the authenticator logs cannot load the keys of the provider yet with the error the provider reports the issuer <A>, not <B>. Keycloak builds its issuer from its hostname setting, so the issuer must be the same for the browsers and for the authenticator. Set KC_HOSTNAME of Keycloak to its public HTTPS address, and SSO_ISSUER to <that address>/realms/<realm>.

The session ends

Your Keycloak session has ended (<reason>): sign in again. All panels were closed. Keycloak refused to refresh the token: the session ended there, or the user was disabled. This is how access ends after a change in Keycloak.

how-to/import-user-attributes.title: Import user attributes
how-to/import-user-attributes.description: Import the user attributes of Data Access Policies from a JSON feed, an HTTPS URL, or an LDAP directory or Active Directory, with the access policy worker.

headings.text: Import from an LDAP directory or Active Directory

how-to/import-user-attributes.html:
Fill the user attributes that the rules of Data Access Policies use, such as department or branch, from a trusted identity source instead of typing them in the console: a JSON feed (a file or an HTTPS URL) exported by an identity provider or HR system, or an LDAP directory or Active Directory. The access policy worker imports the values each cycle, then reconciles the rules, so a change in the source reaches the server's grants and row policies within one interval.

For the trust model of attributes (source, writer, freshness), see Attributes and classifications.

Prerequisites

  • Data Access Policies set up in the admin database (console_admin by default): Set up on one of the tabs Access Tests, Attributes & Classifications, Policy Rules, or Policy Deployments.

  • The service account of the access policy worker, access_policy_worker, created with deploy/service-accounts.sql (see Create service accounts), including the grant used only for imports:

    sql
    GRANT INSERT ON console_admin.dap_user_attributes TO access_policy_worker;

  • The worker: the access-policy-worker service of the Docker Compose deployment or of the Kubernetes deployment, or utils/web-console/access_policy_worker.mjs run with Node.js 18 or later.

  • The ClickHouse user names of the people in the source: the worker stores each value under the user name the source reports, and rules apply it to the ClickHouse user of that name.

One worker imports from one source: set either ATTRIBUTE_FEED or LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_URL, not both. With both, the worker stops at start with "Set ATTRIBUTE_FEED or LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_URL, not both: one worker imports from one source."

Define the attributes

The worker imports only the attributes defined with its source, so define them first, for either kind of source:

  1. Open Administration → Data Access Policies → Attributes & Classifications and select Define attribute.
  2. Fill in:
    • Attribute: the name rules use, for example department.
    • Category: User. The worker imports user attributes only.
    • Source of truth: the source name of the worker, ATTRIBUTE_FEED_SOURCE. Its default is feed for a feed, and ldap for a directory.
    • Writer: access_policy_worker, the account of the worker. Values written by any other user are then Not trusted.
    • Owner: the team responsible for the source.
    • Fresh for (seconds): the longest outage of the source you accept, for example 86400. Each cycle re-confirms every value the source reports, so a value becomes stale only when the source stops reporting it or cannot be read.
  3. Select Review, then Apply.

Repeat for each attribute. Define employment_status the same way if the source reports it: the values disabled, suspended, terminated, and inactive disable the identity for every rule.

Import from a JSON feed

  1. Produce the feed

    The feed is a JSON array of users with their attributes:

    json
    [
    {"user": "alice", "attributes": {"department": "Finance", "employment_status": "active"}},
    {"user": "bob", "attributes": {"department": "Sales", "employment_status": "active"}}
]

    user is the ClickHouse user name. Each value is stored as a string. The worker skips entries without a string user or an attributes object, values that are null, and attributes that are not defined as user attributes with the feed's source.

  2. Configure the worker

    Set these environment variables of the worker:

    VariableValue
    ATTRIBUTE_FEEDThe path of the JSON file, or an https:// URL. Other URL schemes are not supported: anything that does not start with https:// is read as a file path.
    ATTRIBUTE_FEED_SOURCEThe source name of the attribute definitions. Default: feed.
    ATTRIBUTE_FEED_TOKENFor an HTTPS feed: sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>. Optional.
    INTERVAL_SECONDSThe time between cycles. Default: 60.

    In the Docker Compose deployment, set them in .env: ATTRIBUTE_FEED, ATTRIBUTE_FEED_SOURCE, ATTRIBUTE_FEED_TOKEN, and ACCESS_POLICY_INTERVAL_SECONDS for the interval. A file must be inside the container of the worker: mount it into the access-policy-worker service (for example with a volumes entry in a Compose override file) and set ATTRIBUTE_FEED to its path in the container. Then restart the worker:

    bash
    docker compose up -d access-policy-worker

    To run the worker directly:

    bash
    CLICKHOUSE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8123 CLICKHOUSE_USER=access_policy_worker CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD=... \
    ATTRIBUTE_FEED=/var/lib/clickhouse-console/hr-feed.json ATTRIBUTE_FEED_SOURCE=hr INTERVAL_SECONDS=60 \
    node utils/web-console/access_policy_worker.mjs

    Add --once to run one cycle and exit, which is useful to test the configuration.

  3. Keep the feed complete

    Each cycle, the worker writes every reported value with the current time, and removes the values of its source that the feed no longer reports: a user who leaves the feed, or loses an attribute in it, loses the value, and rules on it close for that user.

    Warning

    A readable feed is applied as it is. An empty array removes every value of the source at the next cycle, and rules then revoke what they gave. Produce the feed so that a failed export makes it unreadable (a missing file, a failed HTTPS response, or invalid JSON) rather than empty.

Import from an LDAP directory or Active Directory

The worker reads the users of the directory and the LDAP attributes you map to console attributes, so that the directory is the trusted source of, for example, the department or branch of each user. It connects over LDAPS, or over ldap:// with StartTLS, always checks the certificate of the directory, and uses TLS 1.2 or later; plain LDAP is refused, because the bind sends the password of the service account. It uses paged results, so directories that cap a search, such as Active Directory at 1000 entries, return every user.

  1. Prepare a directory account and the certificate

    Create a read-only service account in the directory that can read the users and the mapped attributes. In the Docker Compose deployment, put its password in ldap/password (mode 600, readable by the worker's user, 1000) and the certificate authority of the directory in ldap/ca.crt, next to compose.yaml.

  2. Define the attributes with the source ldap

    Define each attribute as in Define the attributes, with Source of truth ldap (the default source of a directory import) and Writer access_policy_worker.

  3. Configure the worker

    The worker reads these variables:

    VariableValue
    LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_URLldaps://host[:636], or ldap://host[:389] with LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_STARTTLS=1.
    LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_STARTTLS1 for StartTLS on an ldap:// URL.
    LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_CA_FILEThe certificate authority of the directory. Default: the system's.
    LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_BIND_DNThe DN of the read-only service account. Required.
    LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_PASSWORD_FILEA file with its password, readable by the worker only. Or LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_PASSWORD with the password itself. A bind without a password is refused.
    LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_BASE_DNWhere the users are, for example ou=users,dc=example,dc=org. Required.
    LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_FILTERWhich entries are users. Default: (objectClass=person).
    LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_USERThe LDAP attribute that is the ClickHouse user name. Default: uid; sAMAccountName for Active Directory.
    LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_MAP<attribute>=<LDAP attribute>, comma-separated, for example department=departmentNumber,branch=l. Required.
    ATTRIBUTE_FEED_SOURCEThe source name of the definitions. Default with a directory: ldap.

    With Docker Compose, set them in .env, for an OpenLDAP directory for example:

    bash
    LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_URL=ldaps://ldap.example.com
LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_STARTTLS=0
LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_BIND_DN=cn=console-attributes,ou=services,dc=example,dc=org
LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_BASE_DN=ou=users,dc=example,dc=org
LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_FILTER=(objectClass=person)
LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_USER=uid
LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_MAP=department=departmentNumber,branch=l

    compose.ldap-attributes.yaml sets the source of the worker, ATTRIBUTE_FEED_SOURCE, to ldap itself, whatever .env says, so define the attributes with the source ldap.

    For Active Directory, set LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_USER=sAMAccountName and map the Active Directory attributes, for example LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_MAP=department=department. LDAP attribute names are compared without case.

    compose.ldap-attributes.yaml passes these variables to the access-policy-worker service, clears ATTRIBUTE_FEED, and mounts ./ldap at /etc/clickhouse-console/ldap for the password and certificate files. Start the worker with it:

    bash
    docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.ldap-attributes.yaml up -d access-policy-worker

Each cycle, the worker binds, searches the base DN with the filter, and turns each entry with the user attribute into a user with the mapped attributes. A multi-valued LDAP attribute gives its first value. A changed attribute changes the value; a user who leaves the directory, or loses an attribute, loses the value, and rules on it close for them. Entries without the user attribute are ignored.

Fail-closed behavior

The import never grants access from a value it cannot confirm:

  • The source cannot be read (a missing file, invalid JSON, an HTTPS error, an LDAP connection, TLS, or bind failure): nothing is written, and the cycle goes on to reconcile the rules with the values already stored. The values age: until they pass the freshness limit of their attribute, the access already provisioned stays; after that they are Not trusted, and each rule applies its Missing or stale attribute setting: Revoke removes what the rule gave (row filters show no row), Keep holds what was provisioned.
  • A directory search finds nobody while values exist: the import is refused, not applied, so that a wrong filter or base DN cannot remove every value at once. The values then age as above. This protection applies to the directory only: an empty JSON feed is applied.
  • A search finds only some of the users: the values of the users it does not find are removed, as for users who left.
  • A value written by another user, or reported with another source: Not trusted, and treated as missing.

Verify the import

  1. Read the log of the worker. It writes one JSON object per line; after a successful import:

    json
    {"time": "2026-11-12T09:00:00.000Z", "worker": "...", "message": "attribute feed imported", "values": 2, "removed": 0}

    With a directory, the line also has "source": "ldap" and "from": "ldap". values is the number of values written, and removed the number of values removed.

  2. On Attributes & Classifications, User attribute values shows each value with the source and written by access_policy_worker, the time it was last confirmed, and Status Fresh. Hover a Not trusted badge for the reason.

  3. Query the values directly:

    sql
    SELECT user_name, attribute, value, source, observed_at, updated_by
FROM console_admin.dap_user_attributes FINAL
WHERE NOT deleted
ORDER BY user_name, attribute;

  4. On Policy Rules, select Explain on a rule that uses the attribute: the matched users show the imported values. Policy Deployments → History shows the reconcile entries of the worker.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
attribute feed failed: values keep aging and become stale after their freshness limit in the logThe source could not be read; the error field has the reason. Fix the source: the values stay trusted until their freshness limit.
The attribute feed answered <status>The HTTPS feed returned an error status. Check the URL and ATTRIBUTE_FEED_TOKEN.
The attribute feed must be a JSON arrayThe feed is JSON, but not an array of users.
The log reports the import with "values": 0The attributes are not defined, are not User attributes, or their Source of truth differs from the worker's source (ATTRIBUTE_FEED_SOURCE; with Docker Compose, check .env).
Values show Not trusted with "Written by ..."The Writer of the definition is not access_policy_worker. Select Define attribute again with the same name and the right writer: the new definition replaces the old one.
Values show Not trusted with "Last confirmed ... s ago"The worker has not confirmed them within the freshness limit: the source is unreadable, or the worker is stopped.
attribute feed failed with ACCESS_DENIED in errorThe account lacks INSERT on console_admin.dap_user_attributes, or SELECT on console_admin.*.
cycle failed with an error about a dap_* tableData Access Policies is not set up in the admin database, or ADMIN_DATABASE names another database.
The directory returned no user, and N values exist: refusing to remove them all. Check LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_BASE_DN and LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_FILTER.The search matched no entry with the user attribute. Check the base DN, the filter, and LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_USER (sAMAccountName for Active Directory).
An ldap:// URL needs StartTLS: the bind would send the password in clear. Use ldaps://, or StartTLS.Use an ldaps:// URL, or set LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_STARTTLS=1.
A TLS certificate errorThe certificate of the directory is not signed by LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_CA_FILE (or the system's authorities), or its name does not match the host of the URL.
LDAP bind failed: ...The bind DN or the password is wrong, or the account is locked. The message has the directory's result.
LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_MAP is empty, or LDAP_ATTRIBUTES_BIND_DN is not set.Set the missing variable.
Values exist, but a rule does not match the userThe user name the source reports differs from the ClickHouse user name, or the value differs from the values in the rule's Users selector. Values are compared exactly.

To configure ClickHouse itself to authenticate users against the same directory, see Configure LDAP and LDAP.

how-to/offboard-a-user.title: Offboard a user
how-to/offboard-a-user.description: Remove the access of a person who leaves: suspend the ClickHouse user, revoke its roles, delete it, and check the audit log; for LDAP and single sign-on users, disable them in the directory or identity provider.
how-to/offboard-a-user.html:
Use this procedure to end the access of a person who leaves, or of a service account that is retired, so that new logins are rejected, open sessions lose their privileges, and the change is recorded.

How you offboard depends on where the user comes from. Check its Source on the Users page first:

SourceProcedure
SQL, SQL (replicated), SQL (memory), with a password or another methodA user created with SQL.
SQL with the authentication http (single sign-on)A single sign-on user.
LDAPAn LDAP directory user.
ConfigurationRemove the user from the configuration file (users.xml or a file in users.d). The console cannot change it.

Prerequisites

  • A console user with ALTER USER and DROP USER on the user, for example a role created from the ClickHouse Access Administrator role template whose name pattern matches the user.
  • To revoke roles: ROLE ADMIN, or the roles granted to you WITH ADMIN OPTION.
  • To stop running queries: KILL QUERY.
  • To check the result: SELECT on the console audit log and on system.query_log.

A user created with SQL

  1. Open the user

    On Users, search for the name and select the user. If its page says Protected account, the console does not suspend or delete it. If the protection is no longer needed, select Remove protection for it on the Component Access page first (see Protected accounts).

  2. Suspend the user

    Select Suspend. To end the queries the user is running now, also select Also stop the queries the user is running now (KILL QUERY). Select Review, then Suspend.

    The console runs:

    sql
    ALTER USER alice VALID UNTIL '2000-01-01 00:00:00 UTC';
KILL QUERY WHERE user = 'alice' ASYNC;

    New logins are rejected over every interface, and HTTP clients of the user stop working at their next request. The state of the user becomes Suspended. See Suspending a user for the exact effect.

  3. Revoke the roles and privileges

    Native connections that are already open, such as clickhouse-client and pooled driver connections, keep working after a suspension until they disconnect. To cut them off, revoke what gives them access, which applies to open sessions at their next query:

    1. On the Roles tab, select Revoke for each role.
    2. On the Permissions tab, select Revoke for each direct privilege.

    For example:

    sql
    REVOKE analyst, developer FROM alice;
REVOKE ALL ON *.* FROM alice;

  4. Delete the user

    When the account is no longer needed, select Delete. The dialog lists what depends on the user. Before you confirm, handle these:

    • Views and tables that run as this user (DEFINER): views with SQL SECURITY DEFINER stop working until their definer is changed. Change the definer to a service account first.
    • Quotas naming this user and Row policies naming this user: review them.
    • Queries running now: stop them, or wait for them to finish.

    Type the name of the user and select Review, then Delete. This runs DROP USER alice and cannot be undone. Keeping the user suspended instead preserves its configuration for a later review.

A single sign-on user

A user of single sign-on is IDENTIFIED WITH http and created by the user sync of the token authenticator. Offboard it in the identity provider:

  1. In Keycloak, disable the user, or remove it from every group whose name starts with the role prefix (clickhouse- by default).
  2. The console of a signed-in user cannot refresh the access token any more, so it signs the user out at the next refresh. An access token that was already issued stays valid until it expires, which is 5 minutes by default in Keycloak.
  3. The user sync drops the ClickHouse user within its interval (SSO_SYNC_INTERVAL_SECONDS, 60 seconds by default), and records sso_drop_user in the audit log.

Do not delete such a user in the console while it is still enabled in the provider: the sync creates it again at its next run. Roles you revoke in the console are also granted again if the groups still give them. Without the user sync, delete the user in the console after disabling it in the provider, as for a user created with SQL. See Identity Providers and the user sync reference.

An LDAP directory user

Directory users cannot be suspended or deleted in the console: ClickHouse gets them from the directory at each sign-in.

  1. In the directory, disable the user, or remove it from the groups that give ClickHouse roles.
  2. The change takes effect after the verification_cooldown of the LDAP server configuration (the console's configuration form proposes 300 seconds): until then, the server may reuse a successful password check.

If a local user (SQL or configuration) has the same name, it comes first and is not affected: offboard it as well. See Identity Providers and the LDAP authenticator.

Verify

  1. On Users, the state of the user is Suspended, or the user is no longer listed.
  2. On Audit Activity, the Console actions tab shows the records of the suspension, the revocations, and the deletion, with the result Success. Search for the user name.
  3. The Access changes seen by the server tab shows the statements. A change marked Outside the console was made with SQL or by another tool, such as the user sync.
  4. The Access decisions tab shows queries of the user that the server refused after the revocation.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCause and fix
Suspend or Delete is disabled with Protected account.Remove the protection on the Component Access page first.
The dialog says that the change would leave no platform administrator.The user is the last one who can change the console policy. Grant the Platform Administrator role to another user first.
Suspend is disabled with Your user does not have ALTER USER for this user.You can manage only the users whose names match your grants. Ask an administrator.
The user still runs queries after the suspension.An open native connection. Revoke the roles and privileges, or stop the queries with KILL QUERY.
A deleted single sign-on user comes back.The user is still in a group of the provider. Disable it in the provider.
The partial result says that some steps did not run.The steps marked Done took effect. Review the current state and run the missing steps again.

how-to/recover-access-to-the-console.title: Recover access to the console
how-to/recover-access-to-the-console.description: Recover when the console access policy hides components from everyone, when an administrator is suspended, or when no platform administrator is left.

headings.text: The policy hides components from everyone

how-to/recover-access-to-the-console.html:
Use these procedures when a change locked users out of the console: a policy rule hides components from everyone, an administrator is suspended, or nobody can change the console access policy any more. The console has safeguards against each of these, but a change made with SQL directly can bypass them.

Every procedure works with SQL, from clickhouse-client or any other client, because the console stores nothing of its own outside of ordinary ClickHouse users, roles, and tables. The examples use the default console database console_admin (the admin_database setting; see the configuration reference).

Prerequisites

  • Access to the server with a user that has the privileges named in each procedure. A user defined in a configuration file (users.xml or a file in users.d) with access_management is the most robust choice: SQL statements cannot change, suspend, or delete it.
  • clickhouse-client on the server, or another SQL client.

The policy hides components from everyone

Symptoms: panels or administration pages are missing from the home page and the sidebar for every user, and their addresses say that the console policy does not allow them.

The Component Access page is not governed by the policy. It stays available to the users who can change the policy (INSERT on console_admin.component_policy) or set it up (CREATE TABLE on console_admin.*), so a platform administrator can fix the rules there:

  1. Sign in as a platform administrator and open Component Access.
  2. In Rules for, choose All users, or the role whose rules caused the problem.
  3. Tick Open for the components that must be available again, and select Save rules.

With SQL, insert a rule. A new row for the same subject and component replaces the previous one. For example, to allow the SQL Console for everyone again:

sql
INSERT INTO console_admin.component_policy (subject_type, subject, component, open, view_data, run_queries, administer)
VALUES ('all', '', 'sql', 1, 1, 1, 0);

The component names are the IDs of the console's components, for example sql, dashboard, admin-users, or idp-sso.

To turn the policy off without losing the other console data, empty the table. With no rules, the console shows every component to every user:

sql
TRUNCATE TABLE console_admin.component_policy;

To turn every console administration feature off, drop the database and the reader role. The console then works as if it was never set up:

sql
DROP DATABASE console_admin;
DROP ROLE console_admin_reader;

Warning

The database also holds the audit log, and, when they are set up, the tables of Data Access Policies, Backup & Restore, Clusters, and Identity Providers. Dropping it removes them all. Back it up first if it must be kept, for example with BACKUP DATABASE console_admin TO Disk('backups', 'console_admin.zip') on a server with a backups disk configured.

Users cannot read the policy

Symptoms: one user, or some users, do not see the governed components, and the home page says that the console access policy could not be read.

The console fails closed when the policy table exists but the user cannot read it. Give the user the reader role as a default role:

sql
GRANT console_admin_reader TO alice;
SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO alice;

SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL makes every granted role active at sign-in; to keep a narrower list, name the roles instead. Then the user signs out of the console and in again. For users defined in configuration files, grant SELECT ON console_admin.component_policy in those files. See The reader role.

An administrator is suspended

Symptoms: an administrator cannot sign in, and the Users page shows the state Suspended or Expired.

The console suspends a user by making its authentication methods expire. Any user with ALTER USER on the suspended user can reactivate it:

  1. Sign in as that user and open the suspended user on Users.
  2. Select Reactivate. The dialog shows the expiry the user had before the suspension, from the audit log. Leave Credentials expire (optional) empty for no expiry, or choose a date.
  3. Select Review, then Apply.

With SQL:

sql
ALTER USER alice VALID UNTIL 'infinity';

If no other administrator can sign in, run the statement as a user defined in a configuration file with access_management. The console refuses to suspend your own user and the last platform administrator, so this happens only after changes made with SQL directly or by another tool.

No platform administrator is left

Symptoms: nobody can change the console access policy or the protected accounts, and the Component Access page is missing for everyone who needs it.

Platform administrators are the users with INSERT on console_admin.component_policy. The console refuses to delete or suspend the last of them, to revoke the last role that makes someone one, and to delete such a role, but a DROP USER, REVOKE, or DROP ROLE run directly bypasses these safeguards. To appoint a platform administrator again, run as a user that holds these privileges WITH GRANT OPTION, or as a user defined in a configuration file with access_management:

sql
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON console_admin.component_policy TO alice;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON console_admin.protected_accounts TO alice;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON console_admin.audit_log TO alice;

If a role was created from the Platform Administrator role template (by default console_platform_admin) and still exists, grant it instead:

sql
GRANT console_platform_admin TO alice;

Verify

  1. Sign in to the console as the affected user. The home page and the sidebar list the components again.
  2. On Component Access, the Platform administrators section lists at least one user, and Policy storage shows the expected state.
  3. On Audit Activity, the Access changes seen by the server tab shows your statements, marked Outside the console. Changes to the policy table with SQL are not access-management statements, so they appear in neither tab: find them in system.query_log.

Prevent it

  • Keep a break-glass user defined in a configuration file. SQL statements cannot change it, and it does not depend on the console tables.
  • Protect break-glass and service accounts that are created with SQL on the Component Access page, so that the console does not delete or suspend them (see Protected accounts).
  • Keep at least two platform administrators.
  • Grant ALTER, TRUNCATE, and DROP on the console database only to the server administrators.

how-to/protect-backups.title: Protect backups and server bundles
how-to/protect-backups.description: How to choose and set up the master key of server bundles in the ClickHouse web console, rotate it, test it with a restore rehearsal, and protect the backup storage.
how-to/protect-backups.html:
This guide sets up the master key that encrypts the server bundles of the backup worker, rotates it, proves that it works, and protects the storage of the backups against loss, deletion, and disclosure.

Prerequisites

  • The console with Backup & Restore set up and at least one enabled destination.
  • The backup worker running on the server host, with its service account. With Docker Compose, the commands below use the overlay compose.bundles.yaml of the deployment directory, which mounts the deployment's config.d, a key directory bundle-keys, and a staging directory restore-staging into the worker.
  • The grant for the bundle tables of the worker (included in service-accounts.sql):
    sql
    GRANT CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, INSERT, SELECT, BACKUP ON console_admin.server_bundle* TO backup_worker;

Choose a key provider

Each bundle is encrypted with its own random data key, wrapped by the master key. The master key is never stored with a bundle. Without it, no bundle can be decrypted, so where it lives decides both who can read the bundles and what you need to recover.

BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDERWhere the master key isBundles from the console and on a scheduleNeeded to restore
fileA file on the worker host, readable by its owner onlyYesA copy of the key file, kept out of band
vaultThe Transit secrets engine of HashiCorp Vault; the key never leaves VaultYesVault, reachable from the worker, and a token
passphraseNowhere: derived from a passphrase with scryptNo: a person makes and restores bundles on the worker hostThe passphrase

Choose vault when you run Vault already; file otherwise; passphrase only when no key may be stored on the host and a person can make each bundle.

Use a key file

  1. Create the key and staging directories, then the key:

    bash
    mkdir -p bundle-keys restore-staging && sudo chown 101:101 bundle-keys restore-staging && sudo chmod 700 bundle-keys restore-staging
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.bundles.yaml run --rm backup-worker backup-worker bundle-key-init --key-file /keys/bundle.key

    Without Compose, run node utils/web-console/backup_worker.mjs bundle-key-init --key-file <path> as the user of the worker.

    The command prints the fingerprint of the key:

    text
    Created /keys/bundle.key (readable by its owner only), fingerprint sha256:….

    It refuses to replace an existing file: a replaced key makes every bundle encrypted with it unreadable.

  2. Copy the key out of band, away from this host and from the backups: a password manager, or a sealed envelope. Record the fingerprint with it. The worker never copies the key, and never includes it in a bundle, even when it lies under BUNDLE_PATHS.

  3. Configure the worker. compose.bundles.yaml sets BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER to file by default and BUNDLE_KEY_FILE to /keys/bundle.key. Without Compose, set:

    text
    BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER=file
BUNDLE_KEY_FILE=<path>

    The file must have mode 600: the worker refuses a key file that other users can read.

  4. Start the worker:

    bash
    docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.bundles.yaml up -d backup-worker

Use HashiCorp Vault Transit

  1. In Vault, enable the Transit secrets engine and create a key, for example clickhouse-bundles:

    bash
    vault secrets enable transit
vault write -f transit/keys/clickhouse-bundles

  2. Create a policy that allows only encrypt and decrypt with that key. The worker calls POST /v1/<mount>/encrypt/<key> and POST /v1/<mount>/decrypt/<key>, and nothing else:

    text
    path "transit/encrypt/clickhouse-bundles" {
  capabilities = ["update"]
}
path "transit/decrypt/clickhouse-bundles" {
  capabilities = ["update"]
}

    Save it as bundle-worker.hcl, then create the policy and a token with it:

    bash
    vault policy write clickhouse-bundle-worker bundle-worker.hcl
vault token create -policy=clickhouse-bundle-worker

  3. Give the token to the worker. With Docker Compose, put it into bundle-keys/vault-token with mode 600 (owned by the user 101), and set in .env:

    text
    BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER=vault
VAULT_ADDR=https://vault.example.com:8200
VAULT_TRANSIT_KEY=clickhouse-bundles

    Without Compose, set VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_TRANSIT_KEY, and VAULT_TOKEN or VAULT_TOKEN_FILE; VAULT_TRANSIT_MOUNT if the engine is not mounted at transit, and VAULT_NAMESPACE for a Vault namespace.

  4. Start the worker:

    bash
    docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.bundles.yaml up -d backup-worker

The key appears in the console as vault:<mount>/<key>, for example vault:transit/clickhouse-bundles. Vault must be reachable to restore a bundle: keep its own backups and recovery separate from those of this server.

Use a passphrase

  1. Set BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER=passphrase for the worker. Automatic bundles (BUNDLE_DESTINATION, BUNDLE_EVERY_HOURS) are not possible: the long-running worker never has the passphrase, and the console cannot request bundles.
  2. Make each bundle on the worker host, in a terminal. The passphrase has at least 12 characters, and is read without echo:
    bash
    docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.bundles.yaml run --rm backup-worker backup-worker bundle --destination <name>

    Without Compose: node utils/web-console/backup_worker.mjs bundle --destination <name>.

  3. Keep the passphrase out of band. Restores also need it: backup-worker bundle-restore --bundle <ID> --mode compare|stage.

Verify

  1. On Administration → Backup & Restore → Server state, the Backup worker box shows the provider, the key fingerprint (or vault:<mount>/<key>), the included paths, and no error.
  2. Select Back up the server state…, a Destination, and Request the bundle. After the next cycle of the worker, the bundle is Succeeded, with the key in its Key column.
  3. Select Compare on the bundle, then Request the comparison. The result lists the files that are the same, changed, missing on the host, or not in the bundle. A comparison proves that the master key, the bundle, and the destination all still work: repeat it regularly, for example after every change of the configuration.

To make bundles automatically, set BUNDLE_DESTINATION to the name of a destination and BUNDLE_EVERY_HOURS to an interval, then restart the worker. The box shows Automatic bundles.

Rotate the master key

Each bundle records the key that encrypted it, and the worker refuses to decrypt a bundle made with another key: The bundle was encrypted with the master key …; this worker has …. Keep every old key as long as bundles made with it are kept.

  • Key file. Move the old key aside without deleting it, for example to bundle-keys/bundle-2026-11-12.key, create a new key at /keys/bundle.key with bundle-key-init, copy it out of band with its fingerprint, and restart the worker. New bundles show the new fingerprint. To restore an older bundle, run the restore command with the old key:

    bash
    docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.bundles.yaml run --rm -e BUNDLE_KEY_FILE=/keys/bundle-2026-11-12.key \
    backup-worker backup-worker bundle-restore --bundle <ID> --mode compare

  • Vault Transit. Rotate the key in Vault with vault write -f transit/keys/clickhouse-bundles/rotate. The name of the key, and therefore the key shown in the console, stays the same, and Vault decrypts data keys wrapped with its older versions as long as you keep them decryptable.

  • Passphrase. Use the new passphrase for new bundles. Older bundles still need the passphrase they were made with.

After a rotation, make a bundle and compare it, as in Verify.

Rehearse a recovery

A comparison proves the key; a rehearsal proves the whole recovery. Stage the latest bundle (Stage… on Server state, or bundle-restore --mode stage), then run the recovery rehearsal on the server host with the staging directory:

bash
node utils/web-console/recovery_rehearsal.mjs --url http://127.0.0.1:8123 --user <admin> --password <password> \
    --binary /usr/bin/clickhouse --staged <staging directory of a server bundle>

It starts an isolated server from the staged configuration, restores the latest backup of each database from its real destination, and compares the data. --staged needs a bundle that includes /etc/clickhouse-server, the default of BUNDLE_PATHS; the Compose overlay includes only /deploy/config.d, so omit --staged there. The result is shown as Recovery rehearsed in the inventory. Delete the staging directory afterwards: it holds secrets in clear. See Recover a whole server.

Protect the backup storage

The Overview checks the backups of the last 7 days against the 3-2-1-1 rule (Resilience (3-2-1-1)), and Destinations shows what protects each destination in its Protection column.

RuleHow
Two copiesGive each schedule a Second copy to destination: after each full backup, the worker makes a new, independent full backup of the same databases there. Retention keeps the same number at each destination.
One off-siteMake the second destination an S3 bucket in another place: another region, account, or provider. A disk of the server, and an endpoint on this host, are the same site.
One immutableEnable Object Lock with a default retention on that bucket. Nothing, not even the worker, can then delete a backup before its retention ends: a deletion only adds delete markers, and the console says so. Keep the console retention at least as long as the lock.
Encrypted at restEnable default encryption on the bucket (SSE-KMS, or SSE-S3); the server then needs no encryption setting. For a disk destination, use an encrypted disk. Server bundles are always encrypted by the worker.
Least privilegeGive the server a key that can write and read backups but not delete them, and the worker a separate key that can delete.

Destinations → Recommended S3 permissions and bucket settings has both policies:

json
{
  "server_key": {
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket", "s3:AbortMultipartUpload", "s3:ListMultipartUploadParts"],
    "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::BUCKET", "arn:aws:s3:::BUCKET/PREFIX/*"]
  },
  "worker_key": {
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket", "s3:DeleteObject", "s3:GetEncryptionConfiguration", "s3:GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration", "s3:GetBucketVersioning"],
    "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::BUCKET", "arn:aws:s3:::BUCKET/PREFIX/*"]
  }
}

The server key goes into the destination form (Access key ID, Secret access key); the worker key into the worker's environment, under the destination's Worker credential reference (<REF>_ACCESS_KEY_ID, <REF>_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY). The worker reads the encryption, Object Lock, and versioning of each S3 bucket after every destination test and every 6 hours, with its own key. A setting it cannot read is shown as unknown, never as met.

Also:

  • Do not configure bucket lifecycle rules that expire objects of a backup prefix: they can delete the base of an incremental backup.
  • Do not grant READ ON S3, WRITE ON S3, READ ON DISK, or WRITE ON DISK to users who should not reach every S3 URL or every disk: these privileges are not limited to the destinations.

Troubleshooting

MessageCause and fix
No backup worker makes server bundles.No worker has BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER set. Set it and its key settings, and restart the worker.
BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER is file, but BUNDLE_KEY_FILE is not set.Set BUNDLE_KEY_FILE.
The key file … is readable by other users (mode …): make it 600.Run chmod 600 on the key file.
The bundle was encrypted with the master key …; this worker has ….The bundle was made with another key: restore it with the key whose fingerprint it shows.
The vault key provider needs VAULT_ADDR, a token (VAULT_TOKEN or VAULT_TOKEN_FILE), and VAULT_TRANSIT_KEY.Set the missing variables.
Vault encrypt with the key … failed: HTTP 403 …The token's policy does not allow the operation on that key, or the token expired.
The passphrase must have at least 12 characters.Use a longer passphrase.

how-to/recover-a-server.title: Recover a whole server
how-to/recover-a-server.description: How to recover a whole ClickHouse server with the web console from its server bundle and database backups, and how to rehearse the recovery on an isolated server.
how-to/recover-a-server.html:
This guide rebuilds a lost server from its backups: the configuration and Keeper state from a server bundle, and the databases from the backups of Backup & Restore. It also shows how to rehearse the procedure without touching production.

Prerequisites

Prepare these before you need them, and keep the list with the master key of the server bundles:

  • the version of the images (CONSOLE_VERSION) and of the server;
  • the master key of the server bundles, stored out of band: the key file, access to Vault, or the passphrase (see Protect backups);
  • the credentials of at least one destination, readable without the lost server;
  • server bundles made by the backup worker, and database backups at that destination.

Note

The worker finds a bundle and its destination in the console tables of the server it connects to (CLICKHOUSE_URL). bundle-restore --bundle <ID> therefore works only against a server whose console tables record that bundle; on a server whose console tables are empty, it reports No server bundle <ID>.

Recover

  1. Start a new server from the same images, with an empty data volume: see Deploy with Docker Compose or Deploy on Kubernetes.

  2. Restore the configuration. On the new host, run the worker with the same key settings (BUNDLE_KEY_PROVIDER and BUNDLE_KEY_FILE, or the Vault variables), and stage the latest server bundle:

    bash
    docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.bundles.yaml run --rm backup-worker backup-worker bundle-restore --bundle <ID> --mode stage
